content:
Utley is the harmonic and timbral identity of the record above the rhythm bed. He came in as a working session jazz guitarist (credits including Jeff Beck) and brought a soundtrack-oriented ear — Ennio Morricone for *The Good, The Bad And The Ugly*, John Barry, late-1960s/early-1970s film scoring vocabulary ([Sound on Sound, Adrian Utley: Portishead Sound Shaper](https://www.soundonsound.com/people/adrian-utley-portishead-sound-shaper); [Classic Pop, Classic Album: *Dummy*](https://www.classicpopmag.com/features/classic-album-portisheads-dummy/)). The Morricone dialect is the entry point: vibrato-saturated lead lines, tremolo amp settings, deliberately sparse note choice, a willingness to leave bars empty.

His tracking philosophy is also load-bearing. He printed effects to tape on the way in: "With guitars I always record direct to tape with the effects already on. That's how it used to be done and it's good because you're making a commitment" ([Sound on Sound, Adrian Utley](https://www.soundonsound.com/people/adrian-utley-portishead-sound-shaper)). He used a 1970s Fender Twin Reverb. The album was mastered to quarter-inch analog tape rather than DAT to preserve analog-saturation character on the bass-heavy mixes. Utley plays guitar across most of the record, bass on roughly half the tracks, theremin on "Mysterons," Hammond on "Glory Box," and co-arranged strings on "Roads."

content:
Beth Gibbons's vocal sits at the absolute foreground of every mix. The production posture treats her voice the way a film score treats its lead actor — close, dry, mostly free of obvious effects, with rhythm bed and harmonic layer arranged underneath rather than around it. Both Barrow and Utley describe her as orthogonal to their hip-hop reference frame: "She comes from a different place," Barrow told KEXP, noting her lyrics never use third-person voice and her Devonshire accent shapes pronunciation in ways that read as distinct against any American template ([KEXP, Portishead's Geoff Barrow and Adrian Utley Breakdown *Dummy* 25 Years Later](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)).

Why *Dummy* reads as intimate rather than produced: production accounts describe vocal capture techniques including bouncing to cassette and transmitting Beth's vocals to tape via radio signal for degradation character on specific lines, plus playback through broken amplifiers for re-amped textures ([Classic Pop, Classic Album: *Dummy*](https://www.classicpopmag.com/features/classic-album-portisheads-dummy/)). The principal lead vocal stays clean and close-miced; the noisy and degraded vocal layers sit underneath as texture. Specific microphone choices for *Dummy*-era Gibbons are not authoritatively documented in sources surveyed — published references to a Rode NTK valve mic describe later Portishead sessions (the NTK launched after *Dummy*) and should not be retro-applied here.

content: "Mysterons" opens the album with a tritonal motif derived from Barry Gray's *Thunderbirds* theme. Utley plays theremin on the track, and an ondes martenot — the French electronic keyboard instrument used heavily by Olivier Messiaen and on classic French film scores — is featured for its "sci-fi spooky" upper register ([KEXP, Geoff Barrow and Adrian Utley Breakdown *Dummy*](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)). The track sets the album's grammar in the first 90 seconds: rhythm bed at hip-hop tempo, harmonic centre on Rhodes, lead vocal arriving close, single melodic instrument floating above with film-score affect.

content: "Sour Times" samples Lalo Schifrin's "The Danube Incident" from the 1967 *More Mission: Impossible* album. Barrow sped the sample up to fit Portishead's tempo, which raised Schifrin's arrangement nearly a semitone and left it pitched between conventional keys — what Utley calls "hip-hop tuning," the dissonant in-between character that comes from time-stretching a sampled record rather than transposing it ([WhoSampled, *Sour Times* / *Danube Incident*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/173/Portishead-Sour-Times-Lalo-Schifrin-Danube-Incident/); [KEXP, Geoff Barrow and Adrian Utley Breakdown *Dummy*](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)). The track also samples "Spin It Jig" by Smokey Brooks ([Wikipedia, *Dummy* (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_(album))). John Peel airplay of "Sour Times" was the single that broke the band publicly.

content:
- **"Strangers"** is built on a sample of Weather Report's "Elegant People" (Wayne Shorter's composition from the 1976 *Black Market* album), with the rhythm anchored by a heavily compressed, "knocky" bass-drum sound ([Wikipedia, *Dummy* (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_(album)); [KEXP, Geoff Barrow and Adrian Utley Breakdown *Dummy*](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)).
- **"Wandering Star"** samples War's "Magic Mountain"; the solo section is literally Barrow scratching the intro of "Magic Mountain" in DJ Premier fashion, deliberately minimal — "the song kind of needed a solo, so I just scratched the start" ([KEXP, *Dummy* breakdown](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/); [Wikipedia, *Dummy* (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_(album))). The earlier "Wandering Star samples Weather Report" attribution in the source brief is inverted — Weather Report sits on "Strangers."
- **"Biscuit"** samples Johnnie Ray's 1959 "I'll Never Fall in Love Again," manually slowed down to fit the beat, vocal phrase repeated against itself until it reads as a haunted-house intrusion rather than a quotation ([Wikipedia, *Dummy* (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_(album))).

content:
"Glory Box" is the single most-recognized track on the record and samples Isaac Hayes's "Ike's Rap II" (from the 1971 *Black Moses* medley pairing it with "Help Me Love") ([WhoSampled, *Glory Box* / *Ike's Rap II*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/5/Portishead-Glory-Box-Isaac-Hayes-Ike's-Rap-II/); [Wikipedia, *Glory Box*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Glory_Box)). The bassline is the literal Hayes bassline; the strings are chopped from the same source. Barrow has described the source vinyl as warped and cheap, played quietly with reverb so the warp imparts its own micro-pitch wobble to the sample ([KEXP, *Dummy* breakdown](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)). Utley's overdriven Hammond solo over the final third is the moment the spaghetti-western dialect makes its plainest appearance on the album.

The same track is also Portishead's clearest demonstration of the *Dummy* mix-discipline rule: the sample is not played in the foreground, it is played quietly under the vocal with deliberate noise floor; the impression of presence comes from the vocal sitting forward, not from the sample being loud.

content: "Roads" is the emotional centre of the record. Utley has cited John Carpenter's main theme from *Assault on Precinct 13* as a structural reference — a film-score sustained pulse, "pitched perfectly in terms of emotion" ([KEXP, *Dummy* breakdown](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)). Barrow and Utley co-arranged the strings, performed by Strings Unlimited; Utley has said openly that he was less experienced with string writing than with horn writing and was learning on the job ([Sound on Sound, Adrian Utley](https://www.soundonsound.com/people/adrian-utley-portishead-sound-shaper)). The arrangement is sparse — sustained pads under the Rhodes and the vocal — rather than ornamental, which is the load-bearing decision. The strings hold the room rather than draw attention.

content: Roughly half the record carries no obvious external sample and is essentially a band performance routed through the same vinyl-and-Akai workflow. "Numb" is built on a deliberately unconventional snare sound Utley defended against session pushback; "It Could Be Sweet" is the song that pulled Utley into the band ("I could not believe it…completely blew me away"); "Pedestal" features Barrow's fretless bass, played on a bass whose frets he removed in 1986 to take a rent-paying session ([KEXP, *Dummy* breakdown](https://www.kexp.org/read/2019/8/22/portisheads-geoff-barrow-and-adrian-utley-breakdown-dummy-25-years-later/)); "It's a Fire" is the most Beth-Gibbons-as-composer track, with Gary Baldwin's Hammond carrying the harmonic surface and chord changes Barrow describes as "really strange." The pattern is the same as on the sampled tracks: the band plays it, Barrow routes it through the vinyl-press / floor-walk / re-sample chain, the resulting "record" gets cut into the beat.

content: Before *Dummy* was finished, the band shot a short spy film titled *To Kill a Dead Man*, directed by Alexander Hemming (1994). Beth Gibbons appears as a character; the band wrote and performed the entire score; a still from the film became the *Dummy* cover ([Wikipedia, *To Kill a Dead Man*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/To_Kill_a_Dead_Man); [Far Out Magazine, *To Kill a Dead Man*](https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/to-kill-a-dead-man-portisheads-dummy/)). The instrumental theme — later issued as a "Sour Times" B-side and on the 1995 *Glory Times* compilation — is functionally a Portishead manifesto: slow tempo, Schifrin-adjacent harmonic language, theremin, processed drums, no vocal. That the score rather than the album demos is what landed the Go! Beat deal is itself a thesis: Portishead presented as soundtrack composers first and as a band second, and the label responded to the framing.

content: *Dummy* was mastered to quarter-inch analog tape rather than DAT, a deliberate choice for the warmth and compressed-saturation character analog gave the bass-heavy mixes ([Sound on Sound, Adrian Utley](https://www.soundonsound.com/people/adrian-utley-portishead-sound-shaper)). The mix discipline is consistent: vocal at the front and dry; rhythm bed warm but at conversational volume; sample layer audibly *underneath* the vocal with deliberate noise floor; sustained instruments (theremin, Hammond, strings, guitar leads) used as single voices rather than stacked pads. The record peaked at UK #2, was named record of the year by *Melody Maker* and *The Wire*, and won the 1995 Mercury Prize ([Classic Pop, Classic Album: *Dummy*](https://www.classicpopmag.com/features/classic-album-portisheads-dummy/); [Wikipedia, *Dummy* (album)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dummy_(album))).

content:
- **Sampler:** Akai S1000 — the Massive Attack gift, primary sampling engine across the record ([Reverb, Making Portishead's *Dummy*](https://reverb.com/news/making-portishead-dummy-production-experiments-trip-hop-classic))
- **Sequencing:** Atari 1040ST — sequencer paired with the S1000 ([Reverb, Making Portishead's *Dummy*](https://reverb.com/news/making-portishead-dummy-production-experiments-trip-hop-classic))
- **Tape:** half-inch 16-track for live drum capture; quarter-inch for mastering ([Cuepoint, *Dummy* at 20](https://medium.com/cuepoint/portisheads-dummy-at-20-e7ffdb60668d); [Sound on Sound, Adrian Utley](https://www.soundonsound.com/people/adrian-utley-portishead-sound-shaper))
- **Guitar amp:** Fender Twin Reverb (1970s example, Utley's primary)
- **Keys:** Fender Rhodes, Hammond organ, ondes martenot ("Mysterons"), theremin ("Mysterons")
- **Bass:** Utley's fretless (frets removed 1986) appears on "Pedestal"; otherwise Utley's session bass rig
- **Vocal chain:** specifics for *Dummy*-era Beth Gibbons not authoritatively confirmed in the sources surveyed; published references to the Rode NTK valve mic on Gibbons describe post-*Dummy* sessions and should not be retro-applied
- **Deliberate degradation chain:** vinyl pressing of band-tracked material, floor-distress (walking, kicking), re-sampling through the S1000; cassette bounce-downs; broken-amplifier playback; radio-signal transmission to tape for specific vocal lines

content:
- **Sample your own band as if you didn't know them.** The defining production move on *Dummy* is recording the band, pressing the recording to vinyl, damaging the vinyl, and sampling the damaged vinyl back into the Akai. This breaks the binary that "sampling = lifting from someone else."
- **Vinyl artifact is a timbre, not a flaw.** Surface noise, pitch wobble from warped pressings, and groove damage are foreground textures here, not noise floor to clean up.
- **Commit-on-the-way-in scales.** Utley's "record guitars to tape with effects already on" rule is the same philosophy `corpus/techniques/hardware-sampling-workflow.md` describes for hardware samplers — print decisions early and the resulting audio carries the decision-character.
- **Soundtrack framing changes mix priorities.** When the conceptual model is "film score with a singer" rather than "band with arrangements," the vocal goes to the front, single melodic instruments stay single, and stacked-pad arrangements get cut. *Dummy* is the canonical reference for this re-prioritization.
- **The Bristol lineage is concretely traceable.** The Akai S1000 that built this album was a literal hand-me-down from Massive Attack after *Blue Lines*. The Wild Bunch → Massive Attack → Portishead lineage is not just a scene narrative; it's a chain of custody on the equipment.

content: *Give Up* is the load-bearing reference for two distinct ARLO design conversations. It is the *workflow* example — a record built by two musicians in different cities, who barely knew each other, who shipped audio on physical CD-Rs through the mail and trusted that the asynchronous gap between them would clarify rather than confuse the work. And it is the *aesthetic* example — the album that took Tamborello's IDM-leaning laptop-electronica vocabulary and welded it to confessional indie-rock songwriting in a way that proved enormously durable. By 2013 the album had sold over 1.1 million copies in the U.S. and was certified platinum; Sub Pop counts it as the label's second best-selling release of all time, surpassed only by Nirvana's *Bleach* ([Wikipedia — *Give Up*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Give_Up)). Every subsequent "indie band makes an electronic record" project sits downstream of this template. For ARLO, *Give Up* exemplifies three patterns: (1) asynchronous remote collaboration as a creative constraint, not just a logistical compromise; (2) a single hardware workstation — the Kurzweil K2000RS — treated as a complete studio rather than one voice among many; and (3) indie-electronic crossover built around vulnerability rather than dance-floor energy.

content: The collaboration started two years before the album. Tamborello, recording as Dntel, asked Ben Gibbard (already known as Death Cab for Cutie's songwriter) to contribute vocals to "(This Is) The Dream of Evan and Chan" on Dntel's 2001 album *Life Is Full of Possibilities*. It was the proof of concept: an IDM/glitch instrumental under a fully-sung indie vocal, built by mail without the two meeting in person. Sub Pop A&R Tony Kiewel heard the result and offered the duo an album deal; the band name described the working method ([Wikipedia — The Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Postal_Service); [Life of the Record — The Postal Service](https://lifeoftherecord.com/the-postal-service)). Gibbard later said the Postal Service tracks functioned as "nice breaks" in his concurrent writing for Death Cab's *Transatlanticism* — the two records are companion works of his 2002–2003 output, which the 2023–2024 20th-anniversary tour explicitly acknowledged by pairing them ([Life of the Record — The Postal Service](https://lifeoftherecord.com/the-postal-service)).

content:
The mechanics were physical. Tamborello, in Los Angeles, produced an instrumental sketch — programmed beats, K2000-sourced synth lines, sampled string fragments, structural arrangement — and burned it to a CD-R. He mailed the disc to Gibbard in Seattle. Gibbard received the disc, listened on a portable Discman while walking his neighborhood, and let melody and lyric ideas emerge against Tamborello's already-arranged track. He recorded vocals at home ("Computerworld") and shipped the disc back to Tamborello for further iteration ([MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up); [Life of the Record — The Postal Service](https://lifeoftherecord.com/the-postal-service)). Despite the band name, the actual carriers were FedEx and UPS — both for speed and to avoid losing master discs ([Wikipedia — *Give Up*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Give_Up)).

What matters for the ARLO stack is the *creative consequence*. Tamborello and Gibbard barely knew each other when they started, and the mail delay meant Tamborello had already committed an arrangement before Gibbard ever heard the track. As Tamborello later put it, "We didn't even know each other that well… we were just young and up for anything" — and that separation between arrangement and vocal/lyric decisions actually clarified each contributor's role ([MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up)). The mail delay forced both parties to commit — Tamborello couldn't second-guess once a disc was in the mail, and Gibbard couldn't ask for an instrumental rewrite without restarting the cycle. Constraint as creative driver.

content:
The single most important gear fact about *Give Up* is that nearly the entire instrumental record runs through a **Kurzweil K2000RS** — the rack-mount version of Kurzweil's flagship sampler-synth workstation. The K2000RS provided the bell-tone leads, squelched and rounded bass voices, pad textures, and the chassis for Tamborello's sample manipulation. He controlled it via MIDI from a Macintosh Quadra sequencer and recorded final mixes onto a PowerBook G4 running Cubase 5 ([MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up); [Life of the Record — The Postal Service](https://lifeoftherecord.com/the-postal-service)).

Supporting hardware included a **Clavia Nord Modular**, a **Korg microKORG**, a **Line 6 delay pedal** (used as a creative effect on drum-machine output), and an **Alesis MIDIverb** for reverb and modulation. The mix chassis was a **Mackie 1604** — Tamborello ran eight outputs from the K2000 and eight from the laptop into the Mackie and committed stereo mixes from there ([MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up)).

What is striking from a 2026 vantage is what is *missing*: no bus compression, no side-chain ducking, no parallel-processing aux returns. Tamborello has been candid about this — "I didn't really understand how any of that worked." The absence of mix-bus polish is what gives the record its lo-fi-but-bright character. Drums are unducked and bright; vocals sit forward without being seated in a polished pop bed; the synths breathe. For ARLO this is the *opposite* pattern from a meticulously-engineered electronic record like *Discovery* or *Vespertine* — a producer who treated his sampler-synth as a complete environment and did not reach for the surrounding tools an experienced electronic-pop engineer would have used.

content:
The classical-string textures threaded through the record were not from a sample library and were not played live. Tamborello bought dollar-bin classical LPs, dropped the needle at random places on the record, sampled whatever played into the K2000, and then pitch-shifted, reversed, time-stretched, and re-keyed the result until it fit the track ([MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up)). The blind-sampling method — taking whatever the random needle drop gave you and shaping it after the fact — is the same constraint posture as the OP-1 sketchpad workflow catalogued in `corpus/techniques/hardware-sampling-workflow.md`: the producer commits to a found source and lets the process author the texture, rather than searching a library for the "right" string sound.

The K2000's onboard sampling and DSP did the lifting. Drum patterns were assembled in the **Battery** soft-sampler plugin, then occasionally re-routed out through the Line 6 delay pedal to introduce rhythmic distortion and stutter, then time-corrected back into the grid before being committed to the mix ([MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up)).

content:
"Such Great Heights" did the cultural work. Gibbard said it "came together late in the recording process" and "came out of nowhere," describing the experience as "spiritual transcendence" and noting it was the first time he had written a fully positive love song ([Wikipedia — Such Great Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Such_Great_Heights)).

The iconic hook — the bright, bubbling, music-box bell motif that opens the song and recurs throughout — is a K2000RS patch driven via MIDI, with the bell character coming from the K2000's onboard FM/sample voices and a delay pedal trailing each note ([Grokipedia — Such Great Heights](https://grokipedia.com/page/Such_Great_Heights)). Synth-replication culture has documented the patch extensively; Korg's "Patch of the Week" series rebuilt the "rounded, bubbling synth line" on a modern prologue, confirming the source patch is a relatively straightforward subtractive-plus-delay voice ([KORG USA — Patch of the Week 109](https://www.facebook.com/KORGusa/videos/802001873790572/)). The drums are the second signature element — a tight, squelched kick-snare-clap pattern, forward without compression-driven loudness. Jen Wood (not Jenny Lewis) provided the airy upper-register backing vocal on the studio recording.

The single peaked at #21 on Billboard's Hot 100 Singles Sales chart, spent eleven weeks on the chart, and was certified platinum ([Wikipedia — Such Great Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Such_Great_Heights)). The original was licensed to Target, UPS, Kaiser Permanente, and Ask.com television advertisements.

content:
Sam Beam (Iron & Wine) recorded an acoustic cover of "Such Great Heights" — finger-picked nylon-string guitar, sotto-voce double-tracked vocal, no electronic elements — which was placed on the 2004 *Garden State* soundtrack and used in the film's most-quoted scene. The cover took on a life of its own; it was later licensed to M&M's television commercials and became, for a stretch of the mid-2000s, more culturally visible than the original ([Wikipedia — Such Great Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Such_Great_Heights)).

The propagation pattern matters for ARLO: the original is a synth-pop track that established the song; the acoustic cover is what carried the song into film and advertising; the two versions coexist in cultural memory as different songs that happen to share lyrics and melody. This is the same propagation shape that the corpus catalogs around "Hallelujah" or "Hurt" — a song whose canonical version becomes contested through cover-mediated dissemination.

content: Jenny Lewis of Rilo Kiley contributed backing vocals across roughly half the album and sings the female lead on "Nothing Better," which is structured as a sung dialogue between Gibbard and Lewis. Lewis recorded her parts over the course of several days in Tamborello's bedroom studio after being contacted by Gibbard ([Wikipedia — *Give Up*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Give_Up)). On the 2013 and 2023–2024 reunion tours she joined as the third on-stage member, doubling on keyboards and percussion in addition to vocals.

content: **"The District Sleeps Alone Tonight"** opens with a slow four-on-the-floor kick under a foggy synth pad, situating the record in Washington, D.C. **"Sleeping In"** is the album's brightest track, with its most overt indie-pop chord progression and Lewis's clearest backing vocal. **"We Will Become Silhouettes"** uses a stop-start drum-machine pulse against bouncy synth bass and reads, in retrospect, like post-9/11 apocalypse-pop — the Shins later covered it. **"Brand New Colony"** builds from a single repeated synth motif into a cathartic "everything will change" chant-along outro that became a setlist closer on later tours. **"Natural Anthem"** closes the record with an ambient instrumental outro — Tamborello's least pop-leaning moment, with K2000 and Nord Modular drone-and-swell work for the final two minutes.

content: Sub Pop released *Give Up* on February 19, 2003. It debuted modestly but had unusually long legs — driven by independent radio (KCRW in LA, KITS in San Francisco), picked up by KROQ-FM Los Angeles in January 2004 (a full year post-release), and permanently propelled by the *Garden State* cultural moment in the second half of 2004 ([Wikipedia — Such Great Heights](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Such_Great_Heights)). The album peaked at #45 on the Billboard 200 and was certified platinum. By 2013, U.S. sales exceeded 1.1 million units. Sub Pop frames *Give Up* as the label's second-best-selling album of all time, surpassed only by Nirvana's *Bleach* — a claim repeated across label communications and consistent with the certified-sales math ([Wikipedia — *Give Up*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Give_Up); [MusicRadar — Postal Service interview](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/bands/i-didnt-really-understand-how-any-of-it-worked-we-were-just-young-and-up-for-anything-the-postal-service-on-creating-indie-electronic-classic-give-up)).

content:
In August 2003, six months after the album's release and as it was gaining commercial traction, the United States Postal Service served the band with a cease-and-desist letter, asserting that the band's name caused "tarnishment and dilution" of the agency's trademark on the phrase "postal service" ([Far Out Magazine — Postal Service legal battle](https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/legal-battle-centre-the-postal-service/); [Wikipedia — The Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Postal_Service)).

Rather than litigate, the band — primarily Gibbard, who handled the negotiation directly with USPS representatives — reached a settlement that took the form of a licensing agreement with terms more amicable than the C&D had suggested:

1. The band was permitted to continue using "The Postal Service" as their name.
2. The band agreed to *promote* the U.S. Postal Service in band communications.
3. The band agreed to perform at the U.S. Postal Service's National Executive Conference in Washington, D.C., in November 2004 — which they did.
4. Future copies of *Give Up* and any subsequent releases would include a notice acknowledging the U.S. Postal Service trademark.
5. The U.S. Postal Service was granted permission to monetize the band's music — specifically, to sell copies of their releases on the official USPS website. ([Far Out Magazine — Postal Service legal battle](https://faroutmagazine.co.uk/legal-battle-centre-the-postal-service/); [Medium / Knowledge Stew — The Band That Agreed to Promote the U.S. Postal Service](https://medium.com/knowledge-stew/the-band-that-agreed-to-promote-the-u-s-postal-service-cbccf723cc2a))

Tamborello later told Pitchfork that the affair initially seemed "depressing" but ended up being "kind of fun," noting that "everyone was sort-of in on the joke." Verification confidence on the settlement specifics is high; the band-performs-at-USPS-conference detail and the USPS-sells-band-records detail are corroborated by multiple independent sources.

content: The band reunited in 2013 for the album's tenth anniversary. Sub Pop issued a deluxe reissue with B-sides and two new tracks recorded with Jenny Lewis ("Turn Around," "A Tattered Line of String"). The 2013 tour ran from Coachella in April through a final show at Lollapalooza on August 5, 2013, which both Tamborello and Gibbard publicly called the band's last performance ([Wikipedia — The Postal Service](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Postal_Service)). It wasn't. In 2023, for the 20th anniversary of both *Give Up* and Death Cab's *Transatlanticism*, the Postal Service announced a co-headlining tour with Death Cab — each band performing its anniversary album in full, Gibbard pulling double duty as lead singer of both. The tour ran through 2024, with the final scheduled performance at HFStival in Washington, D.C., on September 21, 2024. Jenny Lewis again joined as the third member.

content: Four transferable patterns: (1) **asynchronous remote collaboration as creative posture, not just logistical compromise** — the mail delay forced commitment and clarified individual contributions; modern cloud-DAW or voice-memo exchanges sit on the same axis. (2) **A single hardware workstation can carry an entire record** — the K2000RS was not one voice among many, it was the studio; an aesthetics agent should recognize when a record's character reduces to one piece of gear plus a producer's vocabulary. (3) **Absence of mix polish can be the signature** — Tamborello's missing compression and side-chain ducking was inexperience, but it gave the record an openness subsequent "properly" engineered indie-electronic records lacked. (4) **The covers-and-licensing tail can outweigh the original release** — *Give Up* sold steadily for two years before *Garden State* / Iron & Wine turned it into a cultural artifact; the cover-and-soundtrack propagation graph deserves first-class treatment.

content: *Purple Rain* is the record Prince made by collapsing four production modes into a single album: a one-man home-studio multi-tracker working at Kiowa Trail in Chanhassen, a band tracking live on a Minneapolis nightclub stage with a remote truck outside, a Hollywood-studio session at Sunset Sound's Studio 3, and a film soundtrack engineered to release with a feature film and a tour. Sessions ran May 1983 – March 1984, with Susan Rogers installed as staff engineer in 1983 after Westlake Audio referred her ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers); [The Current, Susan Rogers on working with Prince](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2018/04/20/susan-rogers-on-working-with-prince-in-the-studio-the-man-i-knew-was-so-human)). The bed tracks for "Purple Rain," "I Would Die 4 U," and "Baby I'm a Star" were captured live at First Avenue on 3 August 1983 during a benefit show for the Minnesota Dance Theatre — David Z ran the recording from a Record Plant remote truck on 24-track tape ([The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue); [The Current, On this Day 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2016/08/03/on-this-day-in-1983-prince-played-purple-rain-for-the-first-time)). "When Doves Cry," written last, was tracked and mixed in a matter of hours at Sunset Sound on 1 March 1984 ([Wikipedia, *When Doves Cry*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Doves_Cry); [MusicRadar, When Doves Cry no bass](https://www.musicradar.com/news/prince-when-doves-cry-no-bass)). Released 25 June 1984 on Warner Bros., the album hit #1 on the Billboard 200 on 4 August 1984, spent 24 consecutive weeks at the top, and has sold over 25 million copies worldwide ([Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album))).

content: The change in billing — *1999* is "Prince," *Purple Rain* is "Prince and The Revolution" — was a real organizational shift, not just a marketing line. On *1999* Prince was still essentially a one-man multi-tracker with the touring band credited as performers; Wendy Melvoin's predecessor Dez Dickerson, plus Lisa Coleman, Bobby Z., Brown Mark, and Dr. Fink had been the road version of "Prince" for the *1999* tour ([Guitar.com, The Revolution interview](https://guitar.com/features/interviews/the-revolution-wendy-melvoin-lisa-coleman-recording-performing-with-prince/); [Wikipedia, Wendy Melvoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Melvoin)). For *Purple Rain*, Dickerson left and Wendy Melvoin — Lisa Coleman's partner, then nineteen — was brought in on rhythm guitar. Wendy's first stage appearance with the band was the August 3 1983 First Avenue show, which is also where the title-track bed was recorded ([Wikipedia, Wendy Melvoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Melvoin); [MusicRadar, Wendy and Lisa](https://www.musicradar.com/news/prince-purple-rain-wendy-and-lisa)). The corpus point: the "and The Revolution" credit on the album spine is the studio recognizing what had already happened on stage.

content: Susan Rogers was working as an electronics technician in Los Angeles when she heard through Westlake Audio that Prince needed a tech in Minneapolis. She called his management and was hired. Her first assignment was a roughly week-long installation: pull out the old console at Kiowa Trail, install a new API unit, and repair the Ampex MM-1200 24-track ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers)). Once the room worked, she stayed — staff engineer from 1983 through 1987, present for *Purple Rain*, *Around the World in a Day*, *Parade*, *Sign o' the Times*, and the shelved *Black Album* ([Wikipedia, Susan Rogers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Susan_Rogers)). Her self-description of the role is precise: "My job was to be the hands and the awake human body that kept this train rolling" ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers)). Rogers later left audio for a doctorate in psychology at McGill and is now Director of the Berklee Music Perception and Cognition Laboratory ([Berklee, Susan Rogers](https://college.berklee.edu/people/susan-rogers); [Berklee Online, Recording with Prince](https://online.berklee.edu/takenote/recording-with-prince-an-interview-with-susan-rogers-from-berklee-online/)). The reason her testimony is the corpus's primary citation anchor for these sessions: she was the only continuous technical presence across Prince's commercial peak, and she has spent the last decade lecturing and writing about it with a cognitive-science vocabulary that most engineer-memoirs lack.

content: Before Paisley Park opened in 1987, Prince worked primarily from a converted bedroom at his Kiowa Trail house in Chanhassen, Minnesota — across from the master bedroom, holding the API console Rogers had installed and the Ampex MM-1200 24-track ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers); [Berklee Online, Recording with Prince](https://online.berklee.edu/takenote/recording-with-prince-an-interview-with-susan-rogers-from-berklee-online/)). Rogers' description of the daily cycle: she would route Prince's vocal mic, mark the patch cord with white tape so he could see where it was, arm the tape machine, put the track on input, and then leave the room. Prince did the lead vocal alone, did the backing stack alone, then she'd come back in and they'd cut the rest of the instruments. At the end of the day she would print a 2-track mix, go to bed, and four hours later they'd start again ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers)). Rogers' framing: Prince was not a perfectionist but a virtuoso — "so fluent on so many instruments that we could go super-fast" — typically completing one song per day, frequently programming drums and keyboards before vocals, with the arrangement already in his head as tape rolled ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers); [Audio Media International, Susan Rogers recalls Prince](https://audiomediainternational.com/in-the-studio-with-prince-susan-rogers-recalls-her-five-years-as-the-stars-staff-engineer/)).

content:
Prince's preferred LA studio for the album was Sunset Sound Studio 3 — its DeMedio console, Lexicon Prime Time delays, EMT plate reverb, and the room's echo chambers later templated Paisley Park ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers)). "When Doves Cry," "The Beautiful Ones," and other studio-only tracks were cut there with Peggy McCreary and David Leonard among the engineers ([Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album))). But the album's defining live source sits in Minneapolis instead.

The benefit show for the Minnesota Dance Theatre at First Avenue on 3 August 1983 is the most consequential live recording in Prince's catalog. Loyce Houlton, the Minnesota Dance Theatre's artistic director, had asked Prince to do a fundraiser for the financially struggling dance company; he agreed, and roughly 1,200 people paid $25 for the show, raising $23,000 ([The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue)). David Z ran the recording from a Record Plant remote truck — "the Black Truck" out of New York — capturing the band on 24-track tape ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers); [The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue)). Three songs from that night made the album: "Purple Rain," "I Would Die 4 U," and "Baby I'm a Star." David Z's own assessment: "there's not very much added or changed to the original performance, especially with the song 'Purple Rain'" ([The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue)). The night was also Wendy Melvoin's first show with the band, meaning the Revolution's classic lineup debuted on tape and on stage simultaneously ([MusicRadar, Wendy and Lisa](https://www.musicradar.com/news/prince-purple-rain-wendy-and-lisa); [Wikipedia, Wendy Melvoin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wendy_Melvoin)).

content: The First Avenue performance of "Purple Rain" ran roughly fourteen minutes. The album version is 8:40. The cut was done at the home studio in September 1983: content edits to bring the length down, plus a bass overdub because wireless bass technology of the period couldn't capture the low end cleanly on a remote truck recording ([The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue); [The Current, On this Day 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2016/08/03/on-this-day-in-1983-prince-played-purple-rain-for-the-first-time)). David Z also enhanced the crowd ambience — his own admission: "I cheated and put a crowd from the Minnesota Vikings in the audience track" ([The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue)). The corpus point: the "live record" framing is technically accurate at the rhythm-and-vocal-bed level, but the released "Purple Rain" is a hybrid object — live band performance with studio surgery on length, low end, and crowd. The string arrangement that closes the song was tracked separately by Lisa Coleman, with Coleman and Wendy Melvoin conducting ([Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album))).

content: "When Doves Cry" was written last, after the rest of the album was done, when director Albert Magnoli asked Prince for a song to score a specific scene. Prince cut it at Sunset Sound on 1 March 1984 — Rogers' account is that it was tracked and mixed in a matter of hours ([MusicRadar, When Doves Cry no bass](https://www.musicradar.com/news/prince-when-doves-cry-no-bass); [Reverb, Prince and the Linn LM-1](https://reverb.com/news/prince-and-the-linn-lm-1)). The famous omission — no bass — was a final-mix decision. The bass line exists on the multi-track tape, but Prince muted it during the last mix pass, telling his engineer some version of "ain't nobody gonna believe I'd do this" ([MusicRadar, When Doves Cry no bass](https://www.musicradar.com/news/prince-when-doves-cry-no-bass)). Rogers' framing: "real genius knows when to show it off and when to just be simple" ([Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers)). Prince also credited a conversation with singer Jill Jones, who'd told him the song was too conventional with the bass in ([Wikipedia, *When Doves Cry*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Doves_Cry)). Matt Fink later disclosed that the baroque synth solo was tracked at half speed and an octave low against a half-speed backing track, then sped up — a classic vari-speed trick borrowed from late-1960s rock production ([Wikipedia, *When Doves Cry*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Doves_Cry)). The single hit #1 on the Billboard Hot 100, stayed five weeks, and was the top-selling single of 1984 ([Wikipedia, *When Doves Cry*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/When_Doves_Cry)).

content: The Linn LM-1 — Roger Linn's 1979 drum computer, the first programmable machine to use 8-bit samples of acoustic drums — was Prince's defining rhythm instrument from *1999* through *Sign o' the Times*. On *Purple Rain*, the LM-1 provides programmed drums on "Darling Nikki," "When Doves Cry," "I Would Die 4 U," and contributes to "Let's Go Crazy" and "The Beautiful Ones" ([Reverb, Prince and the Linn LM-1](https://reverb.com/news/prince-and-the-linn-lm-1); [The Current, Roger Linn interview](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2017/03/01/roger-linn-inventor-of-the-lm1-drum-machine-talks-prince-and-when-doves-cry)). What separated Prince's LM-1 work from other adopters: he retuned the stock samples aggressively (the "knock" in "When Doves Cry" is the LM-1 cross-stick snare tuned down about an octave, per Roger Linn himself), routed individual drum outs through Boss pedals — chorus, flanger, delay, distortion — and played fills manually with his fingers rather than programming them ([The Current, Roger Linn interview](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2017/03/01/roger-linn-inventor-of-the-lm1-drum-machine-talks-prince-and-when-doves-cry); [Tape Op, Susan Rogers interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/117/susan-rogers)). Linn's own framing: "Prince didn't just select a stock beat and press play, but rather used [the LM-1] in unusual and creative ways" ([Reverb, Prince and the Linn LM-1](https://reverb.com/news/prince-and-the-linn-lm-1)). The corpus point: the LM-1 was treated as a sample-playback instrument with effects loops, not as a drum-replacement utility — closer in spirit to how the corpus's hardware-sampling-workflow file describes the Akai S1000 in subsequent decades than to how most contemporary 1984 records used drum machines.

content: "Computer Blue" carries five writers: Prince, John L. Nelson (Prince's father), Wendy Melvoin, Lisa Coleman, and Matt Fink ([Wikipedia, *Computer Blue*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Computer_Blue); [Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album))). The guitar solo is based on a piano instrumental composed by Nelson and his son. The spoken-word intro — Wendy asking Lisa if the water is warm enough — is Wendy Melvoin and Lisa Coleman's voices, the most overt acknowledgement on the record that the Revolution wasn't just a backing band ([The Wire, Prince obituary](https://www.thewire.co.uk/in-writing/essays/prince-1958-2016-is-the-water-warm-enough)). The track was edited substantially for the album from a longer arrangement; the full version surfaced later in Prince's vault releases. *Purple Rain*'s collaborative credits are concentrated here — most of the other tracks remain Prince-only writes.

content: The default assumption on a Prince record is that he played most of the parts. *Purple Rain* complicates that assumption in two directions. On home-studio tracks like "When Doves Cry" and "Darling Nikki," he genuinely is the entire band — programming the LM-1, playing guitar, keyboards, bass (where present), and vocals. On the First Avenue live tracks, the Revolution is functionally the band, with Brown Mark on bass and Bobby Z. on drums doing what their roles say they do; Prince's bass overdub on "Purple Rain" was a fix for the remote-truck wireless capture, not a replacement of Brown Mark's part wholesale ([The Current Rewind, August 3 1983](https://www.thecurrent.org/feature/2020/10/13/the-current-rewind-august-3-1983-prince-purple-rain-debut-first-avenue)). On "Take Me with U," strings arranged by Coleman and Prince and conducted by Coleman and Melvoin run under Prince's lead vocal and Apollonia's harmony — the band is doing band work ([Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album))). The pattern: Prince delegated when the music needed live ensemble feel or specific orchestral arrangement skill (Lisa Coleman's strings), and self-tracked when he wanted the lock-step machine groove of the LM-1 plus overdubs.

content: *Purple Rain* the album and *Purple Rain* the film were released within four weeks of each other in 1984 — soundtrack on 25 June, film on 27 July — with the Purple Rain Tour running November 1984 through April 1985 ([Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album)); [Simon & Schuster, Alan Light *Let's Go Crazy*](https://www.simonandschuster.com/books/Lets-Go-Crazy/Alan-Light/9781476776750)). Alan Light's *Let's Go Crazy: Prince and the Making of Purple Rain* (Atria, 2014) is the standing book-length account. The relevance to the corpus: this is one of the canonical examples of an album planned not as a stand-alone audio object but as part of a multi-format release — most of the technically interesting production decisions (live-tracking the title song at the venue the film also depicts, writing "When Doves Cry" to score a specific scene) flow from that planning, not the other way around. The album debuted at #11 on the Billboard 200 on 14 July 1984, hit #1 on 4 August, spent 24 consecutive weeks at the top, and has sold roughly 25 million copies worldwide (13× Platinum in the US) ([Wikipedia, *Purple Rain*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Purple_Rain_(album))). "When Doves Cry" and "Let's Go Crazy" both went to #1 on the Hot 100; "Purple Rain" peaked at #2. Inducted into the Grammy Hall of Fame (2010) and the Library of Congress National Recording Registry (2012).

content:
- **Live-band-bed plus studio overdub is a legitimate album-side strategy.** The three First Avenue tracks (title, "I Would Die 4 U," "Baby I'm a Star") prove that a remote-truck live recording with post-edits — length cuts, bass replacement, crowd enhancement — can sit on the same album as Sunset Sound studio tracks without seam. The trick is having the live source be good enough that the edits are subtractive, not reconstructive.
- **Deliberate omission is a mix move.** Pulling the bass on "When Doves Cry" in the final mix pass — knowing the part exists on tape — is the production grammar the corpus's `dense-but-clear-mixing` technique file argues for from the other direction. Knowing what to leave out matters as much as knowing what to add.
- **A drum machine becomes an instrument when you use the individual outputs.** Prince's LM-1 sound is inseparable from the Boss pedals patched into the LM-1's per-drum outs. Treat sample-playback gear as a synthesizer with separate voices, not as a single stereo bus.
- **A staff engineer with continuous tenure is a creative asset, not a job description.** Susan Rogers' five-year run captures more useful studio knowledge than any rotating-engineer-of-the-month arrangement would have. The corpus pattern across `bjork-vespertine.md` (Valgeir Sigurðsson), `kate-bush-hounds-of-love.md` (Del Palmer), and this record is the same: artist plus permanent engineer-collaborator is the durable configuration.
- **Multi-instrumentalism is a tempo asset, not just a credit line.** Rogers' "virtuoso, so fluent on so many instruments that we could go super-fast" is the actually-useful description of what Prince's polymath ability did for the sessions — it compressed the band-rehearsal cycle into one person's working memory.
- **Vari-speed is still alive in the 1980s.** The half-speed-and-down-an-octave trick on the "When Doves Cry" baroque synth solo is the same 1960s Beatles technique applied to a 1984 polyphonic-synth part — a reminder that tape-speed manipulation is genre-portable.

content: Public Enemy's second album was recorded in roughly 30 days, mostly at Greene St. Recording in lower Manhattan, with additional tracking at Chung King, Sabella, and the group's own Spectrum City pre-production room on Long Island; the album was finished inside six weeks for an estimated $25,000 in studio costs and released on Def Jam through Columbia on 28 June 1988 ([Wikipedia, *It Takes a Nation*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Takes_a_Nation_of_Millions_to_Hold_Us_Back)). The Bomb Squad — Hank Shocklee, his brother Keith Shocklee, Eric "Vietnam" Sadler, and Chuck D (under the "Carl Ryder" production alias) — built the record's instrumentals out of dozens of sampled fragments per track, treating each sample as a discrete instrumental voice rather than a loop, and explicitly designing every track to function without a written bassline ([KEXP, *The Bomb Squad's Hank Shocklee on the 30th Anniversary*](https://www.kexp.org/read/2018/6/21/bomb-squads-hank-shocklee-30th-anniversary-public-enemys-emit-takes-nation-millions-hold-us-backem/); [Micro-Chop / Medium, *The Bomb Squad Used Sampled 808 Drums Instead of Basslines*](https://medium.com/micro-chop/the-bomb-squad-used-sampled-808-drums-instead-of-basslines-on-it-takes-a-nation-of-millions-to-d681eccf1abb)). Nick Sansano, then a young engineer at Greene St., handled the bulk of tracking and mixing and, by Shocklee's own statement, was "just as important to creating the sound of Public Enemy as we were in terms of producing it and making all the beats" ([Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks: "Black Steel"*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)). Mixing was done by hand on un-automated boards — multiple Bomb Squad members on faders at once, no recall, every pass a performance.

content:
Most 1988 hip-hop production worked from one or two foundational loops per track. The Bomb Squad's working unit was the **individual sample as instrument**. Hank Shocklee, repeatedly across interviews, has framed the philosophy in band terms: "each sample represents a different instrument being played. So this album was coming from a band's perspective but strictly made from records that bands were playing on" ([Tape Op, *Hank Shocklee*](https://tapeop.com/interviews/51/hank-shocklee)). The Bomb Squad would sample a James Brown horn stab as one voice, a different record's snare as another, a third record's noise burst as a third, and trigger them as a small ensemble of pads-as-players rather than as a loop with overdubs. Shocklee told KEXP that on faster tracks like "Bring the Noise" the Bomb Squad accelerated this further — "instead of the samples being long, maybe two bars or four bar loop phrases, they are more like 16th notes" ([KEXP, *30th Anniversary*](https://www.kexp.org/read/2018/6/21/bomb-squads-hank-shocklee-30th-anniversary-public-enemys-emit-takes-nation-millions-hold-us-backem/)).

The transferable move for the ARLO corpus: at the limit of fragmentation, a sample stops being a quotation and becomes a note. The Bomb Squad's sound at peak density is closer to a horn arrangement assembled out of single-frame stills than to looping in any modern sense.

content:
The Bomb Squad's main sampling chain was the E-mu SP-1200, paired with an Akai S900 and an Ensoniq Mirage, with tracking and mixing on un-automated 24-track two-inch tape at Greene St. ([Wikipedia, *It Takes a Nation*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/It_Takes_a_Nation_of_Millions_to_Hold_Us_Back); [Tape Op, *Hank Shocklee*](https://tapeop.com/interviews/51/hank-shocklee); [Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks: "Black Steel"*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)). Shocklee described his sampler progression to Tape Op: the Mirage came first with a roughly three-second sampling window — a constraint he treated as liberating — then the Akai S900 expanded that to about 30 seconds, and the SP-1200 gave him ten seconds divisible across the pads so he could "take bites of stuff and actually play that with keys" ([Tape Op, *Hank Shocklee*](https://tapeop.com/interviews/51/hank-shocklee)).

The signature of the album is in part the signature of those machines. The SP-1200's 12-bit, ~26 kHz crunch is baked into the sample voice itself. On "Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos," Shocklee discovered an accidental lo-fi effect when the SP-1200's output cable was not fully seated — a loose-connection grainy artifact — and instead of correcting it, he ran two passes of the Isaac Hayes piano loop, one with the cable fully connected and one halfway inserted, so the two frequency responses could be combined into the bed ([Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks: "Black Steel"*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)). Cross-link to `corpus/techniques/hardware-sampling-workflow.md` — the *It Takes a Nation* sessions are one of the canonical SP-1200-era documents; the Beastie Boys' *Paul's Boutique* a year later used Emax HD for longer-sample beds, a sibling but distinct hardware path.

content: A defining structural choice on *It Takes a Nation*: the album has, by Shocklee's account, **no written basslines**. "Basslines represent melody," Shocklee has said; without melody, the low end becomes a "low-frequency hum" that serves the energy of the track rather than its harmony ([Micro-Chop, *Sampled 808 Drums Instead of Basslines*](https://medium.com/micro-chop/the-bomb-squad-used-sampled-808-drums-instead-of-basslines-on-it-takes-a-nation-of-millions-to-d681eccf1abb)). Where most 1988 hip-hop placed a programmed bassline at the harmonic center, the Bomb Squad substituted sampled 808 kick hits — pulled off records that had already recorded an 808, not from a fresh 808 — and let the grit and pitch-shift of those second-generation kicks function as the entire low-end voice. The implication for arrangement: every harmonic move on the record is carried by horn-stab samples, piano-loop fragments, and noise rather than by a bass instrument in the traditional sense.

content: The Bomb Squad's sample-source map is dominated by the James Brown / J.B.'s catalog, used not as drum-break source so much as **horn-stab and shriek source**. Shocklee: "everything that P.E. is doing is paying homage to the scream that James Brown used. But we didn't use a human voice scream. We tried to find other sounds that would replicate that" ([Tape Op, *Hank Shocklee*](https://tapeop.com/interviews/51/hank-shocklee)). The most-cited example is "Rebel Without a Pause," whose signature whistling top-end is built from a Maceo-Parker-era J.B.'s alto-saxophone glissando lifted from "The Grunt" ([WhoSampled, *Rebel Without a Pause* sample of *The Grunt*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/804/Public-Enemy-Rebel-Without-a-Pause-The-J.B.%27s-The-Grunt/); [WhoSampled, *Rebel Without a Pause* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Rebel-Without-a-Pause/samples/)).

content:
The following are sample claims documented on WhoSampled. The lists are partial — many of these tracks have a dozen or more documented sources each — but every claim below is corroborated by at least one independent reference.

**"Bring the Noise"** — built on James Brown's "Funky Drummer" (the Clyde Stubblefield break) and "Get Off Your Ass and Jam" by Funkadelic, with Marva Whitney's "It's My Thing" and Malcolm X's "Fire & Fury Grass Roots Speech" among the documented sources ([WhoSampled, *Bring the Noise* sample of *Funky Drummer*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/3148/Public-Enemy-Bring-the-Noise-James-Brown-Funky-Drummer/); [WhoSampled, *Bring the Noise* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Bring-the-Noise/samples/)).

**"Don't Believe the Hype"** — built on Melvin Bliss's "Synthetic Substitution" with James Brown's "I Got Ants in My Pants" and "Escape-Ism," Dyke & the Blazers' "Let a Woman Be a Woman, Let a Man Be a Man," and Whodini's "Fugitive" among the documented sources ([WhoSampled, *Don't Believe the Hype* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Don%27t-Believe-the-Hype/samples/); [WhoSampled, sample of *Synthetic Substitution*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/796/Public-Enemy-Don%27t-Believe-the-Hype-Melvin-Bliss-Synthetic-Substitution/)).

**"Rebel Without a Pause"** (originally a 1987 B-side, included on the album) — the J.B.'s' "The Grunt" sax-shriek as the signature top-end, plus James Brown's "Funky Drummer" and "Get Up Offa That Thing" ([WhoSampled, *Rebel Without a Pause* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Rebel-Without-a-Pause/samples/)).

**"Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos"** — Isaac Hayes's "Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic" (1969, from *Hot Buttered Soul*) provides the high-pitched piano motif; Stevie Wonder's "Living for the City" and the Escorts' "Little Green Apples" appear in additional layers; the track also self-samples Public Enemy's own "Bring the Noise" ([WhoSampled, *Black Steel* sample of *Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/64/Public-Enemy-Black-Steel-in-the-Hour-of-Chaos-Isaac-Hayes-Hyperbolicsyllabicsesquedalymistic/); [WhoSampled, *Black Steel* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Black-Steel-in-the-Hour-of-Chaos/samples/)).

**"Night of the Living Baseheads"** — the J.B.'s' "The Grunt," David Bowie's "Fame," ESG's "UFO," the Temptations' "I Can't Get Next to You," Dennis Coffey & the Detroit Guitar Band's "Scorpio," and Aretha Franklin's "Rock Steady" are among the documented sources ([WhoSampled, *Night of the Living Baseheads* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Night-of-the-Living-Baseheads/samples/)).

**"Caught, Can We Get a Witness?"** — Bar-Kays' "Son of Shaft," Bobby Byrd's "Hot Pants (Bonus Beats)," and James Brown's "Soul Power (Live)" are among the documented sources ([WhoSampled, *Caught, Can We Get a Witness?* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Caught,-Can-We-Get-a-Witness%3F/samples/)).

**"Show 'Em Whatcha Got"** — built around Lafayette Afro Rock Band's "Darkest Light" (the same horn loop later famous as the spine of Jay-Z's "Show Me What You Got") ([WhoSampled, *Show 'Em Whatcha Got* sample of *Darkest Light*](https://www.whosampled.com/sample/1414/Public-Enemy-Show-%27Em-Whatcha-Got-Lafayette-Afro-Rock-Band-Darkest-Light/)).

**"Cold Lampin' with Flavor"** — Flavor Flav's solo turn — documented sources include Sweet's "Funk It Up (David's Song)" and the J.B.'s' "Gimme Some More" ([WhoSampled, *Cold Lampin' With Flavor* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Cold-Lampin%27-With-Flavor/samples/)).

**"Louder Than a Bomb"** — Kool & the Gang's "Who's Gonna Take the Weight," Mountain's "Long Red," and a Beastie Boys self-quote of "Girls" are among the documented sources ([WhoSampled, *Louder Than a Bomb* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Louder-Than-a-Bomb/samples/)).

**"Prophets of Rage"** — James Brown's "Funky Drummer" and "The Payback Mix," Funk, Inc.'s "Kool Is Back," and Earth, Wind & Fire's "Shining Star" are among the documented sources, with self-samples from Public Enemy's "Bring the Noise" and "Miuzi Weighs a Ton" ([WhoSampled, *Prophets of Rage* samples](https://www.whosampled.com/Public-Enemy/Prophets-of-Rage/samples/)).

What ARLO should *not* do with this list: extrapolate beyond it. The Bomb Squad's source map is dense enough that fan-forum and casual-listening sample claims circulate without primary corroboration. Treat any sample assertion as a citation that requires WhoSampled (or equivalent primary-source) corroboration before it ships.

content:
"Black Steel in the Hour of Chaos" is the best-documented session on the record because of a *Sound on Sound* Classic Tracks piece on Nick Sansano's engineering work. Tracking happened at Greene St., the main board was an Amek SSL-style desk with automated flying faders in Studio A, but Sansano moved the mix into a smaller room on an "old Trident board" — and Shocklee credits that Trident with giving the track "the grit, the tension, the bite" ([Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)). Two further moves on the same track are worth pulling out:

- **The no-reverb clause.** "I had a no-reverb clause. No reverb on vocals, nothing. Reverb was a symbol of smoothness; I wanted everything edgy and raw" ([Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)). Across the whole album, the lack of plate or chamber treatment on the vocal is a defining negative-space choice — Chuck D's voice sits dry, immediate, and unmistakably "in front of" the bed rather than placed inside a virtual room.
- **Parallel compression, invented under deadline.** Shocklee describes running the same sample loop in parallel with "massive amounts of compression on it so that it would distort" in the background — a parallel-compression / parallel-distortion technique that has since become a standard production move but in 1988 was an emergent on-the-fly invention.

Flavor Flav's phone-call vocal section on "Black Steel" was recorded by miking a speakerphone for verismo rather than emulating the telephone EQ at mix ([Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)).

content:
Chuck D's baritone is the only consistent low-mid voice on the record. With the bassline removed by design and the rhythmic register dominated by 808 thuds and noise, Chuck's chest-voice baritone fills the harmonic space a bassist or keys player would normally hold. The vocal sits forward and dry, pushing mids, with the no-reverb clause carrying through every track. On "Black Steel," he tracked vocals while ill — "deeper and raspier" than usual — and Shocklee chose to keep the take ([Sound on Sound, *Classic Tracks*](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/classic-tracks-public-enemy-black-steel-hour-chaos)). Specific mic-and-chain detail for Chuck's vocal sessions is not consistently documented in primary sources; cite the *sound* of the take, not a model number.

Flavor Flav's high, jagged, often manic delivery is the counter-voice that makes Chuck's baritone legible — a low, prophetic, declarative voice cut against a high, comic, destabilizing voice. Shocklee has framed Flav as a performer-on-faders too: on "Rebel Without a Pause" Flav was triggering the J.B.'s snare hits live in mix while other Bomb Squad members handled kicks and scratches ([Tape Op, *Hank Shocklee*](https://tapeop.com/interviews/51/hank-shocklee)). "Cold Lampin' with Flavor" is the album's most explicit Flavor showcase — a track structured around his solo voice on a sparser Bomb Squad bed.

content: The "Phil Spector of hip-hop" framing is real, repeatedly applied to Shocklee in critical writing, and explicitly disclaimed by Shocklee himself. The shorthand: where Spector built density out of doubled and tripled live instrumentation in a single live room (the Gold Star "Wall of Sound"), Shocklee built density out of layered sample fragments through samplers and tape. Shocklee's preferred analogy in interviews is **collage** — specifically the visual-art collage tradition of Romare Bearden — rather than Spector's monolithic-orchestra model: "I had a ridiculous record collection. And I wanted to prove that it was the records that inspired me… create this collage, almost like a Romare Bearden kind of a painting" ([Mark Kemp, *Hank Shocklee: The Bomb Behind Public Enemy's Squad*](https://dailykemp.com/2017/06/04/hank-shocklee-the-bomb-behind-public-enemys-squad/)). The distinction matters for ARLO: *Spector and Shocklee both aim at density, but the unit of density is different — overdubbed performers vs. recontextualized recordings.* Both are useful reference points for any user asking "how do I make this denser?"

content: Greene St.'s 1988 setup put the team on un-automated boards — Trident at minimum on the "Black Steel" mix, with the SSL-style Amek in the larger room. Shocklee: "if we had automation, we probably would have loved it because every time… you got to start all over again" ([Tape Op, *Hank Shocklee*](https://tapeop.com/interviews/51/hank-shocklee)). Mixing was a four- or five-handed live performance — faders rehearsed and committed, every pass a take. The album's sense of motion — samples popping in and out of the bed at varying levels — is a direct consequence of the live-mix workflow rather than DAW automation. Cross-link to `corpus/techniques/dense-but-clear-mixing.md`.

content:
*It Takes a Nation* was released in June 1988. **Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. Records, Inc.** — Gilbert O'Sullivan's suit against Biz Markie — was decided in December 1991, with Judge Kevin Duffy opening "Thou shalt not steal" and ruling uncleared sampling a copyright infringement requiring pre-clearance ([Wikipedia, *Grand Upright Music, Ltd. v. Warner Bros. Records Inc.*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grand_Upright_Music%2C_Ltd._v._Warner_Bros._Records_Inc.)). Within months, every sample required individual negotiation; rights-holders demanded large royalty percentages or refused outright. The Bomb Squad's working method — dozens of sources per track — became economically impossible.

*It Takes a Nation* sits inside the closing window — roughly 42 months before Grand Upright. *Fear of a Black Planet* (1990), De La Soul's *3 Feet High and Rising* (1989), and the Beastie Boys' *Paul's Boutique* (1989) all live in the same bracket. After 1991, this kind of record stops being made at this density. That historical bracket is most of why *It Takes a Nation* reads as a canonical reference — it is not just a great record but a record from a creative possibility-space that no longer exists.

content:
Transferable lessons from *It Takes a Nation*:

- **A sample is an instrument, not a quotation.** At sufficient fragmentation, a sampled horn stab functions like a tracked horn.
- **Remove a layer to force the others to work harder.** The no-bassline decision forces 808 kicks, horn stabs, and Chuck's baritone to collectively cover the harmonic space.
- **Negative-space mix moves count.** No reverb on vocals is as defining as any positive effect.
- **Constraints upstream become character downstream.** SP-1200 bit-rate, Mirage memory ceiling, loose-cable accidents, un-automated boards — every constraint is now part of the sonic identity.
- **Hand-mix as performance.** Density rehearsed and committed live reads differently than density edited into a session.

content:
*Kid A* is the album where a guitar band — Thom Yorke, Jonny Greenwood, Ed O'Brien, Colin Greenwood, and Phil Selway, with Nigel Godrich co-producing — deliberately broke the framework that had made them famous. *OK Computer* (1997) had been universally praised, toured exhaustively, and left Yorke creatively flattened. The response was not to refine the guitar-band sound but to disassemble it: trade verse-chorus architecture for textural composition, trade live-room tracking for ProTools editing, trade Yorke-as-lead-singer for Yorke-as-instrument. Recorded January 1999 to April 2000 across Paris, Copenhagen, Gloucestershire, and Oxfordshire and released October 2, 2000, the album debuted at number one in both the UK and the US — Radiohead's first US chart-topper, against a marketing campaign that included no singles, few photoshoots, and an internet-first promotional rollout that anticipated the next decade of label strategy ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A); [Billboard 20-year retrospective](https://www.billboard.com/pro/radiohead-kid-a-album-strategy/)).

For ARLO's purposes, *Kid A* is the canonical case study of a band that already had a "strength in one thing" choosing to abandon it on principle.

content:
The break from *OK Computer*-era Radiohead began in Yorke's listening. Burnt out from touring, he became "disillusioned with the 'mythology' of rock music" and listened "almost exclusively to the electronic music" of Warp Records artists — Aphex Twin, Autechre, Boards of Canada ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A)). The quotable line, paraphrased from his Wikipedia-summarized statements, is the aesthetic thesis of the record: "It was refreshing because the music was all structures and had no human voices in it." He wanted his own voice used "as an instrument rather than having a leading role" ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A)).

Yorke could not write conventional Radiohead material. Early *Kid A* drafts were fragments — "some consisted of little more than sounds or rhythms; few had clear verses or choruses" ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A)). The band's response was to keep recording anyway and figure out the songs in post-production.

content:
Returning Radiohead producer Nigel Godrich was not a neutral collaborator on the electronic turn. According to Yorke, Godrich "didn't understand why, if we had such a strength in one thing, we would want to do something else," and Godrich said that Yorke "did not communicate much" during sessions ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A)). On individual tracks his interventions ran the other way: he was the one who pushed Yorke off the piano and onto a Prophet-5 for "Everything in Its Right Place" after the conventional band arrangement failed ([Wikipedia: Everything in Its Right Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everything_in_Its_Right_Place)).

The pattern that emerges across the literature is a producer who resisted the *premise* of the record while supplying the technical vocabulary that made specific tracks work. Godrich's broader engineering philosophy — analog-spine tracking, dense overdubbing, "slammed" tube compression — is treated in detail in [Nigel Godrich Engineering Method](../artists/nigel-godrich-engineering-method.md). What is specific to *Kid A* is that *Kid A* is where his role expanded from engineer-with-opinions into compositional collaborator, the same role he would play across *Amnesiac* (2001) and that later returned for *In Rainbows* (2007) — see [Radiohead *In Rainbows* Production](../artists/radiohead-in-rainbows-production.md).

content:
The sessions ran across four locations between January 1999 and April 2000 ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A); [Howl & Echoes: Making of *Kid A*](https://howlandechoes.com/2016/10/feature-the-making-of-radiohead-kid-a/)):

- **Guillaume Tell Studios, Paris** (January 1999) — the first attempt. Sessions yielded little usable material. Yorke's verdict on an early "Everything in Its Right Place" pass at Guillaume Tell was the slogan of the entire pivot: "That sounds great, but it sounds like old Radiohead" ([MusicRadar: Radiohead redefined guitar on *Kid A*](https://www.musicradar.com/news/how-radiohead-redefined-the-role-of-guitar-on-their-landmark-album-kid-a-its-scary-everyone-feels-insecure-im-a-guitarist-and-suddenly-its-like-well-there-are-no-guitars-on-this-track-or-drums)). Importantly, Jonny Greenwood acquired his ondes Martenot during the Paris sessions — finding the listing in a Paris music shop and having the instrument mailed to the studio ([The King of Gear: Greenwood and the ondes Martenot](https://thekingofgear.com/post/59984869688/jonny-greenwood-and-the-ondes-martenot)).
- **Medley Studios, Copenhagen** (March 1999) — two weeks, described as unproductive. The session produced "approximately 50 reels of tape, each containing 15 minutes of music, with nothing finished" ([Wikipedia: *Kid A*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kid_A)).
- **Batsford Park mansion, Gloucestershire** (from April 1999) — the breakthrough location. The country-house setup, similar to St. Catherine's Court on *OK Computer*, allowed open-ended experimentation. "Everything in Its Right Place" got rebuilt around the Prophet-5 here ([Wikipedia: Everything in Its Right Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everything_in_Its_Right_Place)).
- **Radiohead's own Oxfordshire studio** (from September 1999) — once their converted-barn facility was complete, the band moved final tracking and overdubbing home and finished the record in April 2000.

The geography is itself a production choice: by the time finishing happened on the band's own equipment, there was no studio clock and no label deadline.

content:
*Kid A* is not the first record to use a DAW. It is, however, the record where Godrich-with-Radiohead crossed the threshold from analog editing to digital editing as the central compositional act. Godrich has described the workflow on the *Kid A* / *Amnesiac* sessions as a hybrid: "mainly used Digidesign's Pro Tools for editing and manipulating audio" and "Steinberg's Cubase for MIDI sequencing" ([Nigel Godrich Producer Tumblr — DAW quotes](https://nigelgodrichproducer.tumblr.com/post/153225174935/old-nigel-quotes-on-recording-with-daws)). Tracking still went to reel-to-reel; the editing was digital ([MusicTech: Landmark Productions: *Kid A*](https://musictech.com/guides/essential-guide/landmark-productions-radiohead-kid-a/)).

A widely-cited summary line: "There is some kind of sound generation or digital editing or arrangement on every track of the *Kid A* and *Amnesiac* albums" ([MusicTech: Landmark Productions: *Kid A*](https://musictech.com/guides/essential-guide/landmark-productions-radiohead-kid-a/)). The aesthetic consequence is a record that retains analog warmth at the source (tape, tube compression, U47-style vocal mics, SSL desks — see [Nigel Godrich Engineering Method](../artists/nigel-godrich-engineering-method.md)) while letting Pro Tools dictate the *form* of each track.

content:
The opening track is the cleanest illustration of the method. Written on piano, it stalled in conventional band arrangements through both the Paris and Copenhagen sessions. Yorke and Godrich rebuilt it in Gloucestershire by transferring the chord movement from piano to a Sequential Circuits Prophet-5 synthesiser, which became the song's harmonic spine ([Wikipedia: Everything in Its Right Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everything_in_Its_Right_Place); [MusicTech: Landmark Productions: *Kid A*](https://musictech.com/guides/essential-guide/landmark-productions-radiohead-kid-a/)).

The signature vocal move is the Pro Tools "scrubbing tool" — Godrich dragging Yorke's vocal track back and forth like a physical tape reel until fragments of the line emerged in non-linear order, then committing those scrubs as additional vocal layers around the main take ([Wikipedia: Everything in Its Right Place](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Everything_in_Its_Right_Place); [MusicRadar feature on the song](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/lots-of-people-say-that-song-is-gibberish-its-not-its-totally-about-that-how-thom-yorke-channelled-his-tour-exhaustion-into-the-track-that-saved-radiohead-from-oblivion)). Pitch-shifting, delay, and reversed vocals layer over the main take to create what one source calls a "hazy sonic fog" ([MusicRadar](https://www.musicradar.com/artists/lots-of-people-say-that-song-is-gibberish-its-not-its-totally-about-that-how-thom-yorke-channelled-his-tour-exhaustion-into-the-track-that-saved-radiohead-from-oblivion)). The technique was — for a major-label rock record in 1999 — genuinely novel. The DAW is functioning as a compositional instrument, not as a tape-replacement editor.

**ARLO anti-hallucination note:** the specific plugin chain on "Everything in Its Right Place" is not documented in primary sources beyond "Pro Tools scrubbing," pitch-shift, and reversal. Treat the *technique* (chop/scrub/repitch a clean vocal take into a textural pad) as solid prior art; do not invent specific plugin names.

content:
If "Everything in Its Right Place" is the album's clearest electronic statement, "How to Disappear Completely" is the clearest demonstration that the electronic shift was textural, not anti-acoustic. The string arrangement, scored by Jonny Greenwood — the band's only formally music-theory-trained member — was performed by the Orchestra of St John's, conducted by John Lubbock, in a single three-hour session on February 4, 2000, at Dorchester Abbey, a twelfth-century church roughly five miles from Radiohead's Oxfordshire studio ([Wikipedia: How to Disappear Completely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Disappear_Completely)). Greenwood chose the Orchestra of St John's because they had previously played Penderecki and Messiaen — the two composers whose harmonic vocabulary he was drawing from ([Wikipedia: How to Disappear Completely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Disappear_Completely)).

The ondes Martenot on this track is Greenwood, multitracked, on the digital ondes he had bought in Paris during the Guillaume Tell sessions. The instrument is a special student model from a fifty-unit run built in 1983 by Maurice Martenot's son — four octaves rather than the standard six, a left-side control panel, and additive-synthesis sliders for overtone shaping ([The King of Gear: Greenwood and the ondes Martenot](https://thekingofgear.com/post/59984869688/jonny-greenwood-and-the-ondes-martenot)). Greenwood acquired all three diffuseurs (the speaker cabinets Maurice Martenot designed) with it and taught himself to play the instrument during the sessions, without a teacher. His ondes parts are mixed quietly under the string section ([Wikipedia: How to Disappear Completely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Disappear_Completely)).

Critically, this is also the first track on the album where Yorke's vocal appears "clearly and without processing" — a long-drawn-out falsetto, his range spanning roughly C♯3 to A4 ([Wikipedia: How to Disappear Completely](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/How_to_Disappear_Completely)). The compositional logic of the record is to make the unprocessed vocal feel rare and earned by surrounding it with processed ones elsewhere.

**Builder attribution note:** the brief that came in mentioned a possible "Solar" instrument by Christine Vorobeichik. Searchable sources do not corroborate that attribution; the well-sourced fact is that the instrument is from the 1983 Maurice Martenot Jr. digital run. ARLO should treat the Christine Vorobeichik attribution as unverified.
