content: Byrne's solo records after Talking Heads' 1991 dissolution can be read as a sustained experiment in his own *How Music Works* thesis: change the context, and the songwriting changes. [*Rei Momo*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rei_Momo) (1989) committed to Latin American forms — rumba, mambo, merengue, cumbia, samba, bomba — recorded with players like Willie Colón and Celia Cruz and co-produced with Steve Lillywhite. *Uh-Oh* (1992) and *David Byrne* (1994) pulled the Latin instrumentation back toward rock-band shapes. *Look Into the Eyeball* (2001) reintroduced lush string arrangements alongside dance grooves. *Grown Backwards* (2004) added operatic aria fragments (Verdi, Bizet) sung straight, treating bel canto as just another available context. *American Utopia* (2018) returned to a rhythm-section ensemble feel set up for a touring stage show. Across all of these, the *voice* and the *plainspoken lyrical register* are continuous; what changes is the room around them. This is exactly the modular aesthetic ARLO's hybrid stack assumes: keep the writer's signature constant, swap the production world.

provenance.section: The Solo Career Arc — Genre as Context

content: A note on the technical legacy of *Bush of Ghosts*: released in 1981, it preceded mainstream sampling culture by several years and used tape-based techniques to do what later sampler workflows automated. Byrne and Eno used vocal recordings from radio, television, and field recordings as the *lead vocal*, treating spoken-word source material the way later producers would treat drum breaks. The compositional implication — that any recorded human utterance can be lifted into a song as a melodic and rhythmic element — directly anticipates the cut-up vocal techniques later associated with Justin Vernon, Bon Iver's *22, A Million*, and a generation of producers building songs out of found vocal phrases. When ARLO suggests using a found radio fragment as the hook of a track, the lineage running through that suggestion starts with *Bush of Ghosts*.

content: Byrne treats live shows as compositional extensions of the writing, not as promotional rituals for finished records. The *Stop Making Sense* tour and film (1983–84, directed by Jonathan Demme) staged the band as a piece of theater — Byrne entered alone with a boombox and "Psycho Killer," then the band assembled one member at a time across the set, building the ensemble visually the way the records build it sonically. Decades later, [*American Utopia*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/American_Utopia_(film)) (2018 tour, 2019–20 Broadway run, 2020 Spike Lee film) took the same instinct further: eleven musicians, all on fully wireless or portable rigs, dressed identically in grey suits and barefoot, choreographed by Annie-B Parson on a bare stage framed by silver-chain curtains ([Sight and Sound interview](https://www.bfi.org.uk/sight-and-sound/interviews/if-there-was-song-spike-lee-loved-wed-see-him-pop-aisle-david-byrne-his-concert-doc-american-utopia)). The staging *is* the arrangement. For ARLO, the takeaway: a song's final form may not be the studio recording — it may be how the song is *embodied* in performance, and writing decisions can be made with that performance in mind from the start.

provenance.section: Live Performance as Compositional Thinking

content: Byrne's long collaboration with choreographer Annie-B Parson — across *Here Lies Love*, the *American Utopia* tour, the Broadway run, and the film — treats movement as another layer of composition. Performers carry their own instruments and route around the stage on choreographed paths, so a drum part isn't just a part, it's *a person walking a specific line while playing it*. The compositional implication is that arrangement decisions (who plays what, when they enter, how long they stay in the mix) can be derived from spatial logic rather than purely musical logic. This is unusual in pop and rare in rock, and it gives Byrne's late-career work a quality of *spatialized arrangement* that's hard to replicate without thinking about bodies in a room.

content: [*How Music Works*](https://www.themarginalian.org/2012/09/13/david-byrne-how-music-works/) (2012, revised 2017) is the closest thing Byrne has written to a methods manual, and it should be treated as the canonical reference for his philosophy. Key claims, paraphrased: (1) context — acoustics, venue, recording technology, format — shapes what music gets made, not the other way around; (2) creators "unconsciously and instinctively make work to fit preexisting formats," and this is a feature, not a failure; (3) songwriting is largely *hunting and pecking* for short modular pieces and then shaping them into something resembling a song; (4) the emotional content arrives *through* the constraints, not in spite of them; (5) genius is "a thing perfectly suited to its context." Paraphrase only — direct quotation should be verified against the book. The five claims together form a usable operating manual for any modular, context-driven writing process, including the kind ARLO is built to support.

content: A recurring Byrne technique is to record vocal improvisations over a finished track as a *first pass*, capturing rhythm and phrasing before the lyric exists, then mining those vocal nonsense-takes for syllabic patterns and accidental phrases that survive into the final lyric. On *Remain in Light* and *Speaking in Tongues*, several finished lyrics began as scat or syllabic placeholders that he then assigned meaning to. This is the same technique Justin Vernon, Bon Iver, and many contemporary producers use under different names ("mumble track," "vibe vocal," "syllabic demo"), and Byrne is one of the clearest historical reference points for it. The technique presumes the *singer-who-writes* frame: the body's rhythmic instinct goes first, the meaning is assigned afterward, and the lyric is judged by whether it *fits the cadence* as much as by what it says.

provenance.section: Stream-of-Consciousness, Improvisation, and the Demo Vocal

content: A condensed working set of heuristics that ARLO can offer when a user is reaching for this aesthetic. Build the bed first — drums, bass, looping instrumental parts — and only then write the vocal. Improvise a syllabic demo vocal over the finished bed before writing any words. Pull lyrical material from non-musical sources (radio voices, sermons, instruction manuals, overheard speech) and resist anything that sounds like a rock lyric. Keep sentences short, declarative, and present-tense; let strangeness come from juxtaposition, not vocabulary. Treat one voice as the lead and use other voices as call-and-response congregation, not as harmony stacks. Build the arrangement from interlocking single-bar parts, not from chord changes. Consider how the song would be staged — who plays what part, where they stand — and let that constrain the arrangement. And when in doubt, change the *context* (room, ensemble, genre frame) before changing the song.

provenance.section: Practical Heuristics for ARLO Sessions in the Byrne Lineage

content: Dijon Duenas — performing as Dijon — is a Baltimore-born, Los Angeles–based singer and producer whose 2021 debut full-length *Absolutely* sits at the seam between R&B, Americana, and what one might call hi-fi-allergic indie soul. Before going solo around 2017, he co-fronted the duo Abhi//Dijon with Abhirath Raju, releasing the EPs *stay up* and *Montana* — work that critics positioned in a "slick, emotional R&B" lineage with a "sturdy, soulful core" ([The FADER: Guide to Dijon](https://www.thefader.com/2025/08/18/guide-to-dijon-discography-abhi-dijon-collaborations)). His solo run through *Sci Fi 1* (2019) and *How Do You Feel About Getting Married?* (2020) gradually braided folk and Americana into the R&B chassis, setting up *Absolutely* as the consolidation record. *Absolutely* released November 5, 2021 on R&R / Warner, runs 31:32, and was named #3 in *The FADER*'s 50 Best Albums of 2021 ([Wikipedia: *Absolutely*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolutely_(Dijon_album))). For ARLO, Dijon is the template for *fidelity-as-aesthetic-choice* in an R&B-leaning songwriting context — a counterweight to glossy contemporary production.

provenance.section: Who Dijon Is, Briefly
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: Recording took place across two physical sites in 2020, the first pandemic year. Dijon described the geography to *The FADER* as "a lot of the record in my house where I'm at right now and then a big chunk of it in upstate New York" ([The FADER interview podcast](https://www.thefader.com/2021/11/16/dijon-fader-interview-podcast-absolutely)). The LA portion was a domestic, untreated home setup; the upstate sessions were a more communal residency, where Dijon brought in collaborator Jack Karaszewski and others to "try for a few nights to make music around a table." That upstate stretch was when Dijon was, by his own account, "extremely obsessed with The Band" and trying to make "a demented version of one of their songs" — a process that crystallized into "Annie." The split locations are audible: rooms ring differently, and the record is happy to let that show.

provenance.section: The Two-Site Recording: LA Home + Upstate New York
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: The methodological core of *Absolutely* is the collapse of demo and master. Dijon told *The FADER*: "I don't do demos or anything like that. I just sit there and I just think about music for as long as I possibly can." Internal pre-recording rumination lasted roughly two years; the actual cutting took only "one to two months" once it started ([The FADER](https://www.thefader.com/2021/11/16/dijon-fader-interview-podcast-absolutely)). The pieces were sung into existence on tape rather than re-performed from a prior reference. He has framed himself as "not much of a refiner," favoring first-take captures and the "beautiful imperfections" that come with them ([The FADER](https://www.thefader.com/2021/11/16/dijon-fader-interview-podcast-absolutely)). For ARLO this is a usable axiom: when songwriting and recording are the same act, every iteration becomes part of the artifact, and there is no "clean" version waiting backstage to be re-tracked.

provenance.section: "Songwriting and Recording Happened Simultaneously"
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: The single most-cited piece of gear-press on *Absolutely* is Dijon's vocal-capture chain: an AKG C414 large-diaphragm condenser, set to its omnidirectional polar pattern, running into a Heritage Audio 1073 preamp (a faithful reissue of the Neve 1073 channel). Every vocal on the record except "The Dress" used this chain, and Dijon's stated rule was to "make it as hot as possible without clipping" — pushing preamp gain aggressively to get input level riding the top of the envelope. He summarized the stance plainly: "The omni polar pattern, that's the sound of the record" ([Reverb News: Dijon Talks Absolutely and His Omnidirectional Process](https://reverb.com/news/dijon-interview), as quoted across [Equipboard's gear breakdown](https://equipboard.com/albums/dijon-absolutely)). Most home recordists avoid omni because it picks up everything the cardioid would reject — floor creaks, snare-side rattle, wall slap. Dijon used the pattern *for* that reason: a 360-degree image of the room as the record's default vocal source.

provenance.section: The AKG C414 in Omni: "That's the Sound of the Record"
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

citation_targets.title: Reverb News: Dijon Talks Absolutely and His Omnidirectional Process

content: Because the omni pattern was capturing a "boxy" untreated home space, the chain compensated downstream rather than upstream — Dijon and engineers used a graphic EQ to "remove most of the mids" and tame the boxiness, which is why much of the record reads "thin" in the lower-mid register on first listen ([Reverb News via Equipboard](https://equipboard.com/albums/dijon-absolutely)). This is a useful inversion for ARLO's suggestion logic: instead of treating the room or repositioning the mic to avoid the problem, *Absolutely* accepts the room's acoustic signature and then carves the mids out post-tracking. The result is a vocal sound that feels close and present without being "warm" in the usual ballad-pop sense — it sits forward, slightly papery, room-tail audible.

provenance.section: Taming the Room with a Graphic EQ
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: The non-acoustic side of the record's sound design ran through a small hardware-plus-DAW stack. Dijon worked with various guitars and keys plus an Elektron Octatrack loaded with breakbeats, "a bit of his Eurorack skiff," and everything recorded into Ableton Live ([Reverb News via Equipboard](https://equipboard.com/albums/dijon-absolutely)). Eurorack made limited but identifiable appearances: a Make Noise *Strega* on "Talk Down" and a looped pluck pattern from a Mutable Instruments *Rings* on "Did You See It?" Additional hardware in his orbit included an Elektron Analog Four and an MPC he could use to sample Eurorack patches. The Octatrack/Eurorack/Ableton triangle is worth flagging for ARLO: it is identical in shape to several artists in the aesthetic stack (the LCD Soundsystem hardware-into-DAW model, James Murphy's analog-synth philosophy) but applied to R&B/folk material rather than dance-punk.

provenance.section: Elektron Octatrack, Eurorack, and Ableton
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: Michael Gordon — recording as mk.gee, and the subject of [the sibling artist file](/Users/cfitt/Dev/arlo/corpus/artists/mk-gee-di-direct-philosophy.md) — is the most consequential collaborator on *Absolutely*. Wikipedia credits him on bass, drums, guitar, piano, synthesizer, and vocals across the record; Dijon describes his "grooves" as the underpinning of many songs and frames their relationship as a "competitive edge in the studio" that introduced new vocabulary and pushed him out of an isolationist working pattern ([The FADER](https://www.thefader.com/2021/11/16/dijon-fader-interview-podcast-absolutely)). Gordon's general DI/refusal-of-amp-tone philosophy is covered in the sibling file and is *not* re-litigated here, but its presence on *Absolutely* is the load-bearing reason the record's guitar tones read so unconventional: thin, plucky, processed, and never doing the "guitar hero" role a song like "Many Times" might invite. The drum aesthetic across the record is similarly Gordon-inflected — Olivia Powell notes that both producers "saturate drums heavily, with echoing snares reminiscent of 1980s production and slightly 'flabby' kicks," and quotes Gordon's approach as "just saturation…play light and then push it hard after" ([Olivia Powell: Dijon and Mk.gee's Intuitive Groove](https://oliviapowell.substack.com/p/dijon-and-mkgees-intuitive-groove)). The Octatrack-loaded breakbeats sit under live drum overdubs (Jack Karaszewski is credited with drum programming) to get a "wet" pocket that does not sound like a programmed kit. The partnership continued into mk.gee's 2024 *Two Star & the Dream Police* and 2025's Justin Bieber *SWAG* and Bon Iver *Sable, Fable*.

provenance.section: Mike Gordon (mk.gee) as Core Collaborator, and Drum Treatment
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: Beyond Gordon, *Absolutely*'s personnel is a small revolving cast. Andrew Sarlo — known for Big Thief, Nick Hakim, and Bon Iver work — is credited as producer, mixer, and programmer, and Dijon said of him that he "rearranged parts and removed elements," a role Dijon "had never trusted anybody with before" ([The FADER](https://www.thefader.com/2021/11/16/dijon-fader-interview-podcast-absolutely)). Jack Karaszewski handled drum programming, synthesis, production, and mixing presence, and was around for much of the upstate sessions; Dijon credited him with understanding that the project needed "a new fidelity for ourselves," because it was "very strange to record stuff as poorly as we do and then expect to either re-track it at a studio or have somebody who wasn't a part of the record manipulate it" — so they "opted for varying fidelities" ([Reverb News via Equipboard](https://equipboard.com/albums/dijon-absolutely)). Noah Le Gros contributed slide guitar. Henry Kwapis also produced.

provenance.section: The Other Hands: Sarlo, Karaszewski, Le Gros
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: The mix stance is consistent with the recording stance: do not pretend the source is something it isn't. Dijon described the mix process as "throwing in a lot of things that already existed within the sessions and increasing them or riding the volumes," with the explicit philosophy of "not trying to enhance what wasn't really enhanced to begin with" ([Reverb News via Equipboard](https://equipboard.com/albums/dijon-absolutely)). In practice this means automation-heavy mixing — volume rides, fader moves, sub-mutes, level pushes — rather than spectral surgery or polish-pass plugin chains. The "varying fidelities" idea is the corollary: different songs and different moments on the record sit at different fidelity levels on purpose, and the mix preserves the gap rather than averaging it out.

provenance.section: Mixing Philosophy: "Increase What's Already There"
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: The aesthetic positioning of *Absolutely* is genre-promiscuous in a deliberate way. Pitchfork's Stephen Kearse described Dijon's voice moving "from coos to wails to murmurs" across folk and soul arrangements; Dijon himself called the record "an abstracted interpretation of what making music feels like to me," blending "rapturous Americana and delicate soul" ([The FADER](https://www.thefader.com/2021/11/16/dijon-fader-interview-podcast-absolutely)). Olivia Powell quotes Dijon naming a shared frustration with Gordon over "the lack of anger that people had at the state of young music," and questioning "why nobody else was as feverishly...reaching" for new ideas ([Olivia Powell](https://oliviapowell.substack.com/p/dijon-and-mkgees-intuitive-groove)). The R&B-Americana-soul fusion is the surface expression of an anti-polish stance — pulling on traditions that *don't* default to glossy modern production as a way to escape glossy modern production. Powell's piece is also the clearest articulation of the record's compositional posture: both Dijon and Gordon embrace "intentional lo-fi" backed by years of experimentation, "messing things up" purposefully — overdriving guitars and layering vocals unevenly because of how it feels, not despite it. The "wetness" (saturation, reverb, room) creates a "slightly anxiety-inducing" quality that amplifies emotional impact. Equally important is what Powell calls "reverence for silence": both artists "treat pauses as compositional elements, using hand movements and vocalizations to punctuate silence." On *Absolutely* this is audible across the record's many mid-song gear-shifts — sudden drops, abrupt re-entries, vocal moments that hang on their own without instrumental support.

provenance.section: R&B / Americana / Soul Fusion, "Intentional Lo-Fi," and Silence
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: Dijon, mk.gee axis, R&B-folk fusion

content: Director Jack Karaszewski's short film *Absolutely* — released December 2021, free on YouTube through end-of-year ([The FADER: Dijon shares short film *Absolutely*](https://www.thefader.com/2021/12/23/dijon-shares-short-film-absolutely)) — frames the record as a live-band, around-the-table experience. It compiles previously released performances of "Big Mike's" and "Many Times" with new versions of "Scratching," "Talk Down," "Annie," and "Rodeo Clown." A moment during "Annie" — Dijon and Gordon trading a three-word phrase back and forth — is the clearest on-camera glimpse of the duo's working chemistry ([The FADER](https://www.thefader.com/2021/12/23/dijon-shares-short-film-absolutely)). For ARLO the film matters because it confirms the record's premise visually: this is music that wants to be heard as a room of people, not a stack of overdubs, even when it is in fact a stack of overdubs.

provenance.section: "Absolutely" the Film, and the Live-in-the-Room Frame

content: Critical reception was strong without being unanimously hot. Pitchfork awarded a 7.2, with Kearse highlighting the "pliant, raspy" voice and the unpredictable arrangements; *The FADER* ranked it #3 of 2021; Clash put it at #44; The Line of Best Fit #41 ([Wikipedia: *Absolutely*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Absolutely_(Dijon_album))). The record's downstream influence has been larger than its initial reception — by 2025, both Dijon and Gordon were core contributors to Justin Bieber's *SWAG* and Bon Iver's *Sable, Fable*, with the toni truale essay arguing that pop itself became the "third party" their aesthetic was now visibly shaping ([toni truale: Dijon, Mk.gee, and the Third Party Called Pop](https://www.tonitruale.com/post/dijon-mk-gee-and-the-third-party-called-pop)). The pop-architecture exposure means *Absolutely*'s production grammar — omni-vocal capture, hot input, in-room imperfection, breakbeat-under-live drums, mk.gee guitar — is now a recognized contemporary register, not a regional curiosity.

content: If a user is gesturing at "Dijon's vocal sound" on a write, the priors worth surfacing are: large-diaphragm condenser in omni rather than cardioid, preamp gain pushed close to clipping, accept the room's reflections as part of the take, then EQ mids down rather than re-tracking. If the gesture is "Dijon's drum feel," the priors are: breakbeat sample loaded into a hardware sampler (Octatrack-style) sitting underneath a live drum overdub, both heavily saturated, snare bright and 1980s-leaning, kick slightly loose. If the gesture is "Dijon's songwriting flow," the prior is: do not demo separately — start the recording with the song still incomplete, let arrangement decisions happen at capture time, and accept first takes. For the broader aesthetic stack, *Absolutely* is the bridge between the bedroom-pop bedroom (mk.gee) and the dance-punk hardware rig (LCD Soundsystem) — same hardware-into-DAW topology, different genre destination.

content: The sonic blueprint for *I Love You, Honeybear* (Sub Pop, 2015) didn't come from a record collection or a producer pitch — it came from a hallucination. In Josh Tillman's own framing, "the massive, deranged shmaltz I heard in my head, and knew had to be the sound of this record, originated a few years ago while Emma and I were hallucinating in Joshua Tree; the same week I wrote the title track" [(Sub Pop release notes via search synthesis)](https://www.subpop.com/releases/father_john_misty/i_love_you_honeybear). Tillman has said he "chased that sound for the entire year and half" the album was being recorded. For ARLO retrieval the operative phrase is "deranged schmaltz": Honeybear is not pastiche Laurel Canyon, it is Laurel Canyon being squinted at through a mushroom-trip lens, with the orchestral lushness pushed past taste and into a kind of theatrical excess. That intent — deliberate over-decoration as a stylistic statement — is the load-bearing fact when modeling this aesthetic, more than any single piece of gear.

content: The studio that hosted *Honeybear* is Jonathan Wilson's Fivestar Studios (often written "Five Star"), which has migrated geographically across Wilson's career. Wilson founded it in Laurel Canyon, relocated it to Echo Park in 2009 where it stayed for about nine years, and as of recent reporting it lives in Topanga, California [(Jonathan Wilson — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Wilson_(musician)). *Honeybear* was tracked primarily at the Echo Park incarnation of Fivestar, with additional sessions at United Recording Studios in Los Angeles, running intermittently from mid-2013 through 2014 [(I Love You, Honeybear — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Love_You,_Honeybear). Wilson's Echo Park room was a tape-first, console-first environment: a Studer A80 24-track and Otari MX-80 for tracking, an Ampex ATR-102 for mixdown, an MCI JH-416A console, Tannoy mains, NS-10 nearfields [(Tape Op interview with Jonathan Wilson)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/96/jonathan-wilson). When someone asks ARLO for "the Honeybear room," that's the spec — not a modern in-the-box LA studio, but a 24-track tape rig with a vintage British/American console and Tannoys.

content: The producer/mix split on *Honeybear* matters for retrieval because it's not Wilson all the way through. Wilson is credited as producer (Tillman co-produces); the album was mixed by Phil Ek and mastered by Greg Calbi at Sterling Sound [(I Love You, Honeybear — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Love_You,_Honeybear). Ek is a Pacific Northwest engineer associated with Built to Spill, Modest Mouse, Fleet Foxes, and The Shins — bands that lean toward open, dry, instrument-forward indie mixing rather than the dense Laurel Canyon plushness Wilson tracked. That contrast is part of why *Honeybear* sounds the way it does: Wilson's arrangements are baroque and overflowing, but Ek's mix gives them indie-rock midrange clarity and avoids letting strings and horns turn into syrup. The vinyl was issued as a double LP at 45 RPM specifically because, per Sub Pop, "due to its length and the wide audio spectrum of the recording, we...decided that the album sounded much better cut at 45 RPM over 2 pieces of vinyl." A wide, hot-mastered double-LP cut is part of the format-level intent of this record, not an afterthought.

content: Wilson's stated production philosophy with Tillman is non-imposing — closer to assembling a room and letting it cook than imposing a template. On *Pure Comedy* he framed it explicitly: "let me do what I do and let's explore and figure this out all while we're having fun" [(Billboard interview with Jonathan Wilson)](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/jonathan-wilson-father-john-misty-pure-comedy-7777039/). In a separate Tape Op profile Wilson emphasized "the integrity of each part of the band, from tuning the drums to the microphone choices," and avoiding the urge to override an artist's natural sound [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/96/jonathan-wilson). For ARLO this is the modeling cue: the Tillman/Wilson sessions are not auteur productions where the producer rewrites the songs. Tillman arrives with songs in finished form, Wilson assembles a band and a tonal palette, and the arc of the session is sonic exploration on top of pre-existing structure. That order — songwriting closed before tracking starts, exploration happens in tone and texture — is the workflow signature.

content: Wilson has been specific about what he tracks Tillman's voice through. In interview he told the press, "Most of the Josh stuff is my 1957 Neumann 47. But then I changed on him. On most stuff these days, I've been using a 67, because I feel like it sort of has such a natural sound, like, to me, it just sounds like the singer" [(Stereogum — "Inside The Making Of Pure Comedy")](https://www.stereogum.com/1938850/inside-the-making-of-pure-comedy-with-jonathan-wilson-father-john-mistys-secret-weapon/news/). Two retrieval consequences: first, the *Fear Fun* / *Honeybear* Tillman vocal sound is a 1957 U47 large-diaphragm tube mic; second, by *Pure Comedy* the regular vocal mic had shifted to a U67. Both are FET-era reference mics, both Neumann, both expensive — but they're different colors. The U47 reads more dramatic and forward in the upper mids; the U67 sits more naturally and is less of a "character" mic. Wilson also uses U47s as overhead mics on drums as a default, separate from his vocal mic choices.

content: *Pure Comedy* (2017) deliberately broke from the Honeybear method. Wilson explained that earlier records were "individually layering instruments" between him and Tillman, while *Pure Comedy* was tracked as a full band performing together [(Billboard)](https://www.billboard.com/music/rock/jonathan-wilson-father-john-misty-pure-comedy-7777039/). The recording was done in March 2016 at United Recording Studios in Los Angeles; "basic tracking and vocals were recorded live, in no more than two takes each" [(Pure Comedy — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_Comedy). The album was mixed by Tillman, Wilson, and engineer Trevor Spencer, and mastered by Bob Ludwig at Gateway Mastering. Orchestral arrangements came from Gavin Bryars (horns on the opener, strings later), Nico Muhly (strings on a late track), and Thomas Bartlett ("Doveman") on piano and keys. Core band: Elijah Thomson on bass, Daniel Bailey on drums and percussion, Keefus Ciancia on keys and samples. This is a very different production posture from *Honeybear* — fewer takes, less overdubbing, more committed performances, named arrangers — and it sounds less ornamental and more like a working ensemble.

content: When Wilson talks about his job on these records, he frames it as a frequency-and-texture problem, not a song-structure problem. From the *Pure Comedy* interviews: "What are the frequencies? The textures? What drums are we going to use? What microphones are we going to use? What's the studio we're going to use?" [(Stereogum)](https://www.stereogum.com/1938850/inside-the-making-of-pure-comedy-with-jonathan-wilson-father-john-mistys-secret-weapon/news/). That's the producer's role as Wilson conceives it: tonal architecture, room choice, mic choice, drum tuning, and frequency arrangement across the mix. The compositional structure is already settled when he and Tillman get into the room. ARLO should treat that as the operating model — when a user is in this aesthetic stack, the questions worth asking are about tone palette and room sound, not about whether the chorus needs a key change.

content: Wilson is, fairly or not, the figurehead of the modern Laurel Canyon revival. He hosted jam nights at his Laurel Canyon compound that drew in veterans from the Electric Flag, the Paul Butterfield Blues Band, and other late-60s/early-70s LA scene-makers, and is "credited with revitalizing the Laurel Canyon music scene" [(Jonathan Wilson — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Wilson_(musician)). But Wilson has publicly resisted the pastiche framing. His stated goal is to "transcend an era" rather than imitate it [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/96/jonathan-wilson). The cross-link to the Zevon anchor in this corpus is real: the lineage Wilson lives in runs through Joni Mitchell, CSN, Neil Young, Warren Zevon, Jackson Browne — late-Laurel-Canyon singer-songwriter craft with serious arrangers attached. But *Honeybear* and *Pure Comedy* are not period-correct emulations; they're records that use that vocabulary (mandolin, lap steel, congas, clarinet, orchestral strings, mellotron-thick keys) toward modern songwriting that wouldn't fit on a 1973 record.

content: Wilson has been on record that *Pure Comedy* "was done under LSD," with the working theory that "we'd all practice the songs and then go in with this hint of something magical" and "see if we could get that to read on the tape as some sort of expansion of consciousness" [(Stereogum)](https://www.stereogum.com/1938850/inside-the-making-of-pure-comedy-with-jonathan-wilson-father-john-mistys-secret-weapon/news/). Wilson clarified he doesn't do it daily — "I don't use it every day, just because I don't want to get into the habit of doing any outside substance regularly" — but the band was on it during tracking. ARLO should note this as part of the record's stated method but not extrapolate it as a general technique recommendation. The retrieval lesson is contextual: *Pure Comedy*'s long-form, drifting, slightly hallucinated pacing — including the seven-minute opener and the thirteen-minute centerpiece — was tracked with that intent. The slowness and the over-arrangement are part of the design.

provenance.section: The LSD Disclosure — Pure Comedy's Stated Method

content: *God's Favorite Customer* (2018) is the record in this trio where Wilson is least central. Tillman effectively self-produced with collaborators Jonathan Rado (Foxygen), Dave Cerminara, and Trevor Spencer doing most of the actual co-producer work across the ten tracks; Wilson is credited on "very special thanks," played bass synthesizer and Crumar on the opener, and mixed selected tracks [(God's Favorite Customer — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/God's_Favorite_Customer). The record was written largely during a six-week period when Tillman was, in his words, "kind of on the straits" and living in a hotel for two months — the Bowery Hotel in New York being the much-reported context. *Customer* is the most direct, least-orchestrated of the three, with shorter songs and a leaner band sound. For ARLO the practical takeaway: when a user invokes "the Father John Misty sound" they almost always mean *Honeybear* or *Pure Comedy*. *Customer* is the same artist with a different production team and a much smaller arrangement footprint, and conflating the three records will produce bad retrievals.

content: Wilson maintains a small set of inviolable gear choices that show up record after record. From the Tape Op profile: U47s as drum overheads on every project, a Fender Princeton amp on every project, and a stated dream signal path of "V72 preamp into a Pultec into a RCA BA-6A" [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/96/jonathan-wilson). He's a tape-saturation advocate who avoids plug-ins and prefers physical effects — real spring and plate reverbs over algorithmic emulations. His engineer at Fivestar is Bryce Gonzales, who builds custom tube compressors used at the facility. ARLO can treat this gear-philosophy stance as a stable retrieval fact: the Wilson-produced Tillman records are tape-tracked, console-summed, with real outboard reverbs and a small number of recurring color devices, not in-the-box productions with plug-in chains. We don't have a documented per-song plug-in list and should not fabricate one — Wilson's whole point is that there largely isn't one.

content: The instrumentation footprint on *Honeybear* and *Pure Comedy* is wider than a standard singer-songwriter record. Documented elements include strings (with arrangements by Paul Jacob Cartwright and Gabriel Noel on *Honeybear*; Bryars, Muhly, and Bartlett on *Pure Comedy*), horns, mandolin, congas, lap steel, clarinet, piano, mellotron-type sustained keys, and the standard rock-band drums/bass/electric guitar core [(I Love You, Honeybear — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Love_You,_Honeybear) [(Pure Comedy — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pure_Comedy). On *Honeybear* Wilson himself played most of the stringed instruments, while Tillman handled vocals and some drums; on *Pure Comedy* the playing was distributed across a tracked band. For ARLO, the retrieval cue is that "Father John Misty arrangement" usually means: an acoustic-guitar-or-piano foundation, a real string section, real horns, lap steel as a lyrical voice, and tasteful mandolin or clarinet color — not synthesizers, not pads, not programmed drums.

content: Within the corpus's hybrid aesthetic, the Tillman/Wilson axis is the lush-folk anchor opposite the Bon Iver processed-folk anchor: both treat the singer-songwriter form seriously, but Bon Iver routes voice through digital harmony rigs and stacks, while Father John Misty routes it through tube mics and real orchestras. The relationship to the Punch Brothers / Billy Strings acoustic-virtuosity anchor is partial — Wilson uses mandolin and acoustic textures, but as one color among many, not as the central instrument family. The relationship to the mk.gee DI-and-reamped-guitar anchor is essentially zero — there's almost no weird-guitar processing in these records, the electric guitars sound like amps in rooms. The relationship to LCD Soundsystem and Charli XCX is contrastive: Tillman/Wilson is the "real instruments, big arrangements, theatrical lyrics" pole; LCD and Charli are the "synthetic textures, machine pulse, blown-out maximalism" pole. When a user is pulling from both poles, ARLO should expect a tension between an organic Wilson-style rhythm section and a programmed Murphy/A.G. Cook-style top.

content: Geese formed in 2016 while the members were still in high school in New York City — split across two private schools, with Cameron Winter (vocals, keys, guitar) and Max Bassin (drums) at Brooklyn Friends School, and Dominic DiGesu (bass), Emily Green (guitar), and then-guitarist Foster Hudson at The Little Red School House & Elisabeth Irwin High School in Manhattan [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geese_(band)). The band's name comes from Green's nickname, "Goose." For the first several years they practiced and recorded in the basement of Bassin's family home in Fort Greene — a room they nicknamed "the Nest," built around recording gear gifted to Bassin by his family. When ARLO retrieves "the basement Geese record," the user almost certainly means *Projector*, recorded in that room during the band's senior year. A self-released early effort, *A Beautiful Memory* (July 13, 2018), predates the basement era and was issued before the band had a label deal — Winter has said in interviews he'd prefer fans not revisit those old high-school recordings [(Stereogum airport interview)](https://stereogum.com/2488636/cameron-winter-previews-warning-talks-geese-and-the-indie-complex-in-impromptu-airport-interview/news).

content:
The four-member touring lineup as of *Getting Killed* (2025) is:

- **Cameron Winter** — lead vocals, keyboards, guitar
- **Emily Green** — guitar
- **Dominic DiGesu** — bass (also credited with drums on *3D Country*)
- **Max Bassin** — drums
- **Sam Revaz** — touring keyboardist (2022–present, not a full member)

Former member **Foster Hudson** (second guitar, 2019–2023) was on both *Projector* and *3D Country* but departed in December 2023, after the *3D Country* cycle — *Getting Killed* is the first Geese studio album without him [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geese_(band)). For retrieval purposes: any "two-guitar Geese arrangement" reference belongs to the 2019–2023 window; the 2025 record is the four-piece.

content: *Projector* is Geese's second studio album and major-label debut, released October 29, 2021 on Partisan Records / Play It Again Sam [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Projector_(Geese_album)). It was tracked at "the Nest" from late 2019 into early 2020, while the band was still in high school, then sat finished for nearly two years before release. The credit chain is unusual and worth getting right: **Geese self-produced the record**, but Speedy Wunderground founder and Squid / black midi / Fontaines D.C. producer **Dan Carey mixed it**, with **Bernie Grundman** mastering. Carey is sometimes mis-credited as the producer in shorthand — he's not. The band's "live set-up" was the operating principle: Winter has said it was the first time they got everyone playing together in the room rather than overdubbing parts. Critically the record landed as a post-punk debut and pulled a Metacritic of 83 from eight reviews. Lead single "Disco" is the canonical entry point. If a user asks for "the angular early-Geese sound" or compares the band to Squid / black midi / Fontaines, the conversation belongs to *Projector*, not the later records.

content:
*3D Country*, released June 23, 2023 on Partisan / PIAS, is the record where Geese stops being a post-punk band [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_Country). It was produced by British producer **James Ford** (Arctic Monkeys, Depeche Mode, Shame, Simian Mobile Disco), recorded at **The Diamond Mine in Queens and Future Sounds**, mixed by **Beatriz Artola**, and mastered by **Matthew Colton**. The conceptual frame is a fever-dream cowboy narrative — an "uptight cowboy" wandering the desert after taking psychedelics, with reality and the concept of self unraveling — and the genre tags pile up: art rock, alternative country, blues rock, post-punk. String arrangements on select tracks come from **Katie Jacoby** (viola), **Tomoko Akaboshi** (violin), and **Alon Bisk** (cello). Singles: "Cowboy Nudes," "3D Country," "Mysterious Love," "I See Myself." Metacritic landed at 78; Pitchfork (Brady Gerber) gave it 6.8 and framed it as Geese "evolving from gritty post-punk into a proudly outrageous jam band" with "newfound emphasis on dynamics and space" [(Pitchfork review summary via search)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3D_Country).

The Ford collaboration is the load-bearing production story. The band did extensive pre-production for the first time — Emily Green's quote is *"We had more resources and it was like kids in a candy store"* — and Winter has explicitly named Ford's role as a stabilizing adult presence: *"I think we needed an adult presence in the room with us, just a grounding, British sort of 'I know what I'm doing' presence"* [(Radio X / Variety summary via search)](https://variety.com/2023/music/news/geese-band-brooklyn-interview-1235812170/). Ford pushed the band into "weirder margins" by encouraging extra takes and helped them streamline maximalist instincts into cohesive song shapes without sanding off the experimentation. The "Geese pivot record" reference always means *3D Country*.

provenance.section: *3D Country* (2023) — The Country/Cowboy Pivot

content:
*Getting Killed*, released September 26, 2025 on Partisan / PIAS, is the fourth Geese studio album and the breakthrough by critical consensus [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Getting_Killed). It was co-produced by the band with **Kenny Beats** (real name Kenneth Blume) and recorded over a ten-day, fourteen-hours-a-day sprint in January 2025 at **Blume's Putnam Hill studio in Los Angeles** while the LA wildfires were burning. Blume is best known for hip-hop production work; this is his most prominent rock-band credit to date. The collaboration began informally in mid-2024 when Blume noticed Geese merch and got curious, then introduced himself to the band at Austin City Limits Festival in October 2024 [(The FADER review)](https://www.thefader.com/2025/09/26/geese-getting-killed-review). What Winter has said about why it clicked: Blume's "enthusiasm for leaving imperfections intact," which Winter framed as a rare and liberating attitude.

The production approach pushed the rhythm section forward — Bassin's drumming has been called "maximum overdrive," with bass and drum performances tracked repeatedly until they could support the experimental textures layered on top. Much of the album came out of extended thirty-minute jams centered on repetitive grooves, which Bassin described as patterns that "feel almost like they don't end" — a useful retrieval anchor when users ask about Geese's relationship to motorik or trance-rock repetition. Sampling shows up too: Blume incorporated Ukrainian choir samples and what reviewers called "auxiliary production clattering" off Bassin's drums on "Taxes." Blume's own framing: *"They wanted these samples not to reinforce music that was already there"* — i.e., samples used as foreign objects, not as glue.

Guest contributors: **JPEGMAFIA** (additional vocals on "Trinidad"), **Nick Lee** (trombone), **Aaron Paris** (violin). Singles: "Taxes" (July 8, 2025), "Trinidad" (July 29, 2025), "100 Horses" (August 26, 2025), with "Au Pays du Cocaine" / "Cobra" following in February 2026. Genre tags broaden again — art rock, experimental rock, with influences from jazz, funk, noise, prog, and motorik repetition. Critical reception was the strongest of the band's career: a Metacritic of 89 ("universal acclaim"), #1 album of 2025 from both *Stereogum* and *The New Yorker*, and a 2026 Brit Award win for International Group. The FADER's review names Sonny Sharrock, Television, Radiohead, and Suicide as the reference field.

provenance.section: *Getting Killed* (2025) — The Kenny Beats Record

content: This is the cross-link that matters for ARLO retrieval. Cameron Winter releases music under two distinct identities — and the production aesthetics are not interchangeable. As Geese frontman he is one of four/five players in a live-tracked rock band that prizes rhythm-section physicality, guitar texture from Emily Green, and (on *Getting Killed*) hip-hop-adjacent sampling and groove repetition. His solo persona, captured on *Heavy Metal* (December 2024) and the follow-up single "Warning" (2026), is essentially a one-room piano-and-voice project with a deliberately retro arrangement vocabulary — different producer, different gear footprint, different vocal aesthetic. See `cameron-winter-heavy-metal-guitar-center-album.md` for the solo-record context; do not conflate. When a user references "Winter's baritone" they may mean either project, but "Winter's solo album" or "Winter's piano songs" specifically means *Heavy Metal*, while "Winter's band" or "the Brooklyn cowboy band" means Geese.

content: In a February 2026 impromptu airport interview with a Sydney TikToker, picked up by *Stereogum*, Winter offered a half-serious meta-framing that's worth knowing because users may reference it [(Stereogum)](https://stereogum.com/2488636/cameron-winter-previews-warning-talks-geese-and-the-indie-complex-in-impromptu-airport-interview/news). Asked what's next for Geese, Winter said: *"We go deeper into the sort of belly of whatever, you know, indie complex is shilling us right now."* Pressed on what the "indie complex" is, he said: *"Oh, it's so complex, so complex. Even I don't know how it works, why we've been chosen as the sort of main product."* Asked if the attention was a lot of pressure, he answered flatly: *"No."* The phrase has stuck as shorthand for the current critical-darling status Geese occupies — back-to-back top-of-year placements, Brit Award, festival headlining — without the band having had a true commercial breakout single. It's a useful retrieval flag for users discussing Geese-as-phenomenon vs. Geese-as-sound.

content:
A few load-bearing intersections for the hybrid aesthetic blending Bon Iver / LCD Soundsystem / Charli XCX / mk.gee / Billy Strings:

- **Repetition-as-form** — *Getting Killed*'s thirty-minute-jam compositional method, with grooves that "feel almost like they don't end," shares DNA with LCD Soundsystem's long-form repetition and motorik patience. Retrieve here when a user wants to think about how a small phrase can carry a long form.
- **Sample-as-foreign-object** — Blume's use of Ukrainian choir samples and auxiliary clatter on *Getting Killed*, deliberately *not* reinforcing what's already there, is a useful counterweight to the Charli-XCX-style sample-as-hook approach. Two opposite philosophies, both maximalist.
- **Live-tracked-in-a-room** — *Projector*'s basement approach is a usable analog for any home-studio user trying to capture a band feel without overdubbing every part. The Geese precedent is: track live, mix with an outside ear.
- **Genre-hopping as identity, not novelty** — *3D Country*'s cowboy/jam-band pivot is a model for ARLO users who worry that mixing acoustic-Americana (Billy Strings / Punch Brothers idioms) with art-rock or dance-punk will read as pastiche. Geese's answer: commit to the conceit, let the production producer ground it.

content: The single most useful frame for understanding how James Murphy makes LCD Soundsystem records is that he reverses where most rock producers spend money. The *guitars* are cheap on purpose, the *bass* is cheap on purpose, even the live drum kit is a single working unit rather than a rotated arsenal — and almost all of the budget, attention, and superstition lives in the synthesizer rack, the outboard signal chain, and the room itself. Multiple gear rundowns place "$100 Squier Telecasters" and "a 1960s Epiphone bass…purchased from eBay for $150" in Murphy's primary tracking lineup ([Mixdown Magazine — Gear Rundown: LCD Soundsystem](https://mixdownmag.com.au/features/rig-rundown-lcd-soundsystem/)), while the synth side of the room is filled with EMS, CS-60, EML and Powertran units that cost orders of magnitude more (see [LCD Synth Sound Design](./lcd-soundsystem-synth-sound-design.md)). The "cheap guitars, expensive synths" framing is a community paraphrase of this observable pattern — Murphy doesn't appear to use that exact phrase verbatim in any primary interview I could verify, so ARLO should describe it as *the cost-inversion stance* rather than quote it.

provenance.section: The Cost-Inversion Stance in One Sentence

provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: LCD Soundsystem, analog character, dance-punk production

content: The clearest Murphy quote about budget-instrument philosophy is about an Epiphone Les Paul Junior — not the Squier — and it reveals the underlying logic. Murphy told [Mixdown Magazine](https://mixdownmag.com.au/features/rig-rundown-lcd-soundsystem/) about choosing the cheap model and modifying it himself rather than buying the high-end Gibson: *"I bought the $70 model and then thought about what I wanted from it…So I had someone modify it, and it still cost me less than the fancy one."* The point is not that cheap gear is automatically better, it's that **the modification reveals the actual want.** When a producer reaches for a Gibson Les Paul they're buying a brand decision; when they reach for a $70 Junior and pay a tech to swap pickups, pot values and bridge, they have to articulate every component choice. That articulation is the producer-vs-consumer move. For ARLO: when a user wants "LCD-style guitar," the answer is almost never an expensive instrument — it's a cheap one in good hands, ideally one whose owner has thought hard about what they want from it.

content: The Squier Telecaster is the working guitar of choice across the LCD catalog according to [Mixdown's rig rundown](https://mixdownmag.com.au/features/rig-rundown-lcd-soundsystem/), which catalogs "$100 Squier Telecasters" in Murphy's tracking lineup. The aesthetic logic is consistent with the broader cost-inversion: a Telecaster's voicing — single-coil bridge bite, thin body, no humbucker mud — leaves room in the same midrange where Murphy is going to put a CS-60 synth-snare and an SH-101 bass. A heavier, fancier guitar (a Les Paul Custom, a Strat with hot pickups) would crowd the midrange where the synths live. The Squier is, in this sense, a *frequency-staging decision* dressed up as a budget decision. Cheap, clean, single-coil, narrow — exactly the slice the synth palette doesn't already occupy.

content: Murphy told [XLR8R](https://xlr8r.com/features/lcd-soundsystem-in-the-studio/) that his bass tracking philosophy is essentially monogamous: *"an old Epiphone bass that I use that has no name from the '60s, that I've recorded everything with through an old Ampeg Portaflex B-15 flip-top bass amp."* [Mixdown](https://mixdownmag.com.au/features/rig-rundown-lcd-soundsystem/) confirms the eBay-$150 purchase price and adds *"Basically bass is always the Epiphone into the Portaflex."* The B-15 is the Motown bass amp — a 15-inch driver in a sealed flip-top cabinet, naturally rolled-off above 4 kHz, with a syrupy mid-bass bump. For a band that runs SH-101 sub-basses, EML Electrocomp 100 deep-end textures, and Moog Taurus pedals against electric bass, having a single, narrow, well-understood electric bass voice that doesn't fight the synthetics is load-bearing. The Epiphone+B-15 chain *sounds like one instrument* in the mix, which is how it survives sitting next to four synthetic low-end sources.

provenance.section: The 1960s Epiphone Bass + Ampeg B-15 as the Single Bass Voice

content: The single most-cited LCD signal-chain detail is the drum capture path. [Mixdown's rig rundown](https://mixdownmag.com.au/features/rig-rundown-lcd-soundsystem/) describes it as: *"This mic usually goes into a Universal Audio preamp, into the DBX 165, into the LA-2A."* That is a three-stage character chain — a transformer-coupled preamp setting the input color, a fast VCA compressor (DBX 165, known for its "punch" and its program-dependent ratio response) doing the heavy lifting on transient shaping, and an LA-2A optical compressor doing the slow, glue-y program-level taming on the way out. The chain is *the LCD drum sound* as much as the 1957 Gretsch jazz kit is. The Vice piece quotes Juan MacLean's now-famous LA-2A line — *"I don't even use it as a compressor, I use it as an $8,000 distortion pedal"* — which captures the DFA attitude toward outboard ([Vice — DFA Records Has More Gear Than You](https://www.vice.com/en/article/kby4nz/dfa-records-has-more-gear-than-you)). The Purple Audio 1176 is also in the rack, used "exclusively for percussion and toms" per the same Vice piece.

provenance.section: The Drum-Bus Signal Chain — UA Preamp → DBX 165 → LA-2A
provenance.scope: artist-anchored — James Murphy's analog-synth-as-character production philosophy
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: LCD Soundsystem, analog character, dance-punk production

content: The DBX 165 is the workhorse of the chain. Vice paraphrases LCD/DFA drummer Pat Mahoney's collaborator Justin Millhiser saying the 165 is *"really practical"* because *"75% of the time I compress something, I want it to do what this does"* ([Vice — DFA Records Has More Gear Than You](https://www.vice.com/en/article/kby4nz/dfa-records-has-more-gear-than-you)). The 165 is a 1970s VCA compressor with program-dependent attack/release behavior and a famously aggressive transient response — it's the box that gives kick drums their characteristic LCD slam without sounding like SSL-bus compression. ARLO should be careful not to invent specific ratio or threshold values for the 165 chain — those weren't disclosed in the sources I could verify — but the *signal-path order* (UA preamp first, 165 in the middle, LA-2A last) is reliable. The 165 also gets vocal duty per the Vice piece, where it's described as "primarily used for vocals."

content: [Mixdown](https://mixdownmag.com.au/features/rig-rundown-lcd-soundsystem/) lists the LCD/Plantain ribbon-and-figure-8 mic palette as: **Beyerdynamic M160** (a short hypercardioid ribbon — famous on guitar amps and as a top-snare mic where you want figure-eight-style rejection), **Beyerdynamic M201** (a dynamic, not technically a ribbon, frequently lumped in because of similar use), **Coles 4033** (a long-ribbon side-address that Coles markets for broadcast/orchestral capture), and **RCA BK5** (a vintage broadcast ribbon — characterful, dark, slow). The Vice DFA gear piece adds the **Neumann TLM-193** as the studio's primary vocal condenser, with Juan MacLean stating *"I've used it for every vocal I've ever done"* and calling it *"very dark, unlike new condenser mics"* ([Vice](https://www.vice.com/en/article/kby4nz/dfa-records-has-more-gear-than-you)). What the sources do **not** disclose is which mic gets used where — i.e., whether the RCA BK5 specifically tracks LCD vocals or a snare bottom or a guitar cab. ARLO should assert the palette but hedge on placement: "Plantain's ribbon palette includes the M160, Coles 4033 and RCA BK5" is sourced; "the RCA BK5 is on Murphy's vocal" is **not** sourced and should not be claimed.

content: Murphy is on record describing his tracking kit as *"1957 Gretsch jazz drums that are what we record everything with, and they sound astonishing"* ([XLR8R — LCD Soundsystem In The Studio](https://xlr8r.com/features/lcd-soundsystem-in-the-studio/)) and elaborating to Mixdown that *"there's just no way to tune them or mic them to make them sound bad, which makes drum recording much easier."* This is a structurally important admission: when the source instrument is already great, the mic palette becomes a *coloring* choice rather than a *fixing* choice. The ribbons aren't being deployed to repair a bad-sounding kit — they're being deployed to ladle on character over an already-musical source. This frames the entire ribbon-mic palette discussion above. Cheap guitars work because they go into the room's character. Expensive ribbons work because they put a fingerprint on a kit that's already great.

content: [The Tape Op DFA/Plantain interview](https://tapeop.com/interviews/38/dfaplantain/) and [SonicScoop's "DFA Studios Opens Its Doors To Outsiders"](https://sonicscoop.com/2012/03/01/dfa-studios-opens-its-doors-to-outsiders/) document Plantain as a basement studio inside DFA's three-story walkup on 13th Street in Manhattan's West Village, originally built in Brooklyn and migrated to the DFA building. The signature architectural feature is the **car-elevator echo chamber**: a working car elevator in the building, fitted with a microphone, used as a variable-depth reverb chamber — *"You can raise or lower the elevator for different amounts of reverb. Most clap tracks, tambourine tracks, all the pianos were recorded using this unique space"* (Tape Op, as paraphrased in secondary coverage). The catch is acoustic: *"There's an air-conditioning unit on the roof that turns on and off, so you have to time it. You have to hope the vocal take is over before the air-conditioner kicks back on."* This is the kind of physical-room asset that no plug-in replaces — and it's why Murphy spent ~2.5 years living in the studio building during the early LCD records, per [Grammy.com's 15th-anniversary piece](https://www.grammy.com/news/lcd-soundsystem-15-how-james-murphy-created-his-singular-vision).

provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: LCD Soundsystem, analog character, dance-punk production

content: Plantain's console is a **John Oram BEQ 24** — an unusual choice, since Oram is a less canonical name than SSL, Neve, or API in commercial-studio circles. The signature move is that Murphy and Andrew Roberts of **Purple Audio** built a custom master section for it, retrofitting Purple's transformer-coupled summing and master-bus circuitry into the Oram frame ([SonicScoop — DFA Studios Opens Its Doors To Outsiders](https://sonicscoop.com/2012/03/01/dfa-studios-opens-its-doors-to-outsiders/)). Purple Audio's standalone master sections are documented on [Purple's product page](https://purpleaudio.com/products/master-section/), and Andrew Roberts is the founder of Purple, designing master-section retrofits for existing consoles since the late 1990s. The DFA Studios Facebook page itself describes the room as having *"a weird Oram BEQ 24 console…we made a custom master section with Purple"* ([DFA Studios Facebook](https://www.facebook.com/DFAstudios/photos/yes-thats-a-weird-oram-beq-24-console-yes-we-made-a-custom-master-section-with-p/181248165259868/)). The lesson for ARLO: Murphy's pattern is to start with an *interesting* but un-prestigious chassis and then bolt on the boutique components he actually cares about. Same logic as the $70 Junior, scaled up to a console.

content: The Plantain layout also includes a Live C room with reversible fabric/maple acoustic panels and a separate Live B "cedar room" for acoustic guitars and strings ([Tape Op DFA/Plantain](https://tapeop.com/interviews/38/dfaplantain/)). The recurring outboard reverb across DFA records is the **AKG BX-10** spring reverb, which Juan MacLean calls a unit that *"absolutely cannot be duplicated by software"* ([Vice — DFA Records Has More Gear Than You](https://www.vice.com/en/article/kby4nz/dfa-records-has-more-gear-than-you)), and which the Vice piece reports sits on "nearly all" of DFA's recordings. There is also a **Roland Space Echo RE-201** for tape-style delay and saturation, and a **Nakamichi Cassette Deck 2** that drums get resampled through for harmonic distortion. None of these are stock plug-in moves — they are physical reverb and tape sources whose sound depends on the specific unit's age and condition, which is exactly Murphy's preferred kind of asset.

content: [Tim Goldsworthy](https://tapeop.com/interviews/38/dfaplantain/) — Murphy's co-producer in the early DFA period — articulated the deeper DFA studio philosophy in his Tape Op interview: *"I like pieces of equipment with lots of knobs on it, which make crazy sounds and which you don't actually have to play anything on."* That single line captures why the Plantain rack is built around synths, ribbons, springs, and tape rather than around session players or virtuoso instruments. The gear *is the performance*. Murphy and Goldsworthy's idea of "playing" the studio is the act of patching, twisting, and committing to a chain — not the act of layering many takes from many players. This connects directly to LCD's tendency to record fewer, weirder layers rather than many clean ones.

content: Murphy is unusually explicit that he engineers his own records. He told [XLR8R](https://xlr8r.com/features/lcd-soundsystem-in-the-studio/) flatly: *"I don't need an engineer. I'm a pretty full-blown engineer."* He works alongside a programmer/assistant — Eric Broucek for the DFA era — but the engineering decisions and the production decisions are flowing through one head. That's structurally important for understanding why LCD records sound so *consistent*. The choice to send the kick mic into a UA preamp, then a DBX 165, then an LA-2A is a *signal-flow* decision, which is engineering; the choice to build the entire "Get Innocuous!" rhythm bed out of resampled CS-60 patches is a *part-writing* decision, which is production. Murphy is making both with the same hands. The collapse of these two roles is rare in studio practice and is one of the reasons LCD records sound like one person's brain.

provenance.section: "I'm a Pretty Full-Blown Engineer" — the Roles Murphy Wears
provenance.scope: artist-anchored — James Murphy's analog-synth-as-character production philosophy
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: LCD Soundsystem, analog character, dance-punk production

content: Across multiple interviews ([XLR8R — Cracked LCD](https://xlr8r.com/features/james-murphy-cracked-lcd/), [Grammy](https://www.grammy.com/news/lcd-soundsystem-15-how-james-murphy-created-his-singular-vision)) Murphy gives a usable working definition without naming it explicitly. **Engineering** is the question of *capture and processing*: which mic, which preamp, what's the gain stage, which compressor, what bus. **Production** is the question of *what gets played and what doesn't*: does this section need a 606 hat or a tambourine, does the vocal enter on bar 16 or bar 32, does the chorus drop the bass entirely. Murphy is *obsessive* about the second category and operates the first category as service to it. He told Grammy *"I lived in the studio"* for two and a half years during the early LCD records, and described overdubbing piano in the building's elevator shaft for "Never As Tired As When I'm Waking Up" — that's both an engineering decision (elevator shaft as reverb chamber) and a production decision (we need *this* sound on *this* song), executed simultaneously. For ARLO, the practical takeaway: when proposing an LCD-style move, propose both decisions together — never just "use this compressor" or just "write this part."

provenance.section: How Murphy Distinguishes Production from Engineering
provenance.scope: artist-anchored — James Murphy's analog-synth-as-character production philosophy
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: LCD Soundsystem, analog character, dance-punk production

content: Murphy told XLR8R: *"I always write vocals in the studio the day that I record them — it's kind of a rule. It has to start from zero and go to recorded finished vocal by the end of the day or else I'm a disaster"* ([XLR8R — Cracked LCD](https://xlr8r.com/features/james-murphy-cracked-lcd/)). This is technically a production rule, not an engineering one, but it informs the whole studio architecture: Plantain has to support write-and-track-in-one-day workflow, which means the engineering chain has to be **always ready, always committed, never neutral.** Murphy doesn't run the LA-2A in a flat-pass-through configuration so he can decide later; he commits to the chain so that the day's vocal lands on tape with the chain's character baked in. The cost-inversion stance feeds into this — cheap guitars and a default bass rig mean fewer instrument decisions to make on a vocal day, freeing brain budget for the production decisions that actually matter.

provenance.section: The Vocal-Day Rule and Why It's a Production Constraint

content: When a user invokes the LCD aesthetic, ARLO's default move set is: (1) propose the *cheap-tracking-instrument, expensive-signal-chain* split — Squier-class guitar, no-name Epiphone-class bass through a B-15-style flip-top amp, character ribbon mics into a clear preamp into a punchy VCA comp into a slow optical comp; (2) treat the room as an instrument — propose a real spring reverb or chamber send, not a plug-in; (3) collapse the producer and engineer roles in the user's own head — if they're asking about a compressor, also ask what part is being played and whether the part should exist; (4) prefer single, well-understood instrument voices (one bass, one kit) over rotated arsenals; (5) when in doubt, route the expensive money toward the signal chain and the synths (see [LCD Synth Sound Design](./lcd-soundsystem-synth-sound-design.md)) and the *cheap* money toward the guitars and the working bass. The aesthetic is *committed signal flow plus restrained part-writing*.

content: *The Tree of Forgiveness* is Prine's eighteenth and final studio album of original material, released April 13, 2018 on his own Oh Boy Records, and it is the first record of new songs he had released in thirteen years — the prior original-material LP was *Fair & Square* in 2005 [(The Tree of Forgiveness — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tree_of_Forgiveness). In the intervening period Prine had survived squamous cell carcinoma of the neck (surgery 1998) and lung cancer (surgery 2013), both of which permanently re-textured his voice — Rolling Stone described his "plainspoken tenor" as having taken on a quality that "creaks like a wide-plank old floor in winter" [(Rolling Stone review)](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/review-john-prine-keeps-finding-fresh-revelations-on-tree-of-forgiveness-628390/). For ARLO retrieval the load-bearing point is that the production brief on this record is essentially: *don't fight the weathered baritone, build a room around it*. Every other choice — sparse acoustic instrumentation, three-mic drum setups, live tracking, harmony vocals from younger acolytes — descends from that premise.

provenance.section: The 13-Year Gap and Why That Frames the Record
provenance.scope: artist-anchored — John Prine's *The Tree of Forgiveness* (2018), produced by Dave Cobb at RCA Studio A, Nashville, and the broader Cobb-led Nashville-revival production lineage it sits inside

content: The room itself is non-trivial to the sound. RCA Studio A at 30 Music Square West in Nashville was built in 1965 by Chet Atkins, Owen Bradley, and Harold Bradley, designed by RCA architect John E. Volkmann to record the large ensembles the Nashville Sound required — the live room is 75 by 45 feet with 25-foot ceilings, the largest tracking room in Nashville at the time it opened [(RCA Studio A — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Studio_A). Dolly Parton cut "Jolene" there; Elvis recorded gospel sides there. After RCA's tenancy ended the room cycled through Music City Music Hall, Javelina Recording Studios, and from 2002 Ben Folds' Grand Victor Sound. In 2014 a developer planned to demolish it for condos, and Folds' public campaign — joined by Mike Curb and local philanthropists who bought the building for around $5.6 million — saved it; it was added to the National Register of Historic Places in 2015 [(Nashville Scene)](https://www.nashvillescene.com/music/features/three-years-after-being-saved-studio-a-still-makes-an-impact/article_68f6aa0b-d892-5b40-b368-13d0b7bf32bc.html). Dave Cobb has leased the studio since 2016 as the base for his Low Country Sound imprint, and a $500,000 restoration was completed in October 2017, including replicated period RCA Victor signage on the exterior [(RCA Studio A — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/RCA_Studio_A). *Tree of Forgiveness* was tracked between July and December 2017, which means it was made in that room essentially the moment the restoration finished.

provenance.section: Dave Cobb's Tenancy of RCA Studio A
provenance.scope: artist-anchored — John Prine's *The Tree of Forgiveness* (2018), produced by Dave Cobb at RCA Studio A, Nashville, and the broader Cobb-led Nashville-revival production lineage it sits inside
provenance.aesthetic-stack-relevance: John Prine, Dave Cobb, Nashville-revival, American songcraft canon, sparse acoustic production

content: Cobb has talked openly about why Studio A is unusual to track in. In Tape Op he said of the live room, "No matter where I put them, it kind of sounds the same. It's bizarre" — meaning that mic placement is forgiving in a way most rooms aren't, which he reads as intentional acoustic design from the 1965 build [(Tape Op #122 — Dave Cobb)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/122/dave-cobb). For ARLO this is a useful concrete fact: the room itself is part of why Cobb-at-Studio-A productions sound consistent across artists. The control room now centers on a 32-channel API Legacy AXS console, with Cobb's personal Helios, Neve, and UA outboard brought in on top [(Mix Online — Dave Cobb Settles into Studio A)](https://www.mixonline.com/recording/profiles/dave-cobb-settles-in-to-rca-studio-a). The Helios is Cobb's prized piece — sourced from Love Studio in Finland — and he has described it as "the best console I've ever heard in my life. It sounds like a record, and that's with no EQ" [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/122/dave-cobb). Don't model an in-the-box modern Nashville sound for this album; model a 1965 room running through API + Helios + tape.

content: The documented Cobb method, which is the method *Tree of Forgiveness* was made with, has four moving parts. First, he records bands live in one room and refuses isolation: "I hate cutting separately. I can't stand it," with vocalists tracking live with the band because "their pitch is way better" with the band in the room [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/122/dave-cobb). Second, he keeps tape rolling continuously, including during run-throughs, because "that's when you usually get your best vocal performance" — usually "between three takes, you got it" [(Universal Audio — Champion of Nashville's New Sound)](https://www.uaudio.com/blog/dave-cobb-nashvilles-new-sound/). Third, he tracks roughly 70% to tape — a Studer A80 figures heavily in his rig — and on past records like Sturgill Simpson's *Metamodern Sounds in Country Music* he printed reverbs and delays live, e.g. a Studer A80 1/4-inch tape machine going into a Studio Technologies Ecoplate III, rather than adding them in mix [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/122/dave-cobb). Fourth, his miking is famously minimal: three mics on drums (kick, snare, overhead — the Neumann U87 frequently as the overhead, positioned low near the drummer's head), Coles 4038 as a primary vocal mic, Spectra Sonics 610 compressor "just barely tickling" the meter [(Tape Op)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/122/dave-cobb). For ARLO the operative descriptor on this kind of session is "fast and analog" — not because Cobb specifies tape speeds publicly, but because the *workflow* is fast: live cuts, three-takes-max, tape rolling, minimal mics, mix-as-you-go.

content: The core band is Prine's longtime road band augmented by Cobb himself. Lead vocal and acoustic guitar are Prine. Electric guitar is Jason Wilber (Prine's longtime band guitarist); fiddle is Amanda Shires; bass is Dave Jacques; drums are Kenneth Blevins. Cobb plays acoustic and 12-string guitar plus mellotron, claps, and kazoo across the record. Brandi Carlile sings harmony on three tracks. Jason Isbell plays electric guitar on one track and slide guitar and background vocals on two others. Amanda Shires sings background vocals in addition to her fiddle parts [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tree_of_Forgiveness). That guest list — Isbell, Shires, Carlile — is itself a piece of cultural mapping: these are the singer-songwriters of the Nashville/Americana revival explicitly framing Prine as their lineage, on a Prine record produced by the producer (Cobb) who made *Southeastern*, *Traveller*, and *By the Way, I Forgive You*.

content: Cobb is one of the central producers of the 2010s Nashville revival. His discography by the time of *Tree of Forgiveness* already included Sturgill Simpson's *High Top Mountain* (2013) and *Metamodern Sounds in Country Music* (2014), Jason Isbell's *Southeastern* (2013) and several follow-ups, Chris Stapleton's 5x-platinum *Traveller* (2015, co-produced and tracked at RCA Studio A as part of the campaign that saved the building), and Brandi Carlile's *By the Way, I Forgive You* (2018) [(Dave Cobb — Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dave_Cobb). He later co-anchored The Highwomen project with Carlile, Shires, Maren Morris, and Natalie Hemby. For ARLO the retrieval point is that when a user asks about "Cobb-produced Nashville sound," they are asking about a coherent stylistic movement — analog, live-tracked, three-mic-drums, no-vocal-isolation, singer-forward, often using Studio A as the literal physical room — and *Tree of Forgiveness* is the elder-statesman entry in that catalog. Prine is the songwriter the rest of the Cobb roster acknowledges as origin.

content: The songs were written before tracking. Prine has said he checked into an Omni hotel in Nashville to finish the album because "after 45 years on the road, I just can conduct myself better in a hotel" [(Uproxx — Tree of Forgiveness interview)](https://uproxx.com/music/john-prine-tree-of-forgiveness-interview/). His writing partners on the record are Pat McLaughlin (longtime Prine co-writer; Nashville journeyman whose cuts include Alan Jackson, Trisha Yearwood, Gary Allan) and Dan Auerbach of The Black Keys, who by 2017 was running Easy Eye Sound and had become a Nashville fixture. In one stretch Prine and Auerbach (with McLaughlin) wrote six songs in two days; two of those made the record, including "Caravan of Fools" [(Uproxx)](https://uproxx.com/music/john-prine-tree-of-forgiveness-interview/). Auerbach himself confirmed on X at release that he co-wrote both "Caravan of Fools" and "Boundless Love" [(Dan Auerbach on X, April 2018)](https://x.com/danauerbach/status/983349530069536768). Prine described having to rework "Boundless Love" after the initial co-write because the lyric didn't feel like him yet — he called Auerbach and said, in his framing, that he needed to "John Prine it up" [(Uproxx)](https://uproxx.com/music/john-prine-tree-of-forgiveness-interview/). That's a useful idiom for ARLO: songs come back from Nashville co-writes feeling generically Nashville, and the final pass is making them feel idiosyncratically authored.

content: Both "Knockin' on Your Screen Door" and "Summer's End" are Prine/McLaughlin co-writes [(Rolling Stone — Screen Door premiere)](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-country/hear-john-prines-ambling-new-song-knockin-on-your-screen-door-119890/). "Knockin' on Your Screen Door" is an uptempo folk song carrying a downbeat narrator — a lonely, broke man whose only listed possession is a George Jones 8-track tape — and it earned Prine a Grammy nomination for Best American Roots Song. "Summer's End" is a tender ballad framed by Rolling Stone as "an open-armed invitation home to a grown child, perhaps, amidst images of inevitable loss," and it won Best Americana Song at the 2019 Americana Music Honors & Awards and was later read in the post-Prine context as a quiet opioid-epidemic lament without ever naming it as such [(Rolling Stone)](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/review-john-prine-keeps-finding-fresh-revelations-on-tree-of-forgiveness-628390/). Both songs sit in a country-folk register Cobb dresses sparingly — acoustic guitar foreground, fiddle and harmony vocals as the color, drums kept low and brushy.

content: "Caravan of Fools" is the song on the record that most obviously bears Auerbach's fingerprints. Critics and the Uproxx interview describe it as an apocalyptic blues lament — its imagery centers on distant drumming, the pounding of hooves, and a procession decked in shiny jewels [(Uproxx)](https://uproxx.com/music/john-prine-tree-of-forgiveness-interview/). For ARLO modeling purposes the relevant point is that *Tree of Forgiveness* is not monochromatic: most of the album lives in country-folk warmth, but "Caravan of Fools" and "Boundless Love" pull in a darker, Easy-Eye-Sound, fuzzed-blues posture that's Auerbach's natural register. Cobb mixes the two registers without smoothing them flat. The track later got further visibility via a Dan Auerbach cover and a sync placement in *Yellowstone* season 4 [(Whiskey Riff)](https://www.whiskeyriff.com/2023/04/13/on-this-date-john-prine-releases-final-studio-album-the-tree-of-forgiveness/).

content: "I Have Met My Love Today" features Brandi Carlile on harmony [(JohnPrine.com press)](https://yougotgold.johnprine.com/press/john-prine-returns-to-songwriting-jaunty-and-dark-on-the-tree-of-forgiveness-). The arrangement is among the sparsest on the record — acoustic guitar, fiddle, restrained rhythm section, two voices. The retrieval handle for ARLO is the deliberate generational pairing: a weathered Prine lead with Carlile's much-higher and much-cleaner harmony sitting above it. This is the same pattern Cobb uses elsewhere — pairing a singular character voice with younger, technically pristine harmony singers (see his Stapleton/Morgane Stapleton and Isbell/Shires work) — and it's a load-bearing texture of the Cobb-Nashville-revival sound writ large.

content: The closer is the song most people now associate with the record. Thematically it is a self-aware afterlife monologue, played with the band-plus-friends raised to a party — claps, kazoo, gang vocals, a deliberately ramshackle feel. Cobb's production note here is to *not* polish: keep the room sound, keep the gang of friends audible, keep the kazoo in [(Wikipedia)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Tree_of_Forgiveness). Rolling Stone characterized the song as a "mix of punchlines, sweet sentimentality and looming void" [(Rolling Stone)](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-album-reviews/review-john-prine-keeps-finding-fresh-revelations-on-tree-of-forgiveness-628390/). The album's other notable themes — mortality, war, drugs, addiction — recur across Prine's catalog and surface again here, but ARLO should describe these themes analytically and never reproduce Prine's lyrics verbatim. Title-level references are sufficient.
