content: A structural distinction Pattison teaches across [*Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*](https://books.google.com/books/about/Songwriting_Essential_Guide_to_Lyric_For.html?id=0XESAQAAQBAJ) and his Berklee courses: the **refrain** and the **chorus** are different structural objects. A refrain is a single repeated line (typically containing the title) attached to the end of each verse — the AABA tradition (think "Yesterday," "Something," "Norwegian Wood"). A chorus is a separate harmonic and lyrical section that repeats — the verse-chorus tradition that dominates contemporary pop. Both contain the title; both serve as the title's repeated return. The craft difference: a single-line refrain must do all its work in one line, so the line must be saturated with the song's argument. A chorus has multiple lines, so the title can be earned by the chorus's other lines rather than by the title-line alone. The workbench implication: when revising, identify which structure the draft is using, and judge the title-line against that structure's demands. A refrain-line judged against a chorus's standard will seem too compressed; a chorus-line judged against a refrain's standard will seem under-saturated.

content: A claim drawn from Switched On Pop's analysis of contemporary pop on the [Switched On Pop podcast](https://switchedonpop.com/episodes) and consistent with Webb's *Tunesmith* on the older tradition: **the strongest titles contain a hook of their own — a sonic, rhythmic, or imagistic compression that makes the title memorable independent of the music**. "Bohemian Rhapsody" hooks on the unexpected pairing of "bohemian" (foreign, exotic) with "rhapsody" (a musical-form word). "Shake It Off" hooks on the rhythmic compression of three monosyllables. "Bad Guy" hooks on the comma between "duh" and the title. The title-as-hook test: does the title, spoken aloud without the melody, have a sonic shape the listener wants to repeat? If yes, the title is doing its own work; the refrain only needs to deliver it. If no, the title needs the melody to carry it, which means the melody must be strong enough to compensate. Both are valid; the craft is knowing which case applies.

provenance.section: The Hook Inside the Title

content: A pattern observable across the canon and named explicitly in [Pattison's verse-development teaching](https://www.patpattison.com/developing-verse-ideas): when the title repeats across the song, each repetition should land *slightly differently* because the verse content before it has shifted what the title means. The first chorus of "By the Time I Get to Phoenix" arrives after verse 1 (he's leaving, she's just waking); the second arrives after verse 2 (more time has passed, she's at lunch); the third arrives after verse 3 (night, she's calling). The title-line is identical; the *weight* the listener gives it changes because the context has changed. Pattison's phrase for the effect: "Each refrain takes its color from what it attaches to." The craft move on revision: read the title-line as it appears after verse 1, then after verse 2, then after verse 3 (and bridge if present). If the line feels identical in weight each time, the verses are not doing developmental work; they are restating rather than developing. The fix is at the verses, not the refrain.

content: A specific Webb-and-Davis move discussed in *Tunesmith* and [Sheila Davis's *The Craft of Lyric Writing*](https://www.amazon.com/Craft-Lyric-Writing-Sheila-Davis/dp/0898792827): the **delayed-meaning title**, where the title's full meaning is not clear at first hearing and only resolves by the last chorus or bridge. The classic case is a title whose surface meaning shifts under the verses — "Wichita Lineman" reads at first as a job description and reveals across the song as a metaphor for distance and longing. The delayed-meaning title trades immediate accessibility for the payoff of recognition on repeat listening. The craft trap: a delayed-meaning title that *never* resolves reads as obscure; a delayed-meaning title that resolves too early loses its power. The Webb-trained instinct: the title's full meaning should arrive in the bridge or final chorus, when the listener has accumulated enough verse content to receive it. The discipline is patience — trusting the listener to hold the question across the verses without spelling out the answer until the song has earned it.

provenance.section: The Title That Earns Itself by the End

content: The hardest diagnosis on a stalled song: **the title is the problem**. Signals that the title rather than the verses is the issue: the verses are strong but the chorus feels small; the chorus melody is strong but the title-words feel arbitrary; multiple revision passes on the chorus do not lift it; the writer hesitates when asked to say the title aloud. Pattison's diagnostic move, drawn from his "essential question" teaching: try titling the draft with five alternative titles, written in the margin without judging them. If one of them produces a small jolt of recognition — *that's the song* — the original title was wrong and the new one is the song's actual argument. The verses may then need light revision to align with the new title, or none at all. The reverse move is also valid: if the title is right and the verses are wrong, the diagnostic produces the opposite jolt — the alternative titles all feel worse, and the writer realizes the verses have drifted from the title's claim. Either way, the title-vs-verses diagnostic catches misalignment that line-level revision cannot.

provenance.section: When the Title Is Wrong — The Diagnostic
provenance.canonical-references: Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Switched On Pop episodes on hook craft (Sloan & Harding); Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: A specific craft point Pattison teaches in revision: the **line immediately before the title-line** does disproportionate work. That line is the handoff — it must deliver the listener into the title's stress pattern, harmonic resolution, and emotional register. A weak setup line dampens the title's arrival; a strong setup line makes the title detonate. The workbench test: read the setup line and the title-line as a couplet, ignoring the rest of the chorus. Does the couplet feel like a unit? Does the setup line make the title-line necessary? If the couplet is the strongest two lines of the chorus, the chorus is structurally sound. If the couplet feels weaker than other chorus lines, the title is being undersold by its own handoff. The fix is usually at the setup line, not the title. Webb's craft instinct, evident across his catalog: the line before the title is often the line he revised most, because that line is the title's launchpad.

provenance.section: The Last Line Before the Title

content: A practical heuristic for the working writer. Signals that refrain-or-title construction is the likely diagnosis. **(1)** "the chorus is flat" — when the chorus's other elements are strong (melody, harmony, arrangement) but the chorus does not land, the title is often the cause. **(2)** "I don't know what to call this song" — the canonical signal that the song's argument has not yet clarified. **(3)** "the title feels generic" — usually a sign the title is summarizing a feeling rather than naming a specific situation. **(4)** "the chorus doesn't feel earned" — covered in `corpus/songwriting/lyric/theme-consistency-checks.md`; the title is usually the focal point of the unearned-chorus diagnosis. **(5)** "the second chorus feels the same as the first" — the refrain is not accumulating weight across the song, usually because the verses are not developing. For each signal, ARLO's first move is the title-as-test pass: ask the user to say the title aloud, then ask whether the verses make that title-line necessary. If the user hesitates on either question, the diagnosis is confirmed.

content: The amateur's belief about songwriting is that the song arrives in a flash and either works or doesn't. The Pattison / working-songwriter consensus is the opposite: **the first draft is the seed; the revision is the craft.** Pattison repeats this across *Writing Better Lyrics* and Berklee lectures, as recorded in the [Sound on Sound interview](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/pat-pattison-writing-better-lyrics). The myth of the spontaneous masterpiece is exactly that — a myth — and the working canon of revision-heavy songwriters confirms it: Dylan, Cohen, Joni Mitchell, Springsteen, Sufjan, Aimee Mann, Lucinda Williams, Phoebe Bridgers. Each has multiple-draft archives or interview testimony about months- or years-long revision arcs on songs the public hears as effortless. This file is named for Dylan because his revision archive is the most extensively catalogued and verifiable, but the discipline he embodies is general. The mission-relevance for ARLO: a stuck musician often believes "the inspiration phase is over and I can't fix this." The truth is that the fixing phase is where the song actually gets made.

content: The [Bob Dylan Archive](https://www.utulsa.edu/academics/colleges/oxley-college-of-health-natural-sciences/our-departments/center-for-american-research/bob-dylan-archive/) at the University of Tulsa's Helmerich Center for American Research, opened to scholars in 2016 after Dylan sold his papers to the George Kaiser Family Foundation, contains roughly **6,000 items including notebooks, draft lyrics, session tapes, and correspondence**. Scholars including Clinton Heylin and Sean Wilentz have published partial accounts of what the archive contains. The headline finding, repeated across the [New York Times coverage](https://www.nytimes.com/2016/03/02/arts/music/bob-dylan-archive-tulsa-oklahoma.html) and the [Wall Street Journal feature](https://www.wsj.com/articles/bob-dylan-archive-opens-1456891202) at the archive's opening: **the same Dylan song often exists in five or more drafted versions**, with verses written, cut, recombined, and rewritten across notebooks and across sessions. The archive corrects the romantic myth: songs like *"Like a Rolling Stone,"* *"Tangled Up in Blue,"* and *"Idiot Wind"* arrived through documented multi-stage revision processes, not single inspired sittings.

content: The most-discussed Dylan revision artifact is *"Tangled Up in Blue."* Dylan recorded the song for *Blood on the Tracks* (1975) in September 1974, then [scrapped most of the album and re-recorded in Minneapolis in December](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blood_on_the_Tracks). The Minneapolis version is the one released. He then continued to revise the lyric in performance, **substantially rewriting verses for the 1984 *Real Live* version**, swapping point of view (third-person to first-person and back), reordering events, and changing key images. Per Wilentz's *Bob Dylan in America* and the [Pitchfork *Blood on the Tracks* feature](https://pitchfork.com/features/article/9999-bob-dylan-blood-on-the-tracks/), the song exists in at least four distinct lyric versions Dylan has performed publicly, plus the notebook drafts in the Tulsa archive. The lesson: a song the listener thinks of as fixed is, for the working writer, a movable target for as long as they keep playing it. Revision does not end at release.

content: Dylan's published statements about revision are characteristically oblique but consistent. In Paul Zollo's [*Songwriters on Songwriting*](https://www.amazon.com/Songwriters-Songwriting-Revised-Paul-Zollo/dp/030680777X) interview — the most-cited primary source on Dylan's process — Dylan describes writing as a process of "uncovering" lines that already exist, then "putting them in the right order." Cameron Crowe's [*Biograph* liner notes](https://www.bobdylan.com/albums/biograph/) from 1985 contain Dylan's own commentary on song after song, repeatedly noting that finished songs began as fragments, were set aside, and were later combined with unrelated fragments to find their form. Dylan's *Chronicles, Volume One* (2004) describes notebooks full of half-songs awaiting their other half. The pattern across primary sources: **Dylan treats the notebook as a reservoir, not a draft.** Songs assemble from accumulated fragments through revision rather than springing whole from a single sitting.

provenance.section: What Dylan Says About His Own Process

content: Pattison's working revision principle, repeated in *Writing Better Lyrics* and audible across the Dylan archive: **each line must earn its place in the song.** The test is not "is the line good in isolation" but "does the line do work this song needs done?" A line can be brilliant and still need to be cut because it does not serve the song the writer is actually making. Pattison's diagnostic — paraphrased in the [Berklee Online prosody article](https://online.berklee.edu/takenote/prosody-in-music-and-songwriting/): for each line, ask: (1) what does this line tell the listener that the previous line did not? (2) what does this line set up that the next line needs? (3) if I cut this line, does the song collapse, or does it tighten? Lines that fail all three should be cut. The Dylan archive contains dozens of cases of brilliant fragments that did not survive into the released versions because they did not earn their place in the final structure.

provenance.section: The "Every Line Earns Its Place" Rule
provenance.canonical-references: *The Bob Dylan Archive* (University of Tulsa, Helmerich Center for American Research); Cameron Crowe's liner notes to *Biograph* (1985); David Hajdu, *Positively 4th Street* (2001); Sean Wilentz, *Bob Dylan in America* (2010); Pat Pattison's revision chapters in *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting* (Dylan interview)

content: The most-cited Pattison revision technique, named in [*Writing Better Lyrics*](https://www.amazon.com/Writing-Better-Lyrics-Pat-Pattison/dp/1582975779) and elaborated across Berklee lectures: the **line-by-line pass** is the smallest unit of revision and the most rigorous. The writer takes one line at a time and asks: (1) is the concrete-noun and action-verb count high enough (see C1)? (2) is the line's rhyme type matching the section function (see C4)? (3) does the line's syllable count and stress pattern match the prosodic demand of the section (see C5)? (4) is this the strongest available verb? (5) is there a stronger noun? (6) is this the most-economical phrasing or are there filler words ("just," "really," "kind of")? The pass is slow, deliberate, and exhausting. It is also the difference between a draft and a song. Pattison teaches that one line-by-line pass per draft is non-negotiable.

provenance.section: The Line-by-Line Pass
provenance.canonical-references: *The Bob Dylan Archive* (University of Tulsa, Helmerich Center for American Research); Cameron Crowe's liner notes to *Biograph* (1985); David Hajdu, *Positively 4th Street* (2001); Sean Wilentz, *Bob Dylan in America* (2010); Pat Pattison's revision chapters in *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting* (Dylan interview)

content: The line-by-line pass operates at the smallest scale; the **verse-by-verse pass** operates at the song-architecture scale. The question per verse: **does this verse develop the previous one, or does it merely restate it?** A second verse that recapitulates the first is the most-common amateur failure (covered in detail in stall file B2). Pattison's rule, paraphrased from Berklee teaching: each verse should advance the song's narrative, emotional, or sensory progression by at least one substantial step. The diagnostic: write a one-sentence summary of each verse. If the summaries are interchangeable, the verses are not earning their separation. The Dylan archive contains evidence of this exact pass — verses written, judged redundant against neighbors, and replaced with verses that advance the song. The pass requires zooming out from the line and asking what each chunk is contributing.

provenance.section: The Verse-by-Verse Pass
provenance.canonical-references: *The Bob Dylan Archive* (University of Tulsa, Helmerich Center for American Research); Cameron Crowe's liner notes to *Biograph* (1985); David Hajdu, *Positively 4th Street* (2001); Sean Wilentz, *Bob Dylan in America* (2010); Pat Pattison's revision chapters in *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting* (Dylan interview)

content: A move shared across Pattison's teaching, Lucinda Williams's [Sodajerker interview](https://www.sodajerker.com/), Aimee Mann's working practice, and Dylan's own kitchen-table revision habit per multiple biographers: **read the draft aloud, slowly, and mark every false note.** A false note is a line that the writer stumbles on, that does not sound like something a person would say, that breaks the song's tonal frame, or that the writer is faintly embarrassed to read out loud. The body knows before the conscious mind does. The pen marks the line; the writer does not stop to fix it; the read-through continues. After the full read, the marked lines get rewritten. The discipline is not to over-think during the read-through — the goal is to surface the false notes, not to immediately solve them. The body's flinch is the diagnostic; the rewriting is downstream.

provenance.section: Read Aloud, Mark the False Notes
provenance.canonical-references: *The Bob Dylan Archive* (University of Tulsa, Helmerich Center for American Research); Cameron Crowe's liner notes to *Biograph* (1985); David Hajdu, *Positively 4th Street* (2001); Sean Wilentz, *Bob Dylan in America* (2010); Pat Pattison's revision chapters in *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting* (Dylan interview)

content: Pattison warns about this explicitly in *Writing Better Lyrics*, and every working songwriter who revises heavily reports the same trap. **A draft can be revised until the life is out of it.** The signs: the lines are technically perfect but feel airless; the emotional intent has been polished off; the song reads as competent but inert. The cause is usually a draft revised too many times in a single sitting, where each pass strips a layer of rawness that the song needed. The countermove, per Pattison and per the working consensus: **time between passes**. Revise. Set the draft down for at least a day, ideally a week. Revise again. The intervening time gives the writer fresh ears and prevents the cumulative over-polishing that destroys a draft. Aimee Mann reports similar discipline in [her Sodajerker episode](https://www.sodajerker.com/) — sitting on drafts for weeks before deciding what to cut.

provenance.section: The Trap of Over-Revision
provenance.canonical-references: *The Bob Dylan Archive* (University of Tulsa, Helmerich Center for American Research); Cameron Crowe's liner notes to *Biograph* (1985); David Hajdu, *Positively 4th Street* (2001); Sean Wilentz, *Bob Dylan in America* (2010); Pat Pattison's revision chapters in *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting* (Dylan interview)

content: A practical schedule. **(1) First draft session** — write to completion, do not revise within the session. **(2) Wait at least 24 hours.** **(3) Second session** — read aloud, mark false notes, do not yet rewrite. **(4) Wait again, ideally a few days.** **(5) Third session** — line-by-line pass, fixing the false notes. **(6) Wait a week.** **(7) Fourth session** — verse-by-verse pass, asking whether each verse develops the previous. **(8) Wait again.** **(9) Read aloud cold, with fresh ears, and ask: would a stranger think this is one song?** The wait times are doing real work — the writer's ear refreshes between passes, and lines that seemed essential in pass 1 reveal themselves as filler in pass 4. This is the discipline the Dylan archive documents: songs treated as objects worth returning to, not single sittings to be defended. Lucinda Williams famously sat on lyrics for years; her perfectionism is documented in [her *Car Wheels on a Gravel Road* sessions](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Car_Wheels_on_a_Gravel_Road), which she re-recorded multiple times across a six-year process.

The pairing is intentional. Revision without material is unproductive; material without revision is a notebook full of fragments. The Dylan practice is the loop between them.

content: Three patterns this discipline corrects. **(1) Single-pass syndrome** — the writer drafts once, calls it done, and is surprised when the song doesn't connect with listeners. The fix is the multi-pass schedule above. **(2) Revision-as-defense** — the writer revises only to remove lines they're embarrassed by, not to make the song stronger. The fix is reframing: revision is offensive (the song is improving), not defensive (the writer is protecting their reputation). **(3) Revision-until-dead** — the writer revises so many times in such close succession that the song's life is polished off. The fix is the time-between-passes discipline. The Dylan archive contains evidence of all three failures in early-career notebooks, and evidence of mature practice that avoids them. Revision is not the opposite of inspiration; it is the discipline that lets inspiration's first products mature into songs.

content: The practical question every revising songwriter eventually faces. **Three honest signals that a draft is done.** (1) The line-by-line pass produces no new changes — every change you try makes the song worse, not better. (2) The verse-by-verse pass shows each verse advancing the previous, with no redundancies. (3) The aloud-read produces no flinches. **If all three are clear, ship it.** The reverse — refusing to ship a draft that passes all three because the writer believes there must be a better version somewhere — is the demo trap (stall file B4). The working consensus across Pattison, Mann, Williams, and the Dylan-via-biographer accounts: at some point, the song is done, and continuing to revise is now harming, not helping. Recognizing that point is itself a craft skill. For ARLO's purposes, the discipline of revision and the discipline of shipping are two halves of the same finishing practice.

provenance.section: When to Stop Revising

content: "Show don't tell" is the most-quoted maxim in English-language songwriting craft, and the easiest to misapply. In Pat Pattison's working framing — repeated across *Writing Better Lyrics* and his Berklee lectures and recorded in the [Berklee Online "Prosody" overview](https://online.berklee.edu/takenote/prosody-in-music-and-songwriting/) and the [Sound on Sound interview](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/pat-pattison-writing-better-lyrics) — the principle is mechanical, not mystical. **Concrete nouns and action verbs activate the listener's senses; abstractions slide off them.** A line that names *a screen door, a kitchen, a Tuesday* gives the listener something to picture. A line that names *love, sadness, freedom* gives them a category. Categories don't land emotionally; instances do. This is a school of thought (Pattison teaches it; so does Sheila Davis; so do Aimee Mann, Lucinda Williams, and John Prine practice it) — not a universal rule, and not the only way to write a good lyric. But for a stuck musician revising a draft, it is the single highest-leverage diagnostic in the kit.

provenance.section: The Principle, Named Honestly
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: Three working writers anchor this school in different American idioms. **Aimee Mann** — across her *Magnolia* soundtrack work and the *Whatever* / *Bachelor No. 2* records — builds whole songs out of specific household objects and overheard speech. In her [Sodajerker on Songwriting episode](https://www.sodajerker.com/), she describes starting from a concrete image and refusing to let the verse "lift off into generality." **Lucinda Williams** — *Car Wheels on a Gravel Road* is the textbook — names roads, cars, weather, and brand-name food until the song reads like a deposition. The album's title track stacks "Sittin' in the kitchen," "screen door slams," "Loretta singin' on the radio" — every line is something you can point at. **John Prine** — in his Paul Zollo interview in *Songwriters on Songwriting* — talks about writing what the eye sees first, what the ear hears next, and never naming the feeling. *Sam Stone*'s "There's a hole in Daddy's arm where all the money goes" tells you about addiction without using the word. Naming this school matters: this is not "the right way to write." It is the school that prizes pictorial precision, and ARLO should retrieve it by name when the user is working in or adjacent to that tradition.

provenance.section: The Aimee Mann / Lucinda Williams / John Prine School
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: A working revision pass Pattison teaches in *Writing Better Lyrics* — paraphrased in [Berklee Press summaries](https://berkleepress.com/) and the [iZotope object-writing guide](https://www.izotope.com/en/learn/object-writing-your-secret-to-vivid-song-lyrics) — is to read each line and ask: **does this line contain a concrete noun, an action verb, and another concrete noun?** Not as a hard rule, but as a smell test. *"She slammed the screen door"* passes (she / slammed / screen door). *"She felt so sad"* fails (no concrete noun, no action verb — "felt" is stative). *"Love is a battlefield"* passes only because both abstractions get pulled into the concrete by the metaphor — and is one reason that song works despite the high abstraction count. The diagnostic isn't "count nouns and verbs." It's "after I read this line, can I draw anything?" If the answer is no, the line is telling, not showing.

provenance.section: The Noun-Verb-Noun Diagnostic
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: Pattison's second revision move, recorded across his books and Sound on Sound interview, is the **context-stripping test**: cover the surrounding lines and read the candidate line cold. If the line still produces an image or a feeling on its own, it's earning its place. If it only "works" because the listener already knows what the song is about, it is a placeholder you wrote when you couldn't think of the real line. The test is brutal — most first-draft lines fail it — and that is the point. The Aimee Mann / Williams / Prine school passes this test by default because every line is anchored in a thing. The test also flags the worst first-draft tic in English-language songwriting: the **placeholder emotion line** ("and I just feel so lost") that the writer intended to replace and forgot to. Run the cover-the-context pass on every chorus you have ever written and you will find at least one.

provenance.section: "Test the Line Without Context"
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: The concrete-noun fixation under-discusses the verb. **Action verbs do the same job nouns do; stative verbs ("is," "feels," "seems," "becomes") leak the energy out of a line.** Compare *"she walks the dog at sunrise"* with *"she's a person who has a dog."* The first earns the image; the second tells you about her. Per the [Berklee Take Note article](https://online.berklee.edu/takenote/prosody-in-music-and-songwriting/), Pattison flags "to be" verbs as the most frequent first-draft offender. A useful revision sweep: highlight every "is / was / am / are / were / be / been / being" in the draft and ask whether a stronger verb is available. Often the line is salvageable; sometimes the whole line goes. Prine's *"There's a hole in Daddy's arm"* uses "is" — but "is" is doing concrete locative work (there is a hole; it is in this place) rather than the abstract identity-claim work it does in *"I am sad."* The distinction is worth keeping.

provenance.section: The Action-Verb Half of the Move

content: The hardest line in popular songwriting to write well is **the one that names the emotion**. *Love, sadness, freedom, lonely, broken, lost, alone* — these words carry no information because the listener has to import their own definition. They are not banned. The school's actual rule, paraphrased from Pattison's teaching and audible in Mann/Williams/Prine practice: **abstract emotion words earn their place when surrounded by enough concrete detail that the abstraction lands as a summary rather than a substitute.** Prine's *"It's a half an inch of water and you think you're gonna drown"* earns its abstract conclusion in the same song because the verses are anchored in concrete agricultural decline. Joni Mitchell can write "I really don't know love at all" at the end of *Both Sides Now* because she spent two full verses on clouds and circus rides first. The trap is using the abstract word *instead* of doing the concrete work. When ARLO sees a draft with three abstraction words in four lines, that's the diagnostic signal.

provenance.section: The Abstract-Emotion-Word Trap
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: A concrete noun is not automatically alive. *Roses, rain, fire, heart, road, stars, wings* — these are concrete in the dictionary sense (you can picture them) but **so over-used that the picture they produce is blurred and generic**. The Mann/Williams/Prine school cuts dead nouns hard. Williams will write "Vicksburg" before she writes "town." Prine writes "Demerol" before "painkiller." Mann writes "Diet Coke" before "drink." The principle, from Pattison's *Writing Better Lyrics* via [Soundfly's Flypaper article on object writing](https://flypaper.soundfly.com/write/how-to-generate-great-songwriting-ideas-with-object-writing-technique/): the freshness of a concrete noun is a function of its specificity. *Rose* is concrete; *the seven dollar rose she bought at the gas station* is specific. The revision move when you find a dead concrete noun: ask what particular instance you can name in its place. If you can't think of one, the noun isn't earning a line.

provenance.section: Concrete-But-Clichéd Nouns — When Roses and Rain Die
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

citation_targets.title: Soundfly's Flypaper article on object writing

content: A proven move in this school is **proper-noun substitution**. Pop's most-cited recent example, discussed in the [Switched On Pop "folklore" episodes](https://switchedonpop.com/), is Taylor Swift's swerve into named objects on *folklore* and *evermore* — *"the old cardigan under someone's bed,"* *"I haven't met the new me yet,"* *"James, Betty, Inez"* as recurring characters. Williams names *Lake Charles, Louisiana*. Prine names *Muhlenberg County* and *Sam Stone*. Mann names *Wise Up* directly to the listener. Proper nouns are the highest-specificity concrete category — a place name does work no descriptor can do, because the listener either knows the place or can look it up. The risk is over-naming (the song becomes an inventory) or naming things the listener can't reach (an obscure street name from your hometown that produces no image for anyone else). The discipline is to name the one thing per verse that does the most pictorial work, not five.

provenance.section: Brand Names, Place Names, Proper Nouns
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: This school is honest enough to name its exception. **Direct emotional statement lands when the song has earned the right to make it.** The last line of Prine's *Hello in There* — "say 'hello in there, hello'" — is a direct address that tells the listener exactly what to do. It works because the previous three verses showed elderly isolation in concrete detail; the telling line is the conclusion, not the substitute. The rule, paraphrased across Pattison's teaching and Sheila Davis's [*The Craft of Lyric Writing*](https://www.amazon.com/Craft-Lyric-Writing-Sheila-Davis/dp/0898792827) (Davis is the second canonical American lyric-writing textbook after Pattison): **show first, then tell — and only if the showing has built up enough pressure that the telling discharges it.** A chorus that tells without verses that showed lands flat. A chorus that tells after verses that showed becomes the hook.

provenance.section: When Telling Beats Showing
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: A move shared across the Mann / Williams / Prine school and recorded in Pattison's revision chapters: **read every draft line aloud, slowly, looking up at the ceiling between lines.** Two failures surface: (1) lines that you stumble on because the syntax doesn't match natural speech, and (2) lines that produce no image when you close your eyes. Williams talks about this in her [Sodajerker episode](https://www.sodajerker.com/) — she rewrites lines until they sound like something she'd actually say. Mann describes the same test as "does it sound like a person." Prine — per his Zollo interview — wrote out loud at his kitchen table, reading drafts to his wife. The diagnostic catches the placeholder lines that survive silent reading. If you cannot picture the line out loud, the listener cannot either.

provenance.section: The Read-Aloud Diagnostic
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: Three failure patterns this school warns against. **(1) Abstraction stacks**: three or more abstract emotion words in four consecutive lines. The line *"I feel so lost and so alone and so afraid"* has no image and three identical syntactic moves; the verse is doing zero work. **(2) Borrowed concretes**: writing about *whiskey* when you don't drink whiskey, *trains* when you have never been on one, *Nashville* when you have never been there. Borrowed concretes ring false because the writer can't supply the specific sensory detail that turns a category into an instance. The school's rule: write the concrete nouns you have actually touched. **(3) Concrete decoration without function**: piling specific details that don't serve the song's emotional center. A verse about a kitchen that names every appliance is not a song; it is an inventory. Pattison's stress test for this — the "theme consistency" pass detailed elsewhere in C8 — is: does each concrete noun connect to what the song is actually about? If not, cut the noun even though it is concrete.

provenance.section: Common Failure Modes
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting Without Boundaries* (2011); Aimee Mann interviews (Sodajerker, NPR); Lucinda Williams interviews in Bill Friskics-Warren's writing and Sodajerker; John Prine interviews (Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; *Beyond Words*, Prine's 2017 book of lyrics + drawings)

content: A practical revision pass that combines all of the above, executable in 20–30 minutes on a draft. **(1)** Highlight every abstract emotion word in the draft. Count them. If the count is over three per verse, you have a telling problem. **(2)** For each abstract word, ask what concrete thing produced the feeling — and write the concrete thing in the margin. Often the margin word is the better line. **(3)** Highlight every "to be" verb. For each, ask whether an action verb is available. **(4)** Run the cover-the-context test on every line in the chorus first (the chorus is where lines repeat and earn the most scrutiny). **(5)** Read the whole draft aloud, slowly. Mark the lines you stumble on. **(6)** Pick the three weakest lines and rewrite them concretely, even if the rewrite is worse-sounding at first. **(7)** Sit on the revision overnight, then read again. The goal of this pass is not to make the lyric "good" — it is to find the placeholder lines and replace them with lines that show. The polishing is downstream.

content: In the Pattison / Davis school — the dominant American craft tradition for English-language songwriting — **specificity beats abstraction roughly 90% of the time in contemporary pop, country, indie, and folk.** This is documented across Pattison's *Writing Better Lyrics* and Sheila Davis's [*The Craft of Lyric Writing*](https://www.amazon.com/Craft-Lyric-Writing-Sheila-Davis/dp/0898792827), and audible in the working practice of Aimee Mann, Lucinda Williams, John Prine, Taylor Swift's later work, and Billie Eilish's lyric craft as analyzed in the [Switched On Pop podcast](https://switchedonpop.com/). The reason — per the [Berklee Online prosody overview](https://online.berklee.edu/takenote/prosody-in-music-and-songwriting/) — is mechanical: concrete sensory detail activates the listener's body and memory; abstractions activate only their dictionary. The default should be specific. **But this is the default, not the universal law.** Some genres and song types reward abstraction. The craft skill is knowing which lever you are pulling on a given line, and why.

provenance.section: The Default Rule, Named as a Default
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: Specificity has three independent axes that often get conflated. **(1) Sensory specificity** — naming what can be seen, heard, smelled, tasted, touched, felt in the body, sensed kinesthetically (the seven senses Pattison enumerates in [*Writing Better Lyrics*](https://www.izotope.com/en/learn/object-writing-your-secret-to-vivid-song-lyrics)). **(2) Particularity** — naming this instance rather than the category: *the green Toyota* rather than *the car*, *Tuesday at 4* rather than *the afternoon*. **(3) Personal-ness** — drawing on the writer's actual experience rather than a generic version of an experience anyone could have. A line can be high on one axis and low on another. *"My heart was on fire"* is sensory (fire, heart) but not particular (anyone's heart, any fire) and not personal (it's a cliché). *"The Camry stalled out at the second light on Westheimer"* is particular and personal but only moderately sensory. The strongest pop lyrics tend to score high on at least two of the three.

provenance.section: What "Specific" Actually Means
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: Three song-types where abstraction is the correct lever. **(1) Anthem and declaration songs** — *"We Are the World," "We Are the Champions," "Imagine," "I Want to Break Free."* These songs need to scale to stadiums and across cultures; specific detail would narrow the audience. The whole rhetorical move is universality, and abstraction is the tool. **(2) Hymn-mode songs** — gospel, devotional, certain country balladry. The mode requires elevated language and category-level claims. **(3) Mantra and chant** — Sia's *"Chandelier,"* Florence's *"Dog Days Are Over,"* large chunks of dance-pop. The chorus is a repeated abstract phrase because the function is sonic incantation, not narrative. **The rule:** when the song's function is collective affirmation, ceremonial declaration, or chant, abstraction is correct. When the song's function is narrative, confession, or witnessing, specificity is correct. Most pop songs are some mix, which is why the question is per-section rather than per-song.

provenance.section: The Exception — When Abstraction Is the Move
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: Billie Eilish's *"Happier Than Ever"* (2021) — analyzed in detail in the [Switched On Pop episode on the song](https://switchedonpop.com/) and in [Sound on Sound's production coverage](https://www.soundonsound.com/) — is a contemporary case study in specificity. The lyric names a specific behavior pattern (*"you call me again, drunk in your Benz, driving home under the influence"*) and a specific complaint (*"you make me hate this city"*). The song scaled to a worldwide hit while keeping its specifics intact. The Switched On Pop hosts cite this as evidence that the streaming-era pop audience tolerates — and rewards — concrete confessional detail at the same scale that 1980s pop reserved for abstraction. Eilish and brother / co-writer Finneas O'Connell consistently take the specific noun: *"three AM,"* *"the bad guy,"* *"my strange addiction."* The lesson is not that all pop should sound like Eilish, but that the "abstraction sells better at scale" assumption is empirically wrong as of 2026.

content: Taylor Swift's pivot on the 2020 *folklore* and *evermore* records — discussed across the [Switched On Pop *folklore* episode](https://switchedonpop.com/) and the [Pitchfork *folklore* review](https://pitchfork.com/reviews/albums/taylor-swift-folklore/) — was a deliberate move from pop's abstract emotional vocabulary into named characters, places, and objects. *"The old cardigan under someone's bed."* *"James, Inez, Betty."* *"The Cornelia Street townhouse."* *"The 1830s without all the racists."* The records were her most critically acclaimed. The Switched On Pop analysis ties this to a broader 2018–2024 trend in mainstream pop: detail returned as a marker of artistic seriousness. ARLO should not generalize this into "specifics always sell" — Swift's pre-*folklore* hits were largely abstract and also sold massively. The honest framing: specificity is no longer a commercial liability the way Brill Building–era producers sometimes believed it was, and for a writer drawn to it, the cultural moment is supportive.

provenance.section: The Swift Case — Named Objects on *folklore* / *evermore*
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: Pattison's central reframe, recorded in [the Sound on Sound interview](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/pat-pattison-writing-better-lyrics): **the universal is reached through the specific, not by skipping past it.** Naming *your* one detail is what makes the listener feel *theirs*. The mechanism is associative — your "screen door slamming on a Sunday afternoon in August" is not a screen door the listener has ever heard, but it activates the listener's stored memory of *their* screen door, *their* August. An abstraction ("summer made me sad") gives them no anchor point, so they recall nothing. This is why John Prine's Muhlenberg County feels like every reader's hometown; why Springsteen's specific New Jersey reads as every listener's town. The principle is paradoxical and load-bearing: **to write for everyone, write for one person, including one detail nobody else has.**

provenance.section: The Universal-Via-Specific Principle
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: A useful diagnostic from Sheila Davis's [*The Craft of Lyric Writing*](https://www.amazon.com/Craft-Lyric-Writing-Sheila-Davis/dp/0898792827), echoed in Pattison's revision chapters: **most clichés are not failed images — they are failed abstractions.** *"My heart is broken."* *"Walking through the rain."* *"Love is a battlefield."* These were once concrete metaphors that lost their concreteness through repetition. The brain processes them as abstractions because the picture has worn off. The revision move: identify the cliché, ask what concrete thing the cliché was originally trying to say, and write the concrete thing instead. *"My heart is broken"* → *"I dropped the plate she gave me and didn't pick up the pieces."* The replacement may not always be better, but the diagnostic flags lines that are doing zero work.

provenance.section: Cliché as Failed Abstraction
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: A working revision pass: **cover the proper nouns in the draft and read the lyric.** If the lyric still means something, the proper nouns are decoration. If the lyric collapses, the proper nouns are doing structural work. The test is from the lyric-craft tradition of editing for compactness — credited in Davis and audible in any successful pop lyric. Two outcomes are informative. **(1)** If the song still works without the place name (you can swap *"Tupelo"* for *"my hometown"* with no loss), the proper noun was added for color but is not earning its keep. Cut or replace it. **(2)** If the song collapses without the proper noun, you have a song whose meaning is structurally place-based. *"Born in the U.S.A."* without the U.S.A. is a different song. *"Empire State of Mind"* without "New York" doesn't exist. Both outcomes are fine — the test is meant to surface what your song is actually about.

provenance.section: The "Cut the Proper Noun" Test
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: Where this question lands varies. **Folk and country (Williams, Prine, Isbell)** reward extreme specificity; the genre's whole rhetorical pose is witnessing. **Indie / alternative (Mann, Sufjan, The National)** reward specificity with literary flair. **Mainstream pop pre-2015** tolerated more abstraction; post-2015 mainstream pop has trended specific (Eilish, Olivia Rodrigo, Swift's later work). **Hip-hop** has always been specific — *names, brands, blocks, dates* — per the analysis in [Paul Edwards' *How to Rap*](https://www.amazon.com/How-Rap-Art-Science-Hip-Hop/dp/1556528167). **Anthemic stadium rock (U2, Coldplay)** still rewards abstraction because the function is collective. **Dance-pop and EDM vocal hooks** reward chant-mode abstraction because the function is communal repetition. **Hymn, gospel, and certain country balladry** require elevated abstract language as a genre marker. The lever-pull decision is genre-aware. ARLO should retrieve this nuance when the user is writing in a tradition that breaks the default.

provenance.section: Genre and Era Boundedness
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: A craft move that splits the difference: **the song states an abstract thesis and proves it with one extended concrete image.** Joni Mitchell's *"Both Sides Now"* states the abstraction *"I really don't know love at all"* but spends the verses on clouds, circus rides, fairy tales. Leonard Cohen's *"Hallelujah"* states a religious abstraction in the chorus and proves it through King David and Bathsheba in the verse. Bob Dylan's *"Like a Rolling Stone"* states a generalized accusation in the chorus but anchors the verses in a specific scene (*Miss Lonely*, the mystery tramp, Napoleon in rags). This is the most-resilient pop song architecture in the canon, partly because it gives the listener both: the abstraction to remember and the specifics to feel. The lesson for revision: if your verses are abstract and your chorus is abstract, the song has no anchor. Move at least one to the concrete.

provenance.section: When the Whole Song Is One Image
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: A working procedure for the per-section choice. **(1) Name the song's function** — narrative, confession, witnessing, anthem, declaration, mantra, hymn. **(2) The default is specific** unless the function is one of the abstract-leaning categories. **(3) Verses almost always reward more specificity than the chorus** because verses do narrative work; choruses do hook work. **(4) The bridge is the place to introduce an abstract conclusion** if the verses have earned it. **(5) When in doubt, write the specific version first; the abstraction is the safer rewrite, not the bolder one.** **(6) Run the "cut the proper noun" test and the cover-the-context test (from C1)** to surface the lines that are leaning on abstraction by default rather than by choice. **(7) Be honest about scale-of-image** — a song with one named brand can land as confessional; a song with five named brands lands as inventory. Calibrate per song. The point of the procedure is to make the specificity-vs-abstraction choice a deliberate craft move per section, not a default reflex.

provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing* (1985); Switched On Pop episodes on Taylor Swift *folklore*/*evermore* and Billie Eilish; Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*

content: Three patterns. **(1) Default-abstract-everywhere** — the writer leans on "I feel," "I want," "I need," "love," "heart," "alone" because those words are easier to find rhymes for. The song reads as generic. **(2) Default-specific-everywhere** — the writer lists detail after detail without an emotional through-line. The song reads as inventory. **(3) Mismatched section function** — abstract verses and concrete chorus, where the architecture should usually be the reverse (concrete verses build to an abstract or anthemic chorus). This last failure is the most-common in earnest indie songwriting: the writer fills the verses with feeling-words and saves the one concrete image for the chorus, where it gets repeated to death. The fix: redistribute. Put the concrete image into the verse where it can do narrative work; let the chorus do its repetition job.

content: The theme-consistency school of lyric revision rests on a single, contested claim: **a song is about one thing, and every line of the lyric must serve that one thing**. This is Pat Pattison's central organizing claim across *Writing Better Lyrics* and his Berklee teaching, and it is echoed by Jimmy Webb in *Tunesmith* and Sheila Davis in *The Craft of Lyric Writing*. The school is not universal — some writers (Joanna Newsom in long form, Bowie in *Berlin* trilogy mode, Sufjan in atmospheric mode) deliberately work in multi-thematic or productively ambiguous registers. But for a stuck musician revising a draft that "isn't working," the most common diagnosis is **theme drift** — the song started about one thing, drifted into another, and the writer cannot say in one sentence what the song is about anymore. The theme-consistency pass is the workbench technique for catching and fixing that drift. Pattison teaches it as "the essential question." Webb teaches it as the title-as-anchor. Both share the underlying claim: if you cannot name what the song is about, the song does not know what it is about, and the listener will feel that.

provenance.section: The Principle — A Song Is About One Thing
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: Pat Pattison's framing across his books and his [lyric tips page at patpattison.com](https://www.patpattison.com/pat-s-lyric-tips) is to ask before writing — and again during revision — **the song's essential question**. The essential question is a single sentence that names what the song is grappling with: *"What does it cost to forgive someone who didn't apologize?"* *"What does it feel like to be in the room your mother used to live in?"* *"Why does the same fight keep happening?"* The essential question is more useful than a one-word topic ("forgiveness," "grief," "frustration") because it carries an *angle* — a question implies a stance the song will take. Every line of the draft can then be stress-tested against the question: does this line move toward the answer, complicate the question, or wander off? Pattison's revision rule, paraphrased from his teaching: **lines that do not engage the essential question are decoration**, no matter how well-written. Cut them. The pass is brutal because most first-draft lyrics contain at least one line the writer loves that doesn't belong; the discipline is to recognize the line is good and cut it anyway because it belongs in a different song.

provenance.section: Pattison's "Essential Question" Frame
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: Jimmy Webb's parallel framing in [*Tunesmith*](https://archive.org/details/tunesmith00jimm) (Hyperion, 1998) approaches theme through the title. Webb's claim, drawn from a writing career anchored by titles that *are* the song's argument ("By the Time I Get to Phoenix," "Wichita Lineman," "MacArthur Park," "The Highwayman"): **if you cannot title the song, you do not know what it is about**. The title is the song's center of gravity; it is the line the listener will remember; it is the candidate phrase for the refrain. Webb's discipline: before declaring the lyric finished, write down the title and read each verse asking whether the verse is doing work the title implies. *"By the Time I Get to Phoenix"* implies distance, time, and travel; verses that don't engage distance or time are off-theme. *"Wichita Lineman"* implies a worker, a place, and a kind of longing; verses that don't engage at least one of those are off-theme. The title-as-test is the Webb version of Pattison's essential question — different vocabulary, same craft move. The two together form the canonical American theme-consistency framework: name the song's one thing, then check every line against it.

provenance.section: Webb's Title-as-Theme Test
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: A practical revision exercise drawn from both Pattison and Webb and reported across Paul Zollo's [*Songwriters on Songwriting*](https://www.amazon.com/Songwriters-Songwriting-Revised-Paul-Zollo/dp/0306812657) interviews: **after the first draft, set the draft aside and write, in one sentence, what the song is actually about.** Do not write what you *wanted* the song to be about; write what the draft has become. Often these are different. A song that started as "what does it cost to forgive" can become, in draft, "I am angry at this person" — same subject, different angle, different song. Naming the actual draft theme is the first step in deciding whether to keep the original theme and revise the draft toward it, or accept the new theme and revise away the original-theme residue. Either choice is legitimate; the wrong choice is to leave both themes in the song. Songs with two themes tend to be songs with no theme — the listener cannot tell which line is doing which work, so the cumulative effect is incoherence.

provenance.section: The "What Is This Song Actually About" Exercise
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: The mechanical version of the theme-consistency check, executable in 15–20 minutes on a complete draft. **(1)** Write the song's theme statement (one sentence) at the top of the page. **(2)** Read each line of the lyric in order. For each line, ask: *does this line engage the theme?* Mark each line: ✓ (engages), ~ (tangentially relates), ✗ (off-theme). **(3)** Scan the marks. If the column has more than one or two ✗ marks in a single verse, the verse is doing different work than the song. **(4)** For each ✗ line, decide: rewrite the line to engage the theme, cut the line, or — if the line is undeniably load-bearing — interrogate whether the theme statement itself is wrong. Sometimes the off-theme line is the line revealing what the song is *really* about. The discipline is the same as Pattison's "essential question" pass: most first-draft lines pass with ~ rather than ✓, and the work of revision is moving them to ✓ or cutting them.

provenance.section: The Line-by-Line Stress Test
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: The hardest line to cut in a draft is the **brilliant line that doesn't belong**. Every working writer in Zollo's archive — John Prine, Paul Simon, Tom Waits, Carole King — describes the same experience: a line they love, that works on its own, that the song cannot accommodate because it is in a different emotional register or argues a different point. The Pattison and Webb discipline is identical: **cut the brilliant off-theme line, and save it in a notebook for the song it actually belongs to.** Working writers across the canon describe maintaining a "scraps" file or notebook of lines that didn't fit but were too good to throw away; weeks or years later, the line finds the song that needs it. The hardest version of this discipline is the brilliant *chorus* line that doesn't belong — these are especially seductive because choruses do so much work — but if the chorus line argues a different point from the verses, the lyric will read as two songs glued together. The Webb test: does the chorus's claim follow from what the verses showed? If not, one of them is in the wrong song.

provenance.section: The Off-Theme Cleverness Trap
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: Theme-consistency is one school of thought, not the only school. There is a legitimate craft case for **productive ambiguity** — songs whose theme is intentionally multiple, whose meaning shifts on rehearings, whose lyric supports several readings. Joni Mitchell's "Both Sides Now," David Bowie's *Hunky Dory* tracks, Bob Dylan's mid-career symbolic work, Sufjan's *Carrie & Lowell* memory songs, Joanna Newsom's narrative-meets-cosmology lyrics — these are not theme-drift, they are *theme-layering*. The distinction the school flags: productive ambiguity is **intentional and architected**. The writer can name what the multiple themes are and why they coexist. Drift is **unintentional and unrecognized**: the writer cannot name what is happening. The diagnostic question: *if a careful listener asked what this song is about, could you give a coherent answer — even a complicated, layered answer?* If yes, you have ambiguity. If you find yourself shrugging or contradicting yourself, you have drift. ARLO should not flatten ambiguity into single-theme orthodoxy. ARLO should flag drift.

provenance.section: Productive Ambiguity vs. Drift
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: A pattern observable in working-writer revision practice and named explicitly in Pattison's teaching: **when a draft is too long and needs cutting, the off-theme lines are almost always the right cuts**. The writer's instinct is often to cut the line that sounds worst; the school's instinct is to cut the line that is *off-topic*, even if it sounds fine. A four-verse song that should be three usually has one verse pulling at a different theme; cutting that verse tightens the song. A six-line bridge that should be four usually has two lines that argue a different point; cutting them sharpens the bridge. The mechanical move: after the theme-statement pass, identify the lines marked ✗ or ~ — these are the cut candidates before any line marked ✓ becomes one. The discipline is hard because off-theme lines often *sound* finished while on-theme lines often need revision. The school's claim is that an on-theme line that needs revision is more valuable than an off-theme line that is already polished, because the song's coherence rests on the on-theme work.

provenance.section: The Cutting Move — Why Off-Theme Lines Are Usually the Cuts
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: A specific Webb claim from *Tunesmith*, paraphrased and echoed in [the Blinkist summary of the book](https://www.blinkist.com/en/books/tunesmith-en): **if you cannot title the song, you do not yet know what the song is about**. The rule is diagnostic, not prescriptive — it doesn't mean every song must title easily, but it means a song that resists every title attempt is probably a song whose theme is not yet clarified. Working writers across genres test this when stuck: try titling the draft with five different titles. If none of them feel right, the song's theme is probably the issue, not the lyric craft. If one title clicks immediately, the click is information: that title names what the song actually is, and the lyric can be revised toward it. The Webb-trained move: when stuck on a chorus or bridge, return to the title question. The title-as-theme test is a faster diagnostic than the line-by-line pass when the writer suspects but cannot pinpoint that the song is unfocused.

provenance.section: The Title-Declares-the-Theme Rule
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

citation_targets.title: the Blinkist summary of the book

content: Choruses are the highest-leverage theme-consistency check, because the chorus is the line the listener will hear most. Pattison's claim across his teaching: **the chorus is the song's argument**. Whatever the chorus repeatedly claims is what the listener will conclude the song is about, regardless of what the verses showed. A chorus that argues "I will love you forever" with verses showing a relationship in collapse will be heard as ironic at best and incoherent at worst — unless the writer is deliberately working that contradiction (a legitimate craft move, but one that must be earned with explicit signals to the listener). The theme-consistency pass at the chorus: read the chorus aloud, write down what it claims in one sentence, then read each verse asking whether the verse builds toward that claim or contradicts it. If a verse contradicts the chorus without explicit signaling, the contradiction will read as drift, not as craft.

provenance.section: The Theme Check at the Chorus
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: The bridge — covered structurally in `corpus/structure/section-function-verse-prechorus-chorus-bridge.md` — is the place where theme is most often broken or most pointedly clarified. Pattison's framing: the bridge should either **deepen the theme** (introduce a new angle on the same question) or **resolve the theme** (deliver the conclusion the verses set up). The failure mode is a bridge that introduces a *different* theme — a song about forgiveness whose bridge is about loneliness reads as a song that lost its argument. The theme-consistency test at the bridge: does the bridge add to what we already know about the essential question, or does it change the subject? If it changes the subject, the bridge is doing the wrong job. The fix is sometimes a rewrite; sometimes the bridge is fine and the *verses* changed subject earlier without the writer noticing. Either way, the bridge-test catches the drift.

provenance.section: The Bridge as Theme Pressure-Point
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: A practical heuristic for ARLO and the working writer. Signals that theme-consistency is the likely diagnosis. **(1)** "I don't know what this song is about anymore" — the canonical signal; the writer is naming the problem. **(2)** "the bridge isn't working" — bridges fail more often from theme drift than from harmonic problems. **(3)** "the second verse doesn't feel as strong" — second verses often drift because the writer has used the strongest material in the first verse and is reaching for new content. **(4)** "the chorus doesn't feel earned" — when the chorus's claim doesn't follow from the verses, the issue is usually theme misalignment rather than the chorus itself. **(5)** "I have a lot of lines I love but it isn't a song" — the classic theme-incoherence signal; the lines are not arguing the same thing. For each signal, ARLO's first move is the essential-question pass: ask the user to state in one sentence what the song is about. If they hesitate, hedge, or contradict themselves, the diagnosis is confirmed.

provenance.section: When ARLO Should Surface a Theme Problem
provenance.canonical-references: Pat Pattison, *Writing Better Lyrics* (2nd ed., 2010); Pat Pattison, *Songwriting: Essential Guide to Lyric Form and Structure*; Jimmy Webb, *Tunesmith: Inside the Art of Songwriting* (Hyperion, 1998); Paul Zollo, *Songwriters on Songwriting*; Sheila Davis, *The Craft of Lyric Writing*; Pat Pattison's lyric tips at patpattison.com

content: This file builds on two general-corpus files — `corpus/harmony/modal-interchange-and-borrowed-chords.md` and `corpus/harmony/secondary-dominants-and-applied-chords.md` — and applies their theory to a single practical job: **shifting the mood of a moment by swapping one chord for a more colorful one.** These are jazz-derived substitutions used in pop, presented move-by-move with the feeling each produces. Mission-fit: when a progression is correct but emotionally flat, a single substitution can add sophistication or drama without rewriting the section. The honest framing: these are advanced colors, easy to overuse, and many great songs need none of them.

provenance.section: Why this file exists
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: A **chord substitution** replaces an expected chord with a different one that serves a similar function but carries a different color. The substitute usually shares notes or function with the original, so the progression still "works," but it sounds richer, more surprising, or more sophisticated. Jazz developed a deep vocabulary of these, and pop has borrowed selectively from it. The key discipline: a substitution should *do a job* — add a specific feeling at a specific moment — not just decorate. Used with intent, one substitution can lift a whole section; used as wallpaper, they muddy a song.

provenance.section: What a substitution is
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: The most-used jazz-adjacent substitution in all of pop is replacing the major **IV** with the minor **iv**, almost always right before returning to I. It's technically modal interchange (covered in `corpus/songwriting/melodic-harmonic/modal-interchange-by-mood.md`), but it functions as the go-to *substitution* for adding bittersweet ache: the IV opens bright, the iv darkens that opening into longing, and the resolution lands wistful. It's a one-note change — the third of the IV drops a half step — with an outsized emotional payoff. **Radiohead's "Creep"** and **The Beatles' "In My Life"** both put IV→iv exactly where the song aches. When a turnaround or chorus feels too sweet, this is the first substitution to reach for.

provenance.section: Move: IV becomes iv (the canonical sad turn)
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: The signature jazz substitution is the **tritone sub**: replace the dominant **V7** with a dominant seventh chord a tritone away — the **♭II7**. In C major, that means replacing G7 with D♭7. It works because both chords contain the same tritone (the interval between the 3rd and ♭7), so the part that creates the pull toward home is identical — only the root changes ([Jazz-Library, *Tritone Substitution*](https://jazz-library.com/articles/tritone-substitution/); [Tritone substitution, Wikipedia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tritone_substitution)). The payoff is a smooth chromatic bass line: instead of G→C, the bass slides D♭→C, a half step into home. The mood it creates is a sophisticated, slightly unexpected resolution — "lounge-y," noir, jazz-ballad color. In pop it's rare and special; drop it on a single cadence where you want the resolution to feel chromatic and elegant rather than bright and obvious.

provenance.section: Move: the tritone substitution (♭II7 for V7)
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: A **secondary dominant** is a dominant chord borrowed from another key to point strongly at a chord that isn't the tonic — written "V/V" ("five of five"), "V/vi," "V/IV," etc. It creates a brief, urgent pull toward the target chord, adding forward momentum and a "leaving the key for a second" brightness. The classic is **V/V** — the dominant of the dominant — which drives hard into the V before the chorus. Dolly Parton's "9 to 5" uses a V/V in its chorus ([Popgrammar, *Secondary Dominants*](https://popgrammar.com/secondary-dominants/)). The mood: energy, lift, forward motion, a momentary harmonic surprise. Use a secondary dominant when a progression feels static and you want to inject drive and pull toward a specific chord. (Full treatment in `corpus/harmony/secondary-dominants-and-applied-chords.md`.)

provenance.section: Move: the secondary dominant (V/x for forward drive)
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: Instead of resolving the dominant home to **I**, resolve it deceptively to **vi**. The ear expects the bright tonic arrival and instead gets the relative minor — a "we didn't land where we expected" feeling that reads as bittersweet, unresolved, or emotionally expansive. A practical application: if a chorus feels like it ends too soon, replace the final V–I with **V–vi** and add another phrase; the listener thought the section was ending, and now it continues, creating a sense of emotional expansion ([Disc Makers Blog, *Secondary Dominant Chords*](https://blog.discmakers.com/2023/02/secondary-dominant-chords/)). The mood: surprise, melancholy, "not quite home yet." Use it to extend a section or to color a cadence that would otherwise resolve too cleanly.

provenance.section: Move: the deceptive resolution (V to vi)
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: Diminished seventh chords make excellent **dramatic passing chords** between two diatonic chords, adding tension and chromatic motion. A diminished chord a half step below a target chord (a leading-tone diminished) pulls into it strongly; placed as a passing chord it creates a brief, suspenseful lean before the resolution. The mood is dramatic, suspenseful, slightly anxious — the "something's about to happen" sound. In pop this often appears as a chromatic passing chord between I and ii, or pushing into V. Use a diminished passing chord when a smooth diatonic step feels too plain and you want a beat of tension between two chords.

provenance.section: Move: the diminished passing chord (♭II°7 and friends)
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: In a minor key (or to darken a major-key predominant), the **iim7♭5** — the half-diminished "two" chord — is the jazz predominant that leads into the dominant with a darker, more sophisticated color than a plain minor ii. It's the front half of the minor ii–V–i, the most fundamental jazz cadence. In pop, substituting a half-diminished ii for a plain ii adds a noir, jazzy, melancholic shading to the approach to the dominant. The mood: sophisticated melancholy, a "torch song" color. Use it when a predominant chord feels too plain and you want the approach to the V to carry weight and shadow.

provenance.section: Move: the iim7♭5 (jazz minor predominant)
provenance.canonical-references: Mark Levine, *The Jazz Theory Book*; Dominic Pedler, *Songwriting Secrets of the Beatles*; Rick Beato, *The Beato Book*; Open Music Theory v2

content: Rather than substituting the V entirely, you can *enrich* it — adding a 9th, 13th, or altering it (♭9, ♯9, ♭5, ♯5) for jazz color. A dominant with tensions sounds lusher and more sophisticated; an altered dominant (the "♭9" sound especially) sounds tense and dramatic, pulling hard to resolve.
