content:
The second verse is the most-feared lyric assignment in songwriting. Pat Pattison's blunt diagnosis in *Writing Better Lyrics* is that verse 2 is where amateur songs collapse — the writer used everything they had in verse 1, the chorus paid it off, and now there is nothing left to say. The cure is structural, not lyrical: a second verse must *develop* the song, not restate it.

The mistake almost every writer makes is treating verse 2 as a parallel of verse 1 — same situation, same scope, same emotional register, just different rhymes. That works in folk and traditional ballads (where the song advances by accumulating verses of similar shape), but it fails in contemporary pop, where the listener has heard the chorus and expects verse 2 to escalate, complicate, or recontextualize what the chorus said.

Jimmy Webb's *Tunesmith* frames the verse 2 problem as a narrative problem: verse 1 sets up the situation, the chorus declares the emotional response, and verse 2 has to make the listener understand *more* — more about why the singer feels this way, more about the consequences, more about the other person, more about the world the song lives in. If verse 2 doesn't add information, the song flatlines.

Sheila Davis in *The Craft of Lyric Writing* offers the simplest test: after the chorus, ask, "What does the listener now want to know?" That question is verse 2. If you cannot name the question, you do not have verse 2 yet — and trying to write it from a blank page is the stall.

The deeper trap: songwriters often *start* a song without knowing what verse 2 will be, then trap themselves into a chorus and verse 1 that pre-spent the song's material. Cave, Cohen, Dylan, and Pattison all describe drafting verse 2 *first* or alongside verse 1 to avoid this.

provenance.section: Why it stalls

content:
### Move 1 — Time shift: change when verse 2 takes place

Verse 1 is the present; verse 2 is the past or the future of the same situation. This is the most-used move in Nashville and in the Sodajerker interview canon — it gives you new material without changing the song's center of gravity. Examples: verse 1 is the morning of the fight; verse 2 is the morning after. Verse 1 is the first kiss; verse 2 is the divorce. Verse 1 is the phone call; verse 2 is the drive home. The chorus stays as the emotional response that binds both moments.

Concrete recipe: write down what's happening in verse 1 as a one-sentence scene. Now write the same sentence shifted to a different point in time — five minutes later, five years later, the night before, the funeral. That's the seed of verse 2.

### Move 2 — POV shift: change whose eyes the verse is in

Verse 1 is from the singer's perspective; verse 2 is from the other person's, or from a third party who witnessed the situation. Pattison teaches this as the "shift the narrator" move — risky if mishandled but powerful when it lands. Sheila Davis warns that the listener has to be able to follow the shift; if the POV change is unclear, the song reads as confused. A common safe version: keep the same singer but have them imagine what the other person is thinking ("She probably tells her friends...").

The risk: POV switches that aren't earned read as gimmicky. Test by reading both verses aloud — does the listener immediately know who is speaking in each?

### Move 3 — Zoom: change the lens width

Verse 1 is the close-up; verse 2 is the wide shot — or the reverse. Verse 1 is the specific detail (the coffee cup on the table, the song on the radio); verse 2 is the larger context (the city, the year, the cultural moment). Or verse 1 names the world and verse 2 zooms into the room. This is the move when the song's material is about the relationship between the personal and the universal — Aimee Mann songs do this frequently, as does Bruce Springsteen's *Nebraska* catalog.

The discipline: each verse owns its lens. Don't switch lenses mid-verse; the listener needs to feel the camera move *between* sections, not within them.

### Move 4 — Consequence: verse 1 is the choice, verse 2 is what happened

Verse 1 sets up an action; verse 2 reveals its result. This is the narrative-logic move and the most Nashville-friendly of the six. Verse 1: "I told you I was leaving / packed the bag, paid the rent." Chorus: "and I never looked back." Verse 2: "Now I sit in the kitchen / of a house I don't recognize." The consequence-move forces the second verse to *advance* the story rather than restate it, and it gives the final chorus weight by anchoring it in earned material.

Jimmy Webb's *Tunesmith* describes this as the "what happened next" question — the same one a screenwriter asks at every act break. If verse 2 doesn't answer it, verse 2 doesn't exist yet.

### Move 5 — Verse-1 shape with new images (the swap)

Keep verse 1's syntactic structure — line lengths, rhyme scheme, prosodic phrasing — but swap every concrete noun and verb for new ones. The song's structure does the work of feeling familiar; the new images do the work of feeling new. Pattison teaches a version of this in his Berklee lectures: the syntactic shape of verse 1 *is* the song's lyric form, and verse 2 inhabits that form with fresh material. This move is especially useful when you love verse 1's prosody and don't want to lose its momentum.

The danger: if the new images don't connect to the chorus's emotional center, you've written two parallel verses that don't *develop*. Combine this move with Move 1 or Move 4 to give verse 2 a directional motion.

### Move 6 — The cut option: there shouldn't be a verse 2

Some songs are one-verse songs. The song says what it has to say in one verse, the chorus pays it off, and a second verse would dilute the emotional concentration. Modern pop has many of these — the post-chorus has absorbed some of the function the second verse used to perform, and song lengths have shortened. If every attempted second verse is filler, the song may want a structure that goes verse-chorus-instrumental-chorus, or verse-chorus-bridge-chorus, with no second verse at all.

The test: write the song without a second verse. If the song is missing something, write verse 2. If the song is complete, verse 2 was always procrastination.

provenance.section: The 6 recovery moves

content:
When ARLO detects the second-verse stall, it pastes these:

1. "What does the chorus tell us happens emotionally? Now — what does the listener want to know *after* hearing that chorus?"
2. "Verse 1 takes place when? If it's the morning, what's the night? If it's the present, what's the past?"
3. "Whose voice is verse 1 in? Whose voice would verse 2 be in if you switched narrators?"
4. "Read me verse 1 out loud. What are the three most specific images in it? Now name three different specific images from the *same situation*."
5. "If the song stopped after the first chorus, what would feel missing? That missing thing is verse 2."
6. "If you couldn't have a verse 2 — only a bridge or instrumental — would the song be worse? Be honest."
7. "What's the consequence of what verse 1 described? If verse 1 is the choice, verse 2 is what happened next."
8. "Sing me verse 1 and the chorus. Now hum the verse 2 melody and tell me — what does the *music* want to say that the words don't yet?"

provenance.section: Socratic prompts ARLO uses verbatim

content:
If you've tried all six moves and verse 2 still feels grafted-on, the song may want a different form. The signals:

- Verse 2 attempts all sound like watered-down versions of verse 1
- The chorus says everything the song has to say; verse 2 is structural padding
- The song's emotional arc is one verse and one chorus — adding more dilutes it
- You can't articulate what the listener doesn't yet know after the first chorus

The move: cut verse 2 entirely. Structure as verse-chorus-bridge-chorus, or verse-chorus-instrumental-chorus, or verse-prechorus-chorus-postchorus-chorus. Many of the strongest modern pop songs do not have a traditional second verse — they replace it with a post-chorus hook (Eilish, Charli XCX) or a beat-switch second half (Travis Scott, hip-hop conventions).

If verse 1 itself is the problem — if it's too long, too dense, or burns through all the song's material — consider splitting it into two shorter verses with the chorus between, so the song goes verse-chorus-verse-chorus and verse 2 is the *second half* of what was originally one long verse.

When to walk away from the song: see [the abandoning-vs-persisting framework](abandoning-vs-persisting.md). If the second-verse problem persists for more than two sessions and none of the six moves opens a door, the song may be a sketch that has reached its natural length. Archive it; the verse-1-and-chorus may seed a different song later.

content:
The fastest way to make a song specific is to start from a single specific thing and excavate outward. Not a theme. Not a feeling. Not "a song about loss." A particular person you met. A photograph of a friend's cat. A meeting in a coffee shop with an actor newly arrived in Hollywood. Aimee Mann's catalog is built this way — most of her songs begin in a small, concrete, observable detail and grow into something larger only because they grew naturally outward from the seed, not because the writer declared the theme first.

This approach is in productive tension with the "object writing" school that Pat Pattison teaches (see [`corpus/lyrics/object-writing-and-sensory-imagery.md`](../../lyrics/object-writing-and-sensory-imagery.md)) where the writer practices the sensory-imagery muscle separately and brings the developed imagery to the song. Mann's variant is more naïve: the seed itself comes from observation, the song is built from the seed, and abstractions are earned by the time the song ends — never declared at the start.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: Aimee Mann interviews with NPR (2017), The Frame/LAist (2017–18), American Songwriter, Stereogum (2021), Performing Songwriter; *Mental Illness* (2017) and *The Forgotten Arm* (2005) album cycles; Paul Zollo's *Songwriters on Songwriting* tradition

content:
Mann has discussed her process across many interviews — NPR, American Songwriter, LAist's *The Frame*, Stereogum, Performing Songwriter, Sodajerker. Two specific song-origin stories anchor the attribution.

"Patient Zero" (from *Mental Illness*, 2017): Mann wrote it after she and her husband Michael Penn met the actor Andrew Garfield at a Hollywood event, shortly after he'd moved to LA. The song became a portrait of someone walking into the machine without quite knowing yet what they were walking into. The seed wasn't "a song about Hollywood." It was that specific meeting with that specific person ([LAist / The Frame](https://laist.com/shows/the-frame/aimee-manns-latest-album-is-mental-illness-but-shes-pretty-sane)).

"Goose Snow Cone" (also *Mental Illness*): Mann started writing it on tour in Ireland, homesick, after seeing an Instagram photo of a friend's cat named Goose. The cat reminded her of a snow cone. The song built outward from that image into a song about homesickness and loneliness, but it began with the actual cat and the actual picture.

A third anchor: Mann has said in multiple interviews that "it's not the story that's told — every story has been told — but it's the way you're telling it." The "way you're telling it" lives in the specifics. Mann lives in the specifics.

provenance.section: Why this is the right name
provenance.canonical-references: Aimee Mann interviews with NPR (2017), The Frame/LAist (2017–18), American Songwriter, Stereogum (2021), Performing Songwriter; *Mental Illness* (2017) and *The Forgotten Arm* (2005) album cycles; Paul Zollo's *Songwriters on Songwriting* tradition

content:
Three premises:

1. **Abstractions in lyrics are not the songwriter's job.** The listener does the abstracting. The writer's job is to provide specific enough material that the listener can do it. A song that *tells* you it's about loneliness rarely is. A song about a cat photo on tour that the writer can't stop looking at often is.

2. **The seed is observed, not invented.** Mann's seeds are real things — actual people, actual photos, actual scenes. Made-up seeds rarely produce real lyrics. The writer has to look at their own life and notice what's actually pulling them.

3. **The song excavates outward.** The seed is one image; the song grows around it. Excavation, not declaration. The writer does not begin by saying "this song is about X." They begin by writing about the seed and letting the song discover what it's about.

provenance.section: What this workflow believes
provenance.canonical-references: Aimee Mann interviews with NPR (2017), The Frame/LAist (2017–18), American Songwriter, Stereogum (2021), Performing Songwriter; *Mental Illness* (2017) and *The Forgotten Arm* (2005) album cycles; Paul Zollo's *Songwriters on Songwriting* tradition

content:
The clean trigger: the user has a feeling but no song. They want to write about loss, longing, change, anger, joy — and every draft they produce comes out as a generic pop statement of that feeling. Mann's response: stop trying to write about the feeling. Find one concrete, specific thing that's been on your mind, and start there.

Other fits:

- The user keeps starting songs with a declared theme and abandoning them three lines in
- The user's lyrics feel like *positions on* the subject rather than *experiences of* the subject
- The user is working on a record and wants the songs to feel particular rather than universal
- The user has piles of journaled abstractions and no songs

provenance.section: When this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: Aimee Mann interviews with NPR (2017), The Frame/LAist (2017–18), American Songwriter, Stereogum (2021), Performing Songwriter; *Mental Illness* (2017) and *The Forgotten Arm* (2005) album cycles; Paul Zollo's *Songwriters on Songwriting* tradition

content:
A practical test that captures Mann's instinct without requiring her to have ever stated it as a rule (ARLO is honest: this is ARLO's articulation, not a Mann quote):

For every line in the draft, look at the nouns and the verbs. Are the nouns concrete? Are the verbs specific?

- *Bad:* "The pain inside is breaking me." (Nouns: pain, inside. Verbs: breaking. Abstractions.)
- *Better:* "I'm peeling labels off the bottles I won't drink." (Nouns: labels, bottles. Verbs: peeling, drink. Concrete actions, concrete objects.)

The second tells you everything about the singer — alcohol, restraint, a kind of fidget. The first tells you nothing because *pain* and *breaking* are not things you can see. The Mann-style writer almost never lets an abstract noun stand alone.

provenance.section: The "noun-verb-noun" diagnostic
provenance.canonical-references: Aimee Mann interviews with NPR (2017), The Frame/LAist (2017–18), American Songwriter, Stereogum (2021), Performing Songwriter; *Mental Illness* (2017) and *The Forgotten Arm* (2005) album cycles; Paul Zollo's *Songwriters on Songwriting* tradition

content:
1. Sit down. No theme. No declared subject. The instruction is *don't start by deciding what the song is about.*

2. Open a notebook or document. Write down whatever specific thing has been in your head this week — a photo, a person, a conversation, a smell. The thing that keeps coming back. If nothing comes back, the workflow isn't the right one today (try [`david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md`](./david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md)).

3. Describe the thing. Two paragraphs of plain prose. What you saw. What they said. Where it was. The Pattison object-writing discipline is helpful here — use the senses. (See [`corpus/lyrics/object-writing-and-sensory-imagery.md`](../../lyrics/object-writing-and-sensory-imagery.md).)

4. Find one line in the description that hits. The one image or phrase you can't stop looking at. That's the song's seed.

5. Write around it. The seed becomes the chorus, the bridge, the opening verse — whichever it most wants to be. Surround it with adjacent specifics. Don't reach for the universal yet.

6. Let the abstraction surface. If the song is doing its work, you'll notice around the third verse or the bridge that the song has become "about" something larger than the seed. You didn't have to declare it; it emerged.

7. Revise the rest of the lyric against the seed. Every line that doesn't sit beside the seed in tone, register, and specificity gets cut or replaced. The seed sets the bar.

content:
Mann's discipline (implied in her process, not stated as a rule): when the image you started with is exhausted, you don't reach for *the abstraction* (the song's "theme"). You reach for *an adjacent image*. The cat photo isn't enough for a whole song; the next image is the hotel window, the next is the dressing room, the next is the call home. Adjacent specifics build outward.

Reaching for the abstraction at the moment the seed runs out is the most common failure mode of attempted Mann-style writing. The abstraction *will* arrive, but only after a chain of adjacent specifics has built the path.

content:
Many Mann songs are character portraits — *Patient Zero*, *Goose Snow Cone*, *Save Me*, *Wise Up*, the whole of *The Forgotten Arm* (a 2005 concept record about a Vietnam vet and his troubled marriage). The character is rarely declared at the start. The song shapes itself around the central figure as it accumulates details — what they wear, what they say, where they are, what they almost said.

For a user trying this workflow on a character song: the seed should be one specific thing the character does or has. The bottle they won't drink. The way they answer the phone. The chair they always sit in. Build outward from there; the character emerges.

content:
A practitioner-to-practitioner detail Mann has shared in interviews: Fiona Apple suggested to her that when stuck, she could try a constraint-based exercise — cutting headlines out of newspapers and rearranging into a poem-fragment. This is the cut-up technique borrowed from Burroughs/Bowie, transmitted writer-to-writer. Mann reports she's used the move when stuck and it works for her.

ARLO's takeaway: even practitioners with deeply specific instincts use rule-bending tools when they run dry. Mann's specificity-first workflow can pair with the cut-up workflow ([`bowie-burroughs-cut-up.md`](./bowie-burroughs-cut-up.md)) when the user is stuck inside specificity itself.

content:
**Picking a seed that's already too abstract.** "Loss" is not a seed. "The yellow chair he died in" is. If the user's seed is named with an abstract noun, push them to the underlying concrete.

**Treating the seed as a metaphor instead of a thing.** The cat photo is a cat photo. Don't say "the cat photo represents my homesickness" — write the cat photo and let the listener notice the homesickness.

**Reaching for the universal in line two.** A common impulse: write the specific image, then immediately follow it with the declared meaning. ("I'm peeling labels off the bottles I won't drink — because I'm broken.") The second line undoes the first. Cut every "because I'm broken" follower.

**Writing too quickly past the seed.** If the song moves past the seed in eight bars, the seed didn't fully express itself. Often the chorus is the seed restated, and the bridge is the moment you finally let the seed acknowledge what it's been about.

**Making the noun-verb-noun test mechanical.** It's a diagnostic, not a rule. Some lines need abstract nouns; some songs benefit from one declarative abstract line as the keystone. The discipline is to know when you're using one — never by default, always by choice.

content:
vs. [Cave letter method](./nick-cave-letter-method.md): both insist on specificity, but Cave's seed is the recipient (a person, addressed) while Mann's seed is the image (a thing, observed). The Cave seed is *who*; the Mann seed is *what*.

vs. [Lynch's catching the big fish](./david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md): Lynch fishes for the seed in meditative practice. Mann picks up the seed from observation and recent memory. Different acquisition routes for similar raw material.

vs. [Bowie cut-up](./bowie-burroughs-cut-up.md): cut-up produces strange juxtaposition; Mann's specificity produces *recognizable* particularity. They sound nothing alike. Both work for different writers.

vs. [Rubin reduction](./rubin-reduction-philosophy.md): Rubin subtracts at the production stage; Mann constrains at the lyric-writing stage. They are compatible.

content: Mann is one school of lyric writing. Pattison teaches object writing as a daily practice that fills the well; Mann observes from her life and excavates. Cave writes to a person; Mann writes from a thing. Bowie cuts up; Mann would never. None of these is the right way. They are different ways into specificity, which is the shared underlying value. ARLO should match the workflow to the user's instinct, not pick favorites.

content:
The producer (or a track-maker) builds the music first — beat, chord progression, sometimes a bass riff or sketch of an arrangement. The lyric and melody — together called the "topline" — are written *over* the existing track. The writer of the topline may never meet the producer. The song's existence depends on this division of labor.

This workflow is the dominant model for hip-hop since its inception (the beat-then-rhyme tradition), for modern pop since the Cheiron/Max Martin era of the 1990s, and for much of contemporary R&B, K-pop, dance, and Latin pop. John Seabrook's *The Song Machine* (Norton, 2015) is the journalistic reference; the formalized lineage runs through Denniz PoP at Cheiron Productions in Stockholm through Max Martin, Shellback, Stargate (Mikkel Eriksen and Tor Erik Hermansen), Dr. Luke, and later toplines from Ester Dean, Bonnie McKee, Julia Michaels, and Justin Tranter.

For songwriters trained in the singer-songwriter tradition — guitar in hand, lyric and music developed together — beat-first feels backwards. It isn't. It's a separate discipline with its own muscles, and many writers thrive in it once they learn the moves.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
Seabrook's term for the modern industrial workflow: a producer creates a track (beat + chord progression + arrangement skeleton), then ships it to one or more topline writers. The topline writer auditions melodies and lyrics over the track. The best ideas get demoed. The demo goes through label A&R and ultimately to an artist (who may add their own writes, may not). Multiple writers may be on the same track; multiple tracks may be in play for the same artist on the same day.

The Seabrook narrative makes the industrial scale visible. But the underlying *workflow* — start from a track, write a melody and lyric over it — is independent of the industrial setting. A bedroom producer who's made a 16-bar Logic loop and now wants a song over it is doing the same workflow at a one-person scale.

provenance.section: The "track-and-hook" model
provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
A lyric-and-melody-first writer makes choices about syllable count, meter, and stress from the inside, building the rhythm of the song from the words and notes simultaneously. A beat-first writer inherits the rhythm from the track and has to find the melody and lyric that *fit the pocket the track already established.*

The pocket is the constraint. The track's snare on 2 and 4, the kick pattern, the rhythmic feel of the chord stabs — these dictate where vocal phrases want to start and end. A topline that fights the pocket sounds wrong; a topline that lives in the pocket sounds inevitable.

For many writers, the constraint is liberating. The blank page has been replaced by a structured field. The job becomes finding what fits, rather than inventing from nothing.

provenance.section: Why this is its own discipline
provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
The most-analyzed beat-first toolkit in modern pop is what the songwriting community has come to call "melodic math" — a set of compositional rules associated with Max Martin and his Cheiron-lineage collaborators. The term was popularized by analyst Asaf Peres and discussed across Switched On Pop, American Songwriter, and music-business outlets.

Verified principles associated with Max Martin's working method:

- **Match syllable count line-to-line.** If line one of the verse is 8 syllables, line two is 8 syllables. Mirror imagery in meter. Adding or removing one syllable changes the melody enough that Martin treats it as a different melody.
- **Land the strong syllable on the strong beat.** The accented word in the line falls on a downbeat or strong subdivision; weak words fall on weak beats.
- **Match the melodic shape across symmetrical sections.** Verse 1 and verse 2 use the same melodic skeleton; the chorus is the chorus is the chorus.
- **Hook previews.** Plant fragments of the hook in the verse or pre-chorus so the chorus feels inevitable when it arrives.
- **Engineer the climax.** The chorus's highest note typically lands on the title or key phrase.

These rules are documented across multiple Switched On Pop and Peres analyses ([Top40 Theory](https://www.top40theory.com/melodic-math-course); [American Songwriter](https://americansongwriter.com/all-those-pop-songs-you-love-thats-not-magic-thats-melodic-math-and-this-is-how-it-works/); [Music Business Worldwide](https://www.musicbusinessworldwide.com/how-max-martins-songwriting-techniques-are-used-to-write-hit-after-hit-after-hit/)). ARLO should call them a *school*, not a universal rule — they describe Martin's practice and a wider lineage, not all of pop.

provenance.section: Max Martin's "melodic math"
provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
Beat-first as a discipline did not begin with Max Martin. The hip-hop tradition — from the 1970s block parties through MC Shan, Rakim, Nas, Eminem, Lauryn Hill, Kendrick Lamar — has always been beat-then-rhyme. The DJ or producer made the beat; the MC wrote to it. The lineage runs through Marley Marl, Pete Rock, DJ Premier, J Dilla, the Neptunes, Pharrell, Kanye, Mike WiLL Made-It, Metro Boomin.

The hip-hop beat-first move differs from pop melodic math in one key respect: the lyric is often more important than the melody, and the pocket is more rhythmic than tonal. But the underlying workflow — start from the track, write the lyric to fit — is the same.

provenance.section: The hip-hop origin
provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
Seabrook's reporting and many Sodajerker interviews describe a recognizable session shape:

1. The producer opens the track. Plays it on loop.
2. The topline writer listens without writing, sometimes for ten or twenty minutes, letting the track suggest a vocal energy and pocket.
3. The writer starts mumbling and humming over the track — what Ester Dean called working from "grunts and groans" toward words, with phrases pulled from a notebook or phone list of stockpiled images.
4. A melodic idea catches. The writer demos it on a scratch vocal mic.
5. Words are filled in, often after the melody is set. The melody-first / lyric-second order is normative in this workflow.
6. The hook is found first if possible — once the chorus is real, verses can be written backwards from it.
7. Demos go through revision passes; ones that don't catch are scrapped after a session.

This is one shape. Some topline writers prefer to write the lyric first and then fit it to the track. Some pairs work word-and-melody together in real time. The common thread is that the *track exists first*.

content:
The clean trigger: the user has a beat, a loop, a track, or an instrumental sketch — and they want a song over it. Or: the user has been forcing lyric-first songwriting and producing the same kind of song over and over, and wants out.

Other fits:

- The user is a producer who's made a track and doesn't know how to write the topline
- The user is a topliner working remotely with producers
- The user writes better with constraints — the open page is hostile, the track is friendly
- The user is in a genre where beat-first is the norm (hip-hop, modern pop, R&B, electronic, dance, Latin)
- The user has a co-write partner who makes tracks but doesn't write lyrics

When this workflow does not fit:

- The user is a fingerpicking singer-songwriter where the lyric, melody, and guitar evolve together as one organism (the workflow can be learned, but the user should know it's a discipline change)
- The user has a story-song where the lyric's narrative arc is the song
- The user is in the early ideation stage and doesn't have a track yet (use [`david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md`](./david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md) or [`tom-cosm-8-bar-loop-cycle.md`](./tom-cosm-8-bar-loop-cycle.md) to build to a track first)

provenance.section: When this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
1. **Listen to the track 5–10 times before writing anything.** Let the pocket land. Notice where the snare hits, where the chord changes are, where the empty space is, where the track wants vocal energy. Do not start writing yet.

2. **Find the empty space.** The places in the loop where there are no big production elements are where the vocal naturally goes. The track's emptiness is the writer's room.

3. **Mumble first.** Vocal melody on nonsense syllables. Don't try to write a lyric yet. The melody comes first because the melody has to fit the pocket; if you start with words, the words will fight the pocket.

4. **Find the chorus first if possible.** The hook is the song's identity. Once the chorus is real, verses can be written to lead into it.

5. **Mirror the meter line-to-line.** If verse-1 line-1 is 9 syllables, verse-1 line-2 wants to be 9 syllables (or a deliberate variation like 11). Verse 2 should match verse 1's syllable count line by line.

6. **Land strong words on strong beats.** Mark the downbeats; the accented words go there.

7. **Plant hook previews.** A fragment of the chorus melody or lyric appearing in the verse or pre-chorus makes the chorus feel inevitable when it lands.

8. **Engineer the climax.** Chorus's highest note typically lands on the title or key phrase. If it doesn't, consider why.

9. **Demo on scratch vocal.** Get it down. Listen back. Edit.

provenance.canonical-references: John Seabrook, *The Song Machine: Inside the Hit Factory* (Norton, 2015); Switched On Pop podcast (Charlie Harding & Nate Sloan) — Max Martin episodes; Asaf Peres / Top40 Theory melodic-math analyses; *Sodajerker on Songwriting* episodes with working topline writers; Cheiron Productions / Denniz PoP lineage materials

content:
**Fighting the pocket.** The most common failure. The writer ignores the track's rhythmic skeleton and tries to phrase the vocal in the patterns they're used to from lyric-first writing. The result is a melody that sounds disconnected from the production. Fix: re-listen to the track and identify the snare hits; phrase the vocal to land *with* them, not *across* them.

**Writing the lyric first.** Lyric-first inside a beat-first workflow tends to produce a topline where the syllable counts don't match the pocket. Even melodic-math writers usually melody-first, lyric-second. The lyric can be drafted as nonsense syllables that mark rhythm, then filled in.

**Ignoring the track's emptiness.** Some sections of the track are dense; some are sparse. The vocal goes in the sparse parts. Stacking vocals on top of an already-busy production decision is a mix problem the topline shouldn't create.

**Not matching meter section-to-section.** Verse 1's first line is 7 syllables; verse 2's first line is 11. The melody can't match unless the writer rewrites — and the listener feels the mismatch even without naming it. The discipline is to lock the syllable count once verse 1 is set.

**Treating the workflow as creatively diminished.** Some writers from the singer-songwriter tradition view beat-first as a lesser discipline. It's a different discipline. Max Martin's catalog is not a body of bad songs; it's a body of songs made under a different set of constraints. The constraints are real and learning to work inside them is a skill.

**Topline shopping the wrong track.** If the track is uninspiring, no topline will save it. The first listen should be a decision: is there a song here? If not, ask for a different track.

content:
In melodic-math pop, the lyric serves the melody. The line "I'm in your eyes, somehow" works because it lands on the right beats and contains the title; the meaning is built from a small palette of accessible imagery.

In hip-hop, the lyric *is* the song. The bars deliver characterization, narrative, wordplay, and meaning, with the beat as the framework. A great hip-hop topline can be intricate prosody (Rakim, MF DOOM, Kendrick Lamar) where the lyric demands re-listening.

Both are beat-first workflows. The internal weight of lyric vs. melody differs by genre. ARLO should not flatten this — when the user is writing pop topline, the melodic-math discipline is the rule; when the user is writing rap bars, the prosody-and-flow discipline (different topic, separate corpus file) takes over.

content: A producer-songwriter who hasn't internalized lyric-and-melody-first writing may stay stuck in beat-first forever — and produce tracks that are sonically inventive but lyrically thin. A singer-songwriter who refuses to learn beat-first will lock out a large portion of contemporary collaboration. ARLO's stance: both disciplines are worth learning, and the user choosing this workflow is deliberately leaning into the beat-first muscle. That's fine.

content:
The cut-up technique: write prose, cut it into fragments, rearrange the fragments. The juxtapositions that survive are often stranger and more truthful than anything you would have written linearly. The method comes from William S. Burroughs and Brion Gysin in the late 1950s, was systematized in Burroughs and Gysin's [*The Third Mind*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Third_Mind), and was adopted by David Bowie in the early 1970s and used across his career — from *Diamond Dogs* (1974) through *Outside* (1995) and the late records *The Next Day* (2013) and *Blackstar* (2016).

The premise for songwriters: a linear lyric can be too on-the-nose. The mind, told to "write a song about X," reaches for clichés about X. The cut-up sidesteps the reaching. The fragments collide and the writer becomes an editor, picking the lines that hit.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: William Burroughs & Brion Gysin, *The Third Mind* (1977 / written 1965–73); David Bowie interviews in the *Daily Mail* (2008), *Cracked Actor* BBC documentary (1975), Charlie Rose (1998); Bowie's "Verbasizer" software (1995, developed with Ty Roberts); Paul Trynka, *Starman: David Bowie — The Definitive Biography*; Chris O'Leary, *Pushing Ahead of the Dame*

content:
Burroughs credited Brion Gysin with discovering the technique in 1959 — Gysin sliced through a stack of newspapers with a Stanley knife and noticed the resulting strips of text formed unexpected sentences. Burroughs systematized it across the 1960s in *The Soft Machine*, *The Ticket That Exploded*, and *Nova Express*, then with Gysin produced *The Third Mind*, the canonical document of the technique.

Bowie discovered Burroughs in the late 1960s and the two met in late 1974 (the interview was published in *Rolling Stone* and is reproduced in multiple Burroughs biographies). The cut-up entered Bowie's working method around the *Diamond Dogs* sessions — Bowie has said in multiple interviews that he initially tried to adapt Orwell's *1984* into a Broadway-style record, was refused the rights by the Orwell estate, and rebuilt the material using cut-ups.

provenance.section: Origin and the Burroughs lineage
provenance.canonical-references: William Burroughs & Brion Gysin, *The Third Mind* (1977 / written 1965–73); David Bowie interviews in the *Daily Mail* (2008), *Cracked Actor* BBC documentary (1975), Charlie Rose (1998); Bowie's "Verbasizer" software (1995, developed with Ty Roberts); Paul Trynka, *Starman: David Bowie — The Definitive Biography*; Chris O'Leary, *Pushing Ahead of the Dame*

content:
The cleanest verbatim account from Bowie is the 2008 *Daily Mail* interview: "You write down a paragraph or two describing several different subjects… and then cut the sentences into four or five-word sections; mix 'em up and reconnect them." He added that he didn't always use the output verbatim: "I'll either take sentences verbatim as it spews them out, or there might be something within a sentence that triggers off an idea."

That's the two-modes acknowledgment. Some Bowie cut-ups are nearly raw output (the *Diamond Dogs* "Sweet Thing / Candidate / Sweet Thing (Reprise)" suite is the canonical example). Some are seed material that triggered an entirely different lyric, with the cut-up itself discarded. ARLO's workflow should honor both modes.

provenance.section: Bowie's own description
provenance.canonical-references: William Burroughs & Brion Gysin, *The Third Mind* (1977 / written 1965–73); David Bowie interviews in the *Daily Mail* (2008), *Cracked Actor* BBC documentary (1975), Charlie Rose (1998); Bowie's "Verbasizer" software (1995, developed with Ty Roberts); Paul Trynka, *Starman: David Bowie — The Definitive Biography*; Chris O'Leary, *Pushing Ahead of the Dame*

content:
By the mid-1990s Bowie wanted a faster cut-up engine. Working with programmer Ty Roberts (later co-founder of Gracenote), Bowie commissioned a Mac application called the [Verbasizer](https://www.vice.com/en/article/the-verbasizer-was-david-bowies-1995-lyric-writing-mac-app/) — described by Roberts as a tool where Bowie would enter 3–25 source sentences, the program would sort the words into grammatical columns (noun, verb, adjective), and then randomize-recombine into new sentences. The output for *Outside* (1995) was, in Bowie's words, "a real kaleidoscope of meanings and topic and nouns and verbs all slamming into each other."

A modern equivalent web tool [Verbasizer.com](https://verbasizer.com/) reproduces the practice. The mechanism — paper-and-scissors, Verbasizer, or modern LLM-as-cut-up-engine — is interchangeable. The cut-up itself is the constant.

content:
The clean trigger: the user has draft lyrics that feel linear, on-the-nose, paint-by-numbers. They might say "this lyric sounds like a Hallmark card" or "every line is the obvious line." The cut-up is the lateral-collision tool to dislodge that.

Other fits:

- The user has reams of journaling/prose about the song's subject and no lyrics
- The user wants imagistic, dream-logic lyrics rather than narrative
- The user is in a sonic-led project (production-first) where the lyric needs to feel as strange as the music
- The user has been writing the same kind of lyric across many songs and needs out

When this workflow does not fit:

- The user is writing a story-song that depends on narrative clarity (Lucinda Williams, John Prine, Townes Van Zandt school) — the cut-up will destroy the through-line they want
- The user is writing for a specific listener (use [`nick-cave-letter-method.md`](./nick-cave-letter-method.md))
- The user is writing a beat-first topline where the lyric has to scan to a rhythmic pocket (cut-up output rarely scans)

provenance.section: What this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: William Burroughs & Brion Gysin, *The Third Mind* (1977 / written 1965–73); David Bowie interviews in the *Daily Mail* (2008), *Cracked Actor* BBC documentary (1975), Charlie Rose (1998); Bowie's "Verbasizer" software (1995, developed with Ty Roberts); Paul Trynka, *Starman: David Bowie — The Definitive Biography*; Chris O'Leary, *Pushing Ahead of the Dame*

content:
1. Pick a subject. Even a vague one — "the year my dad got sick," "what it feels like to leave a city," "the dream I had Tuesday."

2. Write 3–5 paragraphs of prose about it. Don't think songs yet. Just write. Burroughs encouraged using found text too — newspaper headlines, journal entries, conversations overheard, even passages from books that have nothing to do with your subject.

3. Print or hand-copy the prose with wide margins.

4. With scissors, cut the prose into strips of 3–7 words each. Don't be careful — let some cuts fall in the middle of phrases.

5. Mix all the strips. Lay them out on a table in a new order, drawing strips at random or by feel.

6. Read the new sequence aloud.

7. Mark every line that surprises you, that you'd never have written linearly, or that makes you laugh in recognition.

8. Those lines are the seed of the lyric. Build verses and choruses around them, in whatever order they suggest. You'll add connective tissue. The connective tissue is yours; the seed is the cut-up's.

content:
Use [Verbasizer.com](https://verbasizer.com/), a Burroughs-style cut-up tool, or any text-randomization tool. Modern AI chat tools can be used as cut-up partners — ARLO itself can run this — but the discipline is the same: feed in source text, ask for randomized recombination, edit ruthlessly.

A specific recipe: paste 5–10 sentences of your prose draft. Ask for the words to be sorted by part of speech and recombined into 20 new sentences. Read all 20. Mark the 3–5 that hit. Discard the rest. Build the lyric around the marked lines.

content:
Bowie's own implication, across interviews: very little. The cut-up generates a large volume of nonsense in order to surface a few lines of unexpected gold. The proportion is something like 5–20% usable on a generous day. Writers who expect to use 80% of cut-up output will conclude the technique is broken; it isn't, the expectation was.

The editing pass is the work. The cut-up is not the lyric — it's the rough quarry the lyric is extracted from.

content:
Cut-up lyrics have a recognizable signature. They are:

- Image-rich and juxtaposition-led (a single line will hold two unrelated images and the friction is the meaning)
- Loose in narrative through-line (the song circles its subject rather than telling its story)
- Often dream-logical (the cohesion is associative rather than causal)
- Hard to "explain" but easy to feel

This is why Bowie used it most heavily for surreal/dystopian/Gothic material (*Diamond Dogs*, *Outside*, *Hallo Spaceboy*, parts of *Blackstar*) and largely set it aside for the more direct emotional material (*Hunky Dory*, *Heathen*'s ballads, "Where Are We Now"). When the song wants directness, cut-up is the wrong tool.

provenance.section: What it produces lyrically

content:
Verified examples from interviews and biographies:

- *Diamond Dogs* (1974) album generally, with the "Sweet Thing / Candidate / Sweet Thing (Reprise)" suite as the most-cited extended cut-up
- *Outside* (1995) — first major Verbasizer use
- *The Next Day* (2013) and *Blackstar* (2016) — continued use, particularly the more elliptical tracks
- "Hallo Spaceboy" (1995) often cited as cut-up

ARLO should resist attributing specific lines to cut-up generation unless the attribution is in a primary source — Bowie was protective of process and rarely identified which lines were cut-up output vs. which were authored linearly.

provenance.section: Songs Bowie produced with the method
provenance.canonical-references: William Burroughs & Brion Gysin, *The Third Mind* (1977 / written 1965–73); David Bowie interviews in the *Daily Mail* (2008), *Cracked Actor* BBC documentary (1975), Charlie Rose (1998); Bowie's "Verbasizer" software (1995, developed with Ty Roberts); Paul Trynka, *Starman: David Bowie — The Definitive Biography*; Chris O'Leary, *Pushing Ahead of the Dame*

content:
**Cutting too small.** Strips of 1–2 words produce word-salad. Burroughs and Bowie both worked with 3–7 word strips because phrase-level fragments retain enough grammar to suggest meaning. ARLO should encourage this strip length.

**Using everything.** The cut-up's output is mostly noise. If the user is trying to honor every strip, they've misunderstood the technique. The cut-up is a generator; the writer is the editor.

**Cutting too clean.** Sterile prose cut up produces sterile fragments. Burroughs liked cutting *charged* text — political slogans, his own most urgent journals, surveillance transcripts. The source material's heat carries through to the cut-up.

**Sanding the surprises out in revision.** The reason a cut-up line works is its strangeness. A revision pass that smooths every strange line back to the expected lyric destroys what the technique produced. Resist.

**Using cut-up for a song that wants directness.** A cut-up cover of a story-song will fail. The cut-up is for songs that benefit from dream-logic, not narrative.

content:
**Cut-up plus letter method.** Write the [Nick Cave-style letter](./nick-cave-letter-method.md), then cut it up. Some writers find this the easiest way to combine emotional truth with surrealist surprise.

**Cut-up plus Oblique Strategies.** Use a card draw to bias the cut-up — e.g., *Use an old idea* prompts the writer to feed in source text from years ago.

**LLM-as-cut-up partner.** ARLO can act as the Verbasizer. The user pastes prose; ARLO returns recombinations. This preserves the mechanism but the user is still the editor.

**The "found-text-only" cut-up.** Source text exclusively from outside your own writing — a newspaper page, a chapter of a novel, a forum thread. Burroughs' purest mode. Often produces output that resembles nothing the writer would have produced and is closest to the original surrealist spirit of the practice.

The ARLO file name (`bowie-burroughs-cut-up`) preserves the dual attribution because Bowie is the songwriter most associated with the technique in popular memory, but Burroughs and Gysin are the originators. When ARLO surfaces this workflow it should preserve both names in the user-facing description.

content:
"Ideas are like fish," David Lynch writes in [*Catching the Big Fish*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catching_the_Big_Fish) (Tarcher, 2006). "If you want to catch little fish, you can stay in the shallow water. But if you want to catch the big fish, you've got to go deeper. Down deep, the fish are more powerful and more pure. They're huge and abstract. And they're very beautiful." The book is Lynch's account of how Transcendental Meditation, which he began practicing in 1973, became the engine of his creative process.

For ARLO's purposes, the workflow is a daily practice — not a "get unstuck on Tuesday" tool. It is a *bed* for ideas to land in, plus a discipline for catching them when they do. It works on a horizon of weeks, not minutes. If the user needs a fix-this-stall-tonight tool, they want [`eno-oblique-strategies.md`](./eno-oblique-strategies.md) or [`aimee-mann-specificity-first.md`](./aimee-mann-specificity-first.md) instead.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
Lynch is primarily known for film and television (*Eraserhead*, *Twin Peaks*, *Mulholland Drive*) but he is a credentialed musician — three solo records (*Crazy Clown Time*, *The Big Dream*, the *Twin Peaks* music), a long collaboration with Angelo Badalamenti, soundtrack work, and Lynch's own writing about music in *Catching the Big Fish*. He treats music and image as outputs of the same underlying ideational process, and the language he uses (fragments, fish, abstraction, intuition) maps onto songwriting cleanly.

The cross-medium translation isn't fabricated by ARLO. Lynch himself writes about songs and lyrics as fish in the same school as images and scenes. ARLO inherits the framework.

provenance.section: Why a filmmaker's practice belongs in a songwriting corpus
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
There are two parts and they are not the same. Conflating them produces the most common failure mode of this workflow (treating meditation as a creative *exercise* rather than as the preconditions for one).

**Part one is the meditation itself.** TM is a specific technique: 20 minutes, twice a day, eyes closed, seated comfortably, using a mantra given by a certified TM teacher ([TM.org](https://www.tm.org/en-us/blog/david-lynch)). Lynch has practiced it daily, twice a day, since 1973. The practice is *not* visualization or guided imagery or "thinking about your song." It is a specific technique whose mechanism Lynch describes as letting the mind settle to its quietest level.

**Part two is the catching.** When a fragment surfaces — during meditation, after, on a walk, in the shower, in the middle of editing something else — the writer's job is to capture it before it's gone. Lynch is emphatic on this: "If a person forgets an idea that they love, it's a horror." He talks about the big ideas he has lost over the years that he will never get back, and uses that loss as the argument for writing everything down immediately ([The Marginalian](https://www.themarginalian.org/2014/05/09/david-lynch-interview-ideas-creativity/), [Austin Kleon](https://austinkleon.com/2020/09/24/david-lynch-on-ideas/)).

The workflow is the daily pairing of (a) the practice that produces fragments and (b) the capture discipline that doesn't let them escape.

provenance.section: The two parts of the practice
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
Not a finished song. Not even a verse. A fish is:

- A phrase that arrives intact ("the strangest dance," "she came home with the moon")
- A single sonic image (a guitar that sounds like a sigh, drums that drag behind by a tick)
- A character — who the song is *about*, suddenly clear
- A title
- A tempo and a feeling
- An emotional contour — "the song that starts angry and ends laughing"
- A juxtaposition (cathedral and gas station, baby and gun)

What it almost never is: a finished structural plan. That's the work of subsequent sessions, not the fishing trip.

provenance.section: What counts as "a fish"
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
Lynch's two rules for capture, drawn from his interviews and writing:

1. **Write it down immediately.** Don't wait. Don't trust yourself to remember. Have something near you at all times that can record an idea — Lynch favors paper, but a phone voice memo is the modern equivalent. He has compared losing an idea to losing a loved one.

2. **Write it down *as it arrived.*** Don't pre-edit, don't elaborate, don't try to extract the song from the fragment yet. The fish is the fish. Note it, return to the activity you were doing, leave it for the development pass.

For songwriters, the practical translation is: keep a song-fragment notebook (or notes app, or voice memos folder) that is separate from in-progress songs and separate from your journal. Its only contents are fish.

provenance.section: The capture rules
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
Lynch's TM-specific technique is one path; the broader pattern of *protected interiority + immediate capture* is reachable by many means. Sodajerker and other working-songwriter podcasts repeatedly surface the pattern across writers with no TM connection: Paul Simon's morning walk, Joni Mitchell's after-tea hours alone with the guitar, Dylan's "dreamtime" cassette habit. The mechanism is the same: a daily, defended, low-stimulus interval that lets the mind settle until something surfaces.

Writers without a TM background can substitute:

- Twenty minutes of unguided sitting in silence, twice daily
- A long walk without phone or podcast
- Morning pages (Julia Cameron's variant — three handwritten pages, stream-of-consciousness)
- A daily improvisation session at the instrument with no goal of producing anything

ARLO should be honest here: the specific TM-vs-substitute argument is contested. Some writers find TM transformative; others find equivalent benefit in unguided sitting or daily walks; some find no benefit at all. Lynch's *Catching the Big Fish* is the unambiguous primary source for the TM-specific claim. The "find your daily interval" generalization is ARLO's.

content:
The clean trigger: the user has been forcing material that isn't there. They sit down, produce three drafts, none of which are alive, and they feel creatively dry — not blocked, exactly, but barren. The diagnostic question is "have you written a song you liked in the last month?" If no, and the user has been *trying*, this workflow is the right one.

Also fits:

- The user is between projects and wants the next thing to surface organically
- The user has been deep in production/editing for weeks and feels the well is dry
- The user reports their ideas feel "thin" or "small" or "I can only catch little fish"

content:
- The user has a clear assignment with a deadline. Catching the Big Fish is not a sprint tool.
- The user has plenty of material and needs structure/finishing — go to [`rubin-reduction-philosophy.md`](./rubin-reduction-philosophy.md) or [`spoon-two-demos-a-week.md`](./spoon-two-demos-a-week.md).
- The user wants to write a topline over an existing beat — go to [`beat-first-topline-workflow.md`](./beat-first-topline-workflow.md).
- The user is in the middle of finishing a song and is procrastinating by starting a meditation practice. ARLO should call this out gently.

provenance.section: When this workflow does not fit
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
Lynch is famous for the position that the artist need not suffer to produce dark or difficult work. "Let your characters do the suffering" is the line. He argues that inner peace and external edginess can coexist; the popular romance of the tormented artist is, in Lynch's view, a productivity drag dressed up as authenticity.

For a songwriter who has been waiting for a *crisis* to unlock the next song, this is a genuine intervention. The implication: build the daily practice *before* you need it, fish for ideas from a stable baseline, and your output will be both deeper and more sustainable than the periodic-collapse method.

This is one school. Nick Cave, Tom Waits, and many others have written some of their best material out of acute personal turbulence. ARLO should not flatten the disagreement.

provenance.section: The "suffering" question — Lynch's productive heresy
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
**Treating meditation as the creative session.** It isn't. The practice is the preparation; the creative work still happens at the desk or the instrument. Fish don't write themselves.

**Failing to capture.** The bigger failure than not meditating. Lynch is emphatic — most people lose more ideas than they keep. Without the capture discipline, the practice produces fish that get away.

**Trying to develop fragments during meditation.** Notice them, return to the mantra (or to the breath), capture afterward. Forcing development *during* the practice tends to short-circuit both.

**Picking up the notebook only when stuck.** The capture habit has to be ambient. The big fish often surfaces during a phone call or while doing the dishes. The notebook (or phone) is always within arm's reach, or it isn't a practice.

**Expecting big fish quickly.** Lynch's view is that the depth comes with years of practice. A first-month user may catch shallow fish, miss them, get frustrated, and abandon. The workflow runs on a horizon of months. ARLO should set this expectation.

content:
Outside the scope of the workflow itself, but worth naming: the user accumulates a fragment notebook over weeks. Once a week or every fortnight, sit down with the notebook and read everything in it. Some fragments will be cold; some will spark. The ones that spark are the songs that want to be written next.

This is the contact between the Lynch practice and the actual song-finishing work. Cross-link [`dylan-notebook-cassette-discipline.md`](./dylan-notebook-cassette-discipline.md) — Dylan's archive review practice is the development-pass discipline for which Lynch's catching is the input.

provenance.section: The development pass — what the user does with caught fish
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content: Lynch's albums — *Crazy Clown Time* (2011), *The Big Dream* (2013), and the soundtrack work on the 2017 *Twin Peaks: The Return* — were produced over decades but feel like they emerged from the same atmosphere that produced *Inland Empire* and the late films. The catalog is a useful audit of what the practice can produce when sustained. The songs are not radio pop. They are slow, image-led, sonically committed. A user who tries the practice and produces something Lynch-adjacent should not be surprised. Trying the practice and producing late-period Beatles is also possible; the practice doesn't dictate the style, only the depth.

provenance.section: A note on Lynch's own music
provenance.canonical-references: David Lynch, *Catching the Big Fish: Meditation, Consciousness, and Creativity* (Tarcher, 2006); David Lynch Foundation materials; David Lynch interviews with The Marginalian and BFI; David Lynch Theater (Lynch's daily YouTube weather report and creative talks)

content:
The discipline has two parts:

1. **Capture everything.** Every line, every melody, every dream, every overheard phrase. You write it down — not into your head, not "I'll remember it," but onto paper or tape — in the moment it arrives.
2. **Edit ruthlessly later.** Capture and editing are separate phases. While capturing, no judgment. While editing, no mercy. The bridge between them is a quiet sit-down session, often weeks or months later, in which the capture archive becomes the writing material.

This is the practice the [Bob Dylan Archive in Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/) documents through its 100,000+ items of working materials. It is the practice Dylan describes throughout Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner-note interviews. And it is, plainly, the practice that produces a writer who can sit down and finish "Tangled Up in Blue" because he has a notebook full of lines waiting.

For ARLO users, the workflow is one of the most universally applicable in this stream — every writer who has ever lost an idea before they wrote it down has a use for it.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
The [Tulsa archive collection](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/) preserves Dylan's working materials on, as one researcher put it, "notebooks, shards of note pads, hotel stationery, business cards, even bits of brown paper bags." The capture surface is whatever's at hand. The discipline is: *write it before it disappears*.

For *Blood on the Tracks* alone there are three documented notebooks ([No Depression](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/)):
- **The "Red Notebook"** — the famous spiral notebook in which Dylan drafted 17 songs during summer 1974 in Minnesota.
- **Notebook 5** — coverless, worn, containing lyrics interleaved with phone numbers, art-supply lists, daily observations.
- **Notebook 6** — pale marine blue, described as "a gold mine" of compositional material.

Notebook 5 is the model. It's not a *songwriting* notebook in the precious sense — it's a *capture* notebook into which everything goes. Lyrics. Phone numbers. Lists. Things he overheard. The discipline is keeping a single capture surface always to hand, not segregating creative material from ordinary life.

The modern equivalent is the phone — voice memos, a Notes app, a single text file. The discipline is the same: one capture surface, always to hand, no editing during capture.

provenance.section: The capture half — what Dylan actually did
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
The notebooks also document the *opposite* discipline: extreme revision. As [Anne Margaret Daniel](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1) describes, nearly every page contains heavy revisions — "scribbles above, below, and in margins" with words added between lines, words crossed out, lines rewritten. She compares the density of revision to W.B. Yeats and finds Dylan even more thorough.

The two halves are not contradictory. They are sequenced. The capture phase is non-judgmental. The revision phase is ruthless. The notebook is the workspace for both — but on different days, in different states of mind.

Dylan himself, quoted in 1965: *"Now somebody else is going to be allowed to see what I said to myself."* That phrase — *what I said to myself* — is the capture phase. The revision phase is what makes the captured material into songs the world hears.

provenance.section: The revision half — what the notebooks reveal
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
The deep insight: **the same mental state cannot produce material and judge material.** When you're generating, judgment closes the channel. When you're judging, generation feels precious and protective.

The discipline of two phases — capture (no judgment) and edit (no mercy) — is how working writers across genres handle this. It's the same logic behind Pat Pattison's 10-minute object-writing (no editing during the timer), Dorothea Brande's "morning pages" (in *Becoming a Writer*), Anne Lamott's "shitty first drafts," and Mixerman's "decide once, move on" discipline. Dylan ran it longer and at scale: years of capture, then sit-down editing sessions.

The single biggest practical implication for an ARLO user: **the act of capture is not the act of writing the song.** Capturing is its own discipline. You're not allowed to think about whether the line is good. You're allowed to think about whether you got it down before it disappeared.

provenance.section: Why capture and editing must be separate

content:
The honest answer from the archive: *everything*. Hotel-stationery scraps. Phone numbers next to lyric fragments. Observations that may or may not become songs. Words you overheard. Half a melody hummed into the cassette in a car.

A practical filter for modern users: if you would feel a flicker of regret losing the thing, capture it. The flicker is the signal. You don't have to know yet whether it will become something. The job of the capture phase is *not* to evaluate. It's to preserve.

provenance.section: What counts as "worth capturing"
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
The notebook + cassette discipline maps cleanly to phone-based capture:

- **Voice memos** = the cassette. Hum the melody, sing the line, record the chord progression on the guitar. Don't title carefully; the date is fine.
- **Notes app / single text file** = the notebook. Lyric fragments, overheard phrases, titles, images, dream-words. One file, not 40 files. The friction of opening a new file is enough to lose ideas.
- **Photos** = the visual notebook. A chord diagram you drew on a napkin; a shape your hand is making on the neck.

The key discipline: **open the capture surface immediately.** Not later. Not "I'll remember this." Not "I'll write it down at home." Immediately. The five-second delay is the difference between a captured idea and an idea you'll never see again.

provenance.section: The modern equivalent — phone-based capture
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
The other half of the practice — and the half most casual notetakers skip — is the **periodic review**. The captured material does not become songs by itself. It becomes songs because the writer sits down with the capture archive and *reads it back*.

A working version:
- **Weekly or monthly cadence** (Dylan's appears to have been less regular; pick yours).
- **Block 60–90 minutes.** Single session.
- **Read every capture from the period.** Voice memos: listen to all of them in order. Text: scroll the file.
- **Mark the live ones.** A simple tag — star, asterisk, highlight. You're identifying which captures still have heat.
- **For the live ones, draft.** Take a starred fragment and write into it for 20 minutes. See what wants to come out.
- **Archive the rest.** They sit. Some will become songs in six months. Most won't. That's fine.

Without the review, the archive grows unused. With the review, it becomes the well you drink from.

provenance.section: The periodic review pass
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
- "Tangled Up in Blue" exists in multiple drafts in the Red Notebook and others. Verses are rewritten, characters renamed, the time-jumping structure refined draft by draft.
- "Idiot Wind" exists in significantly different lyrical forms across drafts.
- *Blood on the Tracks* was drafted across summer 1974 in Minnesota, then revised heavily before recording, then partially re-recorded in Minneapolis after Dylan's brother's notes. The notebooks document the path.

For a user, the relevant takeaway is not that Dylan revised heavily (which he did) but that the *capture archive made the revision possible*. You can only edit what you have on paper. The capture discipline produces the material that the revision discipline finishes.

provenance.section: Examples from Dylan's archive

content:
- You have ideas during walks, showers, driving, sleep — and you keep losing them.
- You're a lyrics-first writer who works in language.
- You have no capture discipline yet, or your captures are scattered across 40 apps.
- You want to write more without forcing more sessions — the capture lets you accumulate material in life.
- You're stuck in a project and have a *feeling* that there's relevant material in your phone notes from six months ago.

provenance.section: When this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
- You already have more material than you can use. Don't capture more; review what you have.
- You're production-first and your ideas are sonic, not linguistic. (Use A9 or A10 instead — the equivalent practice is recording snippets into your DAW's idea-bin.)
- You're in a tight deadline and need to finish, not generate.
- You're prone to capture-as-procrastination (collecting more material instead of finishing songs). The review phase is the fix here.

provenance.section: When this workflow does NOT fit
provenance.canonical-references: [The Bob Dylan Archive at the Bob Dylan Center, Tulsa](https://bobdylancenter.com/archive/); [Woody Guthrie Center — Bob Dylan Archive](https://woodyguthriecenter.org/archives/collections/bob-dylan-archive/); [Anne Margaret Daniel — Bob Dylan's *Blood On The Tracks* Notebooks](https://www.annemargaretdaniel.com/blog/2018/11/30/bob-dylans-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-1); [No Depression — Dylan's Three *Blood on the Tracks* Notebooks](https://nodepression.org/bob-dylans-three-blood-on-the-tracks-notebooks-not-just-red/); Cameron Crowe's *Biograph* (1985) liner notes interviews; *Bob Dylan: The Lyrics, 1961–2012*

content:
- **Capture without review.** You build a mountain of notes and never read them back. Schedule the review.
- **Capture-as-procrastination.** You always have time to collect more material but never to develop any of it. Force a ratio: for every capture session, one development session.
- **Friction in the capture surface.** You use a notes app that's slow to open, or a notebook that's not in your pocket. Reduce friction or change tools. The five-second delay loses the idea.
- **Captures that aren't legible later.** Voice memos with no context, lyric fragments without dates. Add minimal metadata at capture time — date, location, why you grabbed it.
- **Treating every capture as precious.** It's a capture, not a song. Most won't become anything. The few that do justify the discipline.
