content:
The card deck called [*Oblique Strategies*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oblique_Strategies) — subtitled "Over One Hundred Worthwhile Dilemmas" — was first published in January 1975 by Brian Eno and Peter Schmidt. Each card carries one cryptic instruction. The user, stuck on a creative decision, draws a card and is obliged to consider (or obey) the instruction. The point isn't that the instructions are wise. The point is that they're *lateral*: they refuse the local logic of the problem and force a sideways move.

The cards work because creative stalls are usually pattern-locks. The writer has been making the same kind of choice for the last hour and can no longer see other choices. An external nudge — even a random, slightly absurd one — breaks the lock. Eno and Schmidt understood this; they assembled the deck precisely as a structured interruption tool.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
The deck has two origin streams. Peter Schmidt, a painter, created "The Thoughts Behind the Thoughts" in 1970 — a box of 55 letterpress sentences printed on the backs of discarded prints. Eno, working in the studio in 1974, independently kept a handwritten list of strategies he found himself reaching for under pressure. When the two discovered the overlap, they merged the projects.

The first edition was published in January 1975 in a numbered, signed run of 500 sets — small black box, cards roughly 2¾" × 3¾", phrases drawn variously from I Ching aphorism, studio observation, and lateral provocation. Subsequent editions appeared in 1978 and (after Schmidt's death in 1980) in 1996 and 2001. The current authorized edition is sold by Eno's shop and remains the canonical print form ([enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)).

ARLO should preserve the attribution: Schmidt is the co-author. The deck is not just "Eno's cards."

provenance.section: Origin — two parallel projects
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
To resist the temptation to invent cards, ARLO should only cite verbatim cards documented from authoritative sources. From the Wikipedia entry (sourced to the published decks), verified card texts include:

- *Use an old idea.*
- *State the problem in words as clearly as possible.*
- *Only one element of each kind.*
- *What would your closest friend do?*
- *What to increase? What to reduce?*
- *Are there sections? Consider transitions.*
- *Try faking it!*
- *Honour thy error as a hidden intention.*
- *Ask your body.*
- *Work at a different speed.*

Other widely-circulated cards (e.g., *Emphasise differences*; *Make it as similar as possible*; *Repetition is a form of change*; *Use unqualified people*; *Abandon normal instruments*; *Look closely at the most embarrassing details and amplify*; *The most important thing is the thing most easily forgotten*) appear in multiple secondary citations including session accounts of the Berlin Trilogy. Cards beyond these published lists ARLO should NOT invent.

provenance.section: Verified card texts
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
The most-cited Eno usage is the Berlin Trilogy with David Bowie — *Low* (1977), *"Heroes"* (1977), and *Lodger* (1979) — though card usage was heaviest on the latter two. The session account for *"Heroes"* track "Sense of Doubt" is documented: Bowie drew *Emphasise the differences* and Eno drew *Make it as similar as possible*, and the two worked from those simultaneous instructions to produce the track. *Lodger* sessions saw heavier deployment — "Boys Keep Swinging" had band members swap instruments (drummer on guitar, etc.), "Move On" reused "All the Young Dudes" chords reversed, "Red Money" used backing tracks lifted from Iggy Pop's *The Idiot*. These are session-documented uses, not later mythology.

Eno also used the cards on his ambient records and as a producer on U2 and Talking Heads sessions; multiple other artists (Coldplay, R.E.M., LCD Soundsystem, MGMT, Phoenix, Bauhaus, The B-52's) have reported using the deck. The longevity is the evidence the practice works for many kinds of writers.

provenance.section: How Eno actually used the cards
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
There are two ways to use the deck and Eno is on record about both.

**Draw and obey.** The user makes the random draw a hard contract. Whatever the card says, the next move is dictated by it. This is the version most associated with the Berlin sessions — Bowie reportedly took the cards seriously and would obey them. The discipline is brutal but it guarantees the lock is broken.

**Draw and consider.** The user draws and reads, treats the card as a *prompt to think differently* but reserves the right to ignore the literal instruction. Most modern users adopt this mode. The risk is that the user smuggles in the original lock by rationalizing the card away ("doesn't apply here") and continues making the stuck choice.

ARLO's default for an opt-in workflow: draw-and-obey for the first card. If the user wants out, they have to draw a *second* card before discarding the first.

provenance.section: The "draw and obey" vs "draw and consider" question
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
The clean trigger: the user has been working on the same section for more than 30 minutes and is making the same kind of choice repeatedly. The signature is loops of "what if I changed it to X… no, that's worse… what if Y… no… what if Z…" where X, Y, and Z are all the same shape of choice.

Other fits:

- The user knows the song is finished but can't stop tweaking
- The user keeps writing the same chord progression for every demo
- The user has a section that almost works but won't commit to what's wrong
- The user is locked into a single arrangement idea and can't audition alternatives

provenance.section: When this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
- The user hasn't started yet (the cards work *against* a stuck state; they don't manufacture one to break)
- The user is in a meditation/reflection workflow (`david-lynch-catching-big-fish`)
- The user is in a stricter discipline workflow (`tom-cosm-8-bar-loop-cycle`, `spoon-two-demos-a-week`) — the cards' lateralism can sabotage these
- The user is in a co-write with someone who is not in on the practice (the cards work badly when half the room doesn't trust them)

provenance.section: When this workflow does not fit
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
The deck was assembled for studio and visual-art use. Songwriters have informally extended the practice with task-specific decks. ARLO can use the original deck as-is, or assemble a songwriting-specific deck along these lines (without inventing fake Eno cards):

- *Cut the last thing you added.*
- *Move the bridge to the second verse.*
- *Write the line you would not want anyone to hear.*
- *Halve the syllable count.*
- *Change the narrator.*
- *Replace the rhyme with a different rhyme on the same vowel.*
- *Start the song in the chorus.*
- *Sing the verse over a kick that's twice as fast.*

These are *ARLO-original* songwriting-specific moves, not attributed to Eno. The mechanism is the same as Eno's deck — external constraint forces lateral motion — but the attribution must stay honest.

provenance.section: Adapting Eno's deck for songwriting specifically
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content: App and web implementations exist ([obliquestrategies.ca](https://obliquestrategies.ca/), the Oblique Strategies iOS app, browser plugins). They preserve the deck's contents but lose two features of the physical deck: the *commitment* of having pulled a physical card (harder to redo), and the *unhurried* pace of unboxing the deck (it's a ritual, not a refresh). ARLO can offer digital draws, but the recommendation should be: draw once, write the card on paper, work to it, *then* allow a second draw if needed.

provenance.section: Digital implementations and what they preserve
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
The biggest failure mode is overusing the deck. If the user is drawing a card every five minutes, the cards have become the work instead of the interruption. The deck's value is *scarcity* — one or two draws per session, used at known stuck-points, returned to the work between. Eno himself has been clear that the cards are for emergencies, not for routine production.

If ARLO sees a user reaching for the cards on every section of every song, the workflow has eaten the writer. Switch to a non-card workflow.

provenance.section: The "draw too often" failure mode
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
**Drawing until you get a card you like.** This defeats the deck. Either obey the first card or commit to drawing-and-considering as the rule.

**Rationalizing the card into the original lock.** "*Use an old idea* — well, I'm using an old idea, that's the verse I already had." If the card endorses the current move, redraw or skip; the deck is only useful when it dislodges.

**Treating the card as content rather than constraint.** A card that says *Honour thy error as a hidden intention* is not a lyric. It's an instruction to look at the broken thing and decide it's actually finished.

**Using the deck to feel productive while finishing nothing.** The cards are most dangerous in the hands of a chronic procrastinator. The card is the prompt; the user still has to do the work.

provenance.section: Common failure modes
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content:
The cards pair well with:

- [`waits-break-the-demo.md`](./waits-break-the-demo.md) — Eno's lateral nudge often produces a *Waits-style* break of the polished demo.
- [`rubin-reduction-philosophy.md`](./rubin-reduction-philosophy.md) — the cards' *What to reduce?* prompt is the Rubin question.
- [`bowie-burroughs-cut-up.md`](./bowie-burroughs-cut-up.md) — Bowie used both the cards and Burroughs cut-up in the same era; they share an ancestor (lateral-move as method).

provenance.section: Cross-references to other ARLO workflows
provenance.canonical-references: Brian Eno & Peter Schmidt, *Oblique Strategies* (first edition January 1975, current edition via [enoshop.co.uk](https://enoshop.co.uk/products/oblique-strategies)); Eno, *A Year With Swollen Appendices* (1996); David Sheppard, *On Some Faraway Beach: The Life and Times of Brian Eno*; the Berlin Trilogy Bowie sessions (*Low*, *"Heroes"*, *Lodger*)

content: Some working writers find Oblique Strategies transformative. Others find them gimmicky. Eno himself has said the cards are "for when you need them," which is closer to a fire extinguisher than a daily practice. ARLO should not over-sell. Try one card. If the lock breaks, the workflow worked. If it doesn't, draw a second card. If two cards in, no lock has broken, the cards aren't the right tool today.

content:
Joni Mitchell built her songwriting around a single, radical claim: **the tuning is the song.** Change the tuning, the chord shapes change. The chord shapes change, the harmonic vocabulary changes. The harmonic vocabulary changes, the melody and the emotion change. By the time the tuning is set, half the song is already decided — into the wood of the guitar.

Mitchell has used over 50 different alternate tunings across her catalog ([Acoustic Guitar](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/)). The [JoniMitchell.com database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm) catalogs roughly 45 distinct essential patterns, with more than 60 apparent tunings counting capo positions and letter-name variants. Only two of her songs are in standard tuning ("Tin Angel" and "Urge for Going"). Everything else lives in an invented harmonic environment.

This workflow is named after Joni because she pushes it furthest, but it's a tradition: Nick Drake, Richard Thompson, John Martyn, Sandy Denny, Stephen Stills, the entire DADGAD-and-beyond folk lineage, plus modern players like Andy McKee and Kaki King all work this way. If you play guitar and your songs keep coming out sounding the same, the tuning-first approach is the most reliable lateral move available.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
The mechanic is concrete: a new tuning produces unfamiliar chord shapes which produce unfamiliar music. Your left hand cannot rely on muscle memory; it has to find shapes. The shapes you find are the shapes that *fit the hand on this tuning* — not the shapes any guitarist would reach for.

Mitchell's own description in [Acoustic Guitar](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/): *"You're twiddling and you find the tuning. Now the left hand has to learn where the chords are, because it's a whole new ballpark, right?"* That phrase — *whole new ballpark* — is exactly the songwriting effect. You can't write a Joni song in standard tuning because Joni's hand isn't moving the way standard tuning moves a hand.

She also says, more philosophically: *"It's only through error that discovery is made, and in order to discover you have to set up some sort of situation with a random element — a strange attractor, using contemporary physics terms."* The tuning is the strange attractor. It introduces error on purpose.

provenance.section: How a tuning produces a song
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
Mitchell describes the tuning-discovery as both intuitive and environmental. She'll twist the pegs until "these chords I was getting by twisting the knobs on the guitar until I could get these chords that I heard inside that suited me, they feel like my feelings."

She has also written tunings to the *day*. For "The Magdalene Laundries" from *Turbulent Indigo* she tuned to "the day in a certain place, taking the pitch of birdsongs and the general frequency" ([Acoustic Guitar](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/)). The tuning is B F# B E A E.

For most working guitarists, the practical version is less mystical: pick a tuning, sit with it, find a shape that surprises you, follow the shape.

provenance.section: Joni's discovery process — how she finds a tuning
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
A starter list from her catalog ([JoniMitchell.com](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm), [Acoustic Guitar](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/)):

- **D modal (DADGBD)** — early-era Joni; folk-rooted, open and ambiguous.
- **Open G (DGDGBD)** — "Marcie", "Nathan LaFraneer", "Little Green" (capo 5).
- **Open D (DADF#AD)** — blues-derived, common starting point.
- **CGDGBD** — used on "Sweet Bird" and "Cold Blue Steel" — slightly darker open-tonal feel.
- **Open E (EBEG#BE)** — "Both Sides Now", "Big Yellow Taxi" (early arrangements), "Chelsea Morning".
- **BF#C#EF#B** — the *Hejira* tuning; floating, ambiguous, characteristic of her mid-70s sound.
- **DADEAD** — "Slouching towards Bethlehem", "Cool Water" — close to DADGAD with a sus character.
- **C#G#D#F#G#C#** — "My Secret Place" — low and shimmering.
- **BF#BEAE** — "The Magdalene Laundries" — exceptionally low; haunted.

She systematized her own naming convention because the existing notation didn't scale. The Joni system: write the low-string letter, then the fret-numbers needed to tune each successive open string. Standard tuning in Joni notation is "E 55545". The "Marcie" tuning DGDGBD is "D 57543" ([Howard Wright's notation explainer](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); [JoniMitchell.com](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm)).

provenance.section: Canonical Joni tunings to try
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
When you sit with an unfamiliar tuning, **don't try to play the chords you already know.** That is the failure mode. You re-derive standard-tuning shapes and end up writing a standard-tuning song that happens to be in weird tuning.

The Joni discipline is closer to this:
1. Drop into the tuning. Strum the open strings.
2. Move one finger to a fret. Listen. Move it to a different fret. Listen.
3. Find a *shape* — a finger placement — that produces a sound you want to keep hearing.
4. Move that shape up and down the neck. Each fret is a new chord because the tuning is open.
5. Find a second shape that goes well with the first.
6. *Now* you have a progression — and you have no idea what the chords are called, and you don't need to.

The chord names are post-hoc. Mitchell herself often couldn't and didn't name the chords she was playing; she described them by feel and by shape.

provenance.section: The "shape, not chord" approach
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
Once you have two or three shapes that move together, the writing process is:

1. **Find the song's tempo and meter** by strumming or fingerpicking the shapes naturally. Don't force a meter; let the tuning suggest one.
2. **Sing nonsense over it.** The harmonic ambiguity of open tunings (lots of unresolved sus and add chords) often invites a vocal that floats above rather than locking to the root. Sing until you find a melody that fits the hand-of-the-tuning.
3. **Let the lyric come from the feel.** Mitchell's tunings *suggest* emotional registers — open G feels warm and pastoral; the *Hejira* tunings feel road-and-distance; the very low tunings feel underground. Trust the register.
4. **Don't transcribe to standard tuning until you have to.** If you have to teach the song to a band, the chords have names, you can find them. But while you're writing, keep it in the tuning's vocabulary.

content:
Mitchell uses capo extensively. "Little Green" is the Marcie tuning (DGDGBD) with a capo on fret 5, transposing the open strings to GCGCEG. This is how she expanded her tuning library — same pattern, different absolute pitches, different range for her voice.

The pragmatic implication: you can re-use a tuning pattern at different capo positions to fit different vocal ranges or different emotional registers. The pattern is the harmonic identity; the capo is the pitch slot.

content:
- You're a guitarist whose songs all sound the same — same shapes, same progressions, same feel.
- You've exhausted standard-tuning chord vocabulary and want new harmonic territory without learning jazz voicings.
- You're writing a song that wants ambiguity (lots of unresolved chords, droning notes, sus colors).
- You write best at the instrument with your hands, not at a piano or notation.
- You're stuck in a writing rut and need a structural reset.

provenance.section: When this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
- You don't play guitar. Pianists have a piano-only analogue (write the song in a key you don't normally use), but the tuning-first move specifically isn't available.
- You're writing for a band that doesn't want a single-guitar-driven song.
- The song needs to be performed at sessions where re-tuning between songs is impractical (open-mic, busking).
- You're a co-writer working with someone who plays standard-tuning lead — they'll have to navigate the unfamiliar chords too.
- You're writing a specific arranged production and the tuning's harmonic ambiguity will get buried.

provenance.section: When this workflow does NOT fit
provenance.canonical-references: [Acoustic Guitar — The Guitar-Tuning Odyssey of Joni Mitchell](https://acousticguitar.com/the-guitar-tuning-odyssey-of-joni-mitchell/); [JoniMitchell.com tuning patterns database](https://jonimitchell.com/music/tuningpatterns.cfm); [Guitar Player — Joni Mitchell on inventing her own guitar tunings](https://www.guitarplayer.com/guitarists/i-got-my-fingers-rapped-with-a-ruler-they-said-why-would-you-want-to-compose-music-joni-mitchell-on-why-she-invented-her-own-guitar-language-from-more-than-50-tunings); [Howard Wright — Joni Mitchell guitar notation system](https://www.hakwright.co.uk/music/joni_notation.html); Malka Marom, *Joni Mitchell: In Her Own Words*

content:
- **Standard-tuning shapes in disguise.** You re-derive familiar shapes and end up writing a song you could have written in standard tuning. Discipline: only use shapes that *only work in this tuning*.
- **Tuning-as-cosmetics.** You write a standard-tuning song, then tune the guitar weird for the recording. That's not this workflow; that's overdub texture.
- **No commit.** You keep changing the tuning every session. The tuning is supposed to be the song's environment. Commit to one tuning for one song.
- **Capo confusion.** Re-tuning your strings AND capoing introduces enough complexity that transcribing the song later becomes painful. Notate as you go.
- **Lost in the strings.** Open tunings have a lot of sympathetic resonance; you may write a 6-minute song you can't edit. Set a length constraint up front.

content:
The deep principle — *introduce a structural change to your instrument that breaks muscle memory* — applies beyond guitar:

- **Pianists:** write in a key with lots of black keys you don't normally use. F# major. Db major.
- **Keyboardists:** swap to an unfamiliar synth patch and let the patch's affordances dictate the writing.
- **DAW writers:** force a tempo or time signature you don't use (5/8, 6/4, 87 BPM).
- **Singers:** write to a melody an octave outside your usual range.

The mechanic is the same: a structural constraint that produces a *whole new ballpark*.

content:
Music Row in Nashville operates on a documented, repeatable co-writing protocol that has produced the majority of mainstream country songs (and a large share of the modern country-pop, country-rock, and Nashville-affiliated singer-songwriter material) for several decades. The protocol is not a vibe; it is a working method with concrete rules. Writers who learn the protocol can walk into a room cold and have a finished song by the end of the day.

This file documents the protocol as taught by NSAI (Nashville Songwriters Association International), as written by Jason Blume in *Six Steps to Songwriting Success*, and as discussed in interviews with working Music Row writers (Liz Rose, Bobby Braddock, Don Schlitz, Holly Gleason, Don Henry, and others). The protocol applies most cleanly to Nashville country and country-adjacent writing; it adapts for pop and other co-writing contexts but should not be assumed universal.

The single most important framing: **this is a *room* discipline.** Most of what follows breaks down if writers are working asynchronously over email and file-shares.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: Jason Blume, *Six Steps to Songwriting Success* (Revised Edition, Penguin Random House); [NSAI — So You're Lookin' to Co-Write](https://www.nashvillesongwriters.com/so-you-re-lookin-co-write); [NSAI — 5 Tips for Co-Writing](https://www.nashvillesongwriters.com/5-tips-co-writing); [NSAI — Royalties & Rights Summary](https://www.nashvillesongwriters.com/royalties-rights-summary); [NSAI — Basics of Co-Writing (George Teren)](https://nashvillemusicguide.com/nsai-the-basics-of-co-writing/); [LANDR — Songwriting Splits Explained](https://blog.landr.com/songwriting-splits-explained/); [Songpact — Co-Writing Splits Guide](https://songpact.com/songpact-blog/co-writing-splits-co-writer-agreements-guide); [American Songwriter — Jason Blume profile](https://americansongwriter.com/jason-blume-offers-steps-to-success/); Holly Gleason — *Woman Walk the Line* (University of Texas Press, 2017)

content:
The typical Nashville co-write session: **2–3 writers**, occasionally 4. Sessions run **roughly 3 hours**, with a hard cap around 4. The aim is **one song per session**. If you don't have a song at the end, you have a draft to finish later — but the discipline is to finish.

Roles in the room vary by writer combination, but a common configuration is **one strong topliner (melody), one strong lyricist, and one strong "hooker"** (someone whose strength is hook concepts and titles). Writers often rotate roles depending on the song. Some sessions add a track producer who brings a beat/track ([Songpact](https://songpact.com/songpact-blog/co-writing-splits-co-writer-agreements-guide)); this is increasingly common in country-pop and is the bridge to the modern toplining workflow (A8).

The room has a single working table or guitar circle. Phones are mostly off. The vibe is professional but warm — closer to a doctors-collaborating-on-a-case than to a jam session. NSAI's [5 Tips for Co-Writing](https://www.nashvillesongwriters.com/5-tips-co-writing) explicitly encourages "allowing time for connection" — first-time co-writes start with conversation, catching up, getting to know each other before any songwriting starts.

provenance.section: The room — who, how many, how long

content:
Working Nashville writers do not show up empty-handed. NSAI's workshop guidance ([George Teren](https://nashvillemusicguide.com/nsai-the-basics-of-co-writing/)) calls this the "pre-writing" phase: before the session, each writer accumulates **titles, hook concepts, and partial ideas** in a personal list. Some writers maintain a running "title book" they bring to every session.

Before the session begins, the writers share what they brought. The first half-hour is often spent hunting for a concept — a title, a hook, an angle — that "has legs." A concept has legs when:

- The writers can all imagine the chorus.
- It's specific enough to write toward but open enough to develop.
- It's not too close to a recent hit.
- It connects to a current commercial slot (a specific artist, a specific genre direction).

Once the concept is picked, the song's *target* is also often named: "this is for [artist], or for [type of artist], or for the cut date next month." The target shapes the writing.

content:
The Music Row convention is **write the chorus first**. This is doctrinal in NSAI's teaching and in Blume's *Six Steps*. The reasoning:

- The chorus carries the title (which is usually the hook).
- If the chorus doesn't work, the verses won't save it.
- Writing the chorus first forces the writers to agree on what the song is actually about.

Once the chorus is solid, verses follow. The bridge (if there is one) is often written last. Many modern country songs skip the bridge or use a minimal "tag" instead. The structure decisions are usually informed by what's getting radio play in the relevant slot.

content:
The protocol has two opposing modes that the writers move between:

- **Generative mode** (early): no bad ideas. Anything goes. Throw out lines, melodies, concepts without judgment. This protects the creative flow and keeps the room open. NSAI's *5 Tips* explicitly notes: "you can fix a song that's rough around the edges, but you can't fix a song you don't write."
- **Editorial mode** (later): ruthless. The writers actively cut lines that don't serve the song. Killed darlings include your own best line if it doesn't fit. The discipline of letting your best line go for the song's sake is one of the protocol's hardest demands.

A working room can shift between modes multiple times per session. Skilled writers signal the shift verbally ("OK, let's tighten this"). Less experienced writers can stall in either mode — too generative and the song never closes; too editorial and nothing gets written.

content:
A working convention: **any writer can veto any line**, but the veto comes with an obligation. You don't just say "no" — you say *"what if instead...?"* and propose. This keeps the room collaborative rather than adversarial. NSAI's workshops teach this directly: avoid settling for mediocrity, but propose alternatives rather than block.

Working writers describe the discipline as needing strong opinions, lightly held. You advocate hard for what you think serves the song, but you let go quickly when the room moves a different direction. The Golden Rule, per NSAI's George Teren: "Do unto your co-writers what you would have your co-writer do unto you."

content:
The split sheet is the **contractual record of who owns what percentage of the song**. It is signed at the end of the session, before anyone leaves the room. Skipping or deferring the split-sheet conversation is one of the protocol's named failure modes — disputes years later are vastly harder to resolve than a five-minute conversation in the room.

### What the split sheet contains

Per [Songpact's guide](https://songpact.com/songpact-blog/co-writing-splits-co-writer-agreements-guide):

- **Song title** (working title is fine).
- **Writer names**, full legal names.
- **Agreed percentages**, summing to 100%.
- **PRO membership** for each writer (ASCAP, BMI, SESAC, or international equivalent).
- **IPI / CAE numbers** — the international identifier for each writer.
- **Publisher information** if a writer has a publisher.
- **Contact info** — email, phone.

The sheet doesn't have to be elaborate. A photo of a handwritten sheet, or a digital one signed in Songpact/Splitsifter/email, is enough. What matters is *that it exists* and is signed by all writers the day of the session.

### The Nashville Rule — equal splits

The default Music Row convention is **equal splits between everyone in the room**, regardless of who contributed what. Three writers = 33⅓% each. Two writers + a producer who brought the track = often three-way equal, sometimes producer gets a different cut.

The reasoning ([LANDR](https://blog.landr.com/songwriting-splits-explained/)): contribution is genuinely hard to quantify. The lyricist who wrote one perfect line may have done more than the topliner who wrote four mediocre verses. Equal splits avoid an unwinnable post-hoc argument. They also preserve the relationship — co-writers who fight about splits don't write together again.

### The "change a word, get a third" convention

A controversial Nashville convention: if a writer with star-level leverage changes a single word, they get a full writer credit and corresponding percentage. Whether you accept this depends on your situation. The honest version of the rule: leverage matters in splits. Writers who are willing to walk away from a deal preserve negotiation power. Writers who need the cut will accept terms that reflect that need.

### Contribution-based alternative

Some writers prefer **contribution-based splits**: percentages that reflect actual input. Lyrics 50%, melody 40%, arrangement 10%, for example. This is more common in pop and rock contexts than in classic Nashville. The discipline is the same: agree before recording, sign before leaving the room.

content:
The aspirational version of the protocol is "finish in the room." A song that leaves the session unfinished often dies in email rounds. But experienced writers recognize when the room has done what it can:

- **Finish in the room** when: chorus, verses, bridge if needed, all sections complete; you can play the song from start to finish; everyone leaves with the same demo file or working lyric sheet.
- **Take it home** when: there's a structural question that needs sitting with; a verse isn't landing and a fresh ear will help; the room is fading and forcing the close will hurt the song.

If you take it home, the protocol still wants a finishing deadline. NSAI workshop guidance: agree on a return date before leaving. "We'll have V2 and bridge by Friday." Otherwise the song stalls indefinitely.

content:
A real Nashville co-write can be uncomfortable. Three creative people in a room for three hours produces friction. Working writers have signals:

- **Hour 1 with no concept.** Probably the wrong room or the wrong day. NSAI's *5 Tips* explicitly says "sometimes your writing session turns into a therapy session, and that is ok!" — but the session also has to remain a writing session at some level.
- **Two writers carrying the third.** Either reset the room dynamic or accept that this session is one of those where one writer pulled back. Adjust splits if it's structural; let it go if it's a one-off.
- **A line you love that no one wants.** The veto is in play. Either propose-and-let-go, or save the line for another song.
- **Genuine creative mismatch.** Some writer pairs don't work. Finish the session politely, mark each other off the list, move on.
- **Push through or call it.** Around the 2.5-hour mark, working writers know: is there a song here, or are we manufacturing? If the latter, finish what you have and call it.

content:
The Music Row protocol doesn't end at the session. The song moves into:

- **Demo recording.** Sometimes the writers record the demo themselves; sometimes a publisher commissions a demo (a "tape day"). The demo is what gets pitched.
- **Publisher pitch.** Each writer's publisher (or the unattached writer themselves) pitches the song to artists, A&R, producers. Many songs are written for specific cut dates; others are pitched cold.
- **Cuts and royalties.** If the song is recorded by an artist, royalties flow through the PROs to the writers per the split sheet. This is why the split sheet is contractually load-bearing.

This downstream isn't optional in the Music Row context — it's why the protocol exists. The protocol is shaped by the goal: write commercial songs that get cut. A first-time co-writer doesn't have to engage the full downstream, but the protocol's shape is informed by it.

content:
The room protocol adapts cleanly to pop co-writes, less cleanly to indie collaborative writing. Pop adaptations:
- Often more writers in the room (4–6 for major-label sessions).
- Producer + topliner + lyricist roles more separated.
- Splits often pre-negotiated by publishers before the session.

Indie adaptations:
- Smaller rooms (2 writers).
- Equal splits are still the default.
- Less pre-write structure; more jamming.
- The split sheet discipline is *still* worth preserving even in casual indie co-writes.

- You're writing for a commercial slot (artist cut, sync, publisher pitch).
- You write better with structure and other writers in the room.
- You're a strong specialist (lyricist OR topliner OR hooker) and want to partner with complementary writers.

content:
- You're a solo writer who works best alone.
- You're writing personal-confessional material with no commercial intent.
- The co-writer in question isn't on the same protocol page (mismatched expectations destroy sessions).
- You're allergic to the chorus-first discipline (some songs really do start from the verse).
- You're in a stem-trading remote collaboration, not a room. The protocol adapts but a lot of its discipline depends on the room.

content:
- **Skipping the split sheet.** Highest-priority failure. Always sign before leaving.
- **Hour-1 generative drift.** No concept by hour 1. Force a concept by hour 1.5 or end early.
- **Stuck in editorial mode.** The room kills every line. Reset to generative, agree to come back to editing in 30 minutes.
- **Writers not on the same time scale.** One writer wants 6 hours, another wants 2. Agree on length at the start.
- **Mismatched stakes.** One writer treats it as a session for a cut date; another treats it as casual. Discuss the target before starting.
- **Veto without proposal.** Killing lines without "what if instead" — the room turns adversarial. Enforce the proposal rule.
- **Taking the song home without a deadline.** Songs die in indefinite email rounds. Agree the return date in the room.

content:
This workflow recipe is a synthesis. Nick Cave has not, on the public record, described "write the song as a letter to a specific person" as a named method. What he *has* documented — across [The Red Hand Files](https://www.theredhandfiles.com/), his book-length conversation [*Faith, Hope and Carnage*](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Faith,_Hope,_and_Carnage) with Seán O'Hagan, and interviews — is a constellation of practices that this workflow stitches into one operational recipe. Treat the recipe as Cave-adjacent, not Cave-canonical. The constituent moves are verifiable; the bundle is the ARLO-side construction.

The premise: when a lyric keeps coming out vague, abstract, or universal, the writer has lost contact with the actual person, moment, or feeling that originated it. Reaching back to a single recipient — writing the song *to* someone — restores the contact. The song then hides inside the letter, and the writer's job in the second pass is to extract it.

provenance.section: The premise — honest about what this is
provenance.canonical-references: Nick Cave, *The Red Hand Files* (theredhandfiles.com); Nick Cave & Seán O'Hagan, *Faith, Hope and Carnage* (Canongate, 2022); Nick Cave interviews in Interview Magazine, NPR, Kill Your Darlings, Sharp Magazine

content:
Three documented Cave practices justify the attribution.

First, The Red Hand Files is itself a letter project. Since 2018, Cave has answered fan questions in weekly email letters laid out on cream-coloured paper, signed "with love, Nick." The Cambridge University Press chapter on the Files calls them an exercise in epistolary spiritual intimacy ([Cambridge / *Epistolary Entanglements*](https://www.cambridge.org/core/books/abs/epistolary-entanglements-in-film-media-and-the-visual-arts/spiritual-intimacies-of-the-red-hand-files-how-long-will-i-be-alone/A8FE7169B308D3A41708F7909AA1BAA4)). The format isn't decorative; Cave has chosen direct address as his prose mode.

Second, Cave repeatedly describes songs as emerging from a single concrete image. In his 2014 NPR interview he describes [*Ghosteen* growing from "the image of a huge ice sculpture of a man melting slowly in the sun"](https://www.npr.org/2014/09/16/348727370/nick-cave-the-creative-process-is-an-altered-state-in-itself). In the Kill Your Darlings interview he describes writing "As The Waters Cover The Sea" by observing his wife and transforming the ordinary moment into the visionary ([Kill Your Darlings](https://www.killyourdarlings.com.au/article/gerard-elson-in-conversation-with-nick-cave/)).

Third, Cave treats songwriting as a daily desk job. The Line of Best Fit summary of [Red Hand Files Issue #218](https://www.thelineofbestfit.com/news/latest-news/nick-cave-important-part-of-songwriting-is-to-sit-down-at-desk-pick-up-pen) reports him saying the most important undertaking of his day is "to simply sit down at my desk and pick up my pen," and that songs arrive only "when I am at work." Long-form interviews confirm he keeps roughly 9-to-5 hours in a bare office when a record is being written.

The letter method is the songwriter's-bench fusion of these three: the form (letter), the seed (one concrete image of one real person), and the discipline (sit down and write the letter even when nothing is coming).

content:
The clean trigger condition: the user has a strong emotion attached to a real person or real event, but every draft they produce comes out as a universal pop statement that could be about anyone. The classic signature is the line that uses the word *we* or *somebody* when it should use a name.

Adjacent fits: the writer is grieving, in love, furious at one person specifically, or wrestling with an unresolved conversation. Cave's own *Skeleton Tree* and *Ghosteen* both emerged from grief over the death of his son Arthur and circle the dead without ever pretending to address the universal ([Wikipedia / Ghosteen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ghosteen)).

Mis-fits: a purely sonic exploration where no real person is the subject; a producer-led track waiting for a topline; a beat-first workflow where the lyric exists to fit a rhythmic pocket. In those cases see [`beat-first-topline-workflow.md`](./beat-first-topline-workflow.md) instead.

content:
Two recipient archetypes, with different consequences.

**The unreachable recipient.** Someone dead, gone, estranged, or far away. The letter will never be read by them. This loosens the writer's editing — they're free to say the thing they couldn't say. Cave's *Skeleton Tree* is the towering example: the songs cluster around Arthur without naming him in a way that closes the door.

**The reachable recipient.** Someone who could, in theory, read this. The constraint is sharper. The writer must reckon with consequences. The discipline tends to produce more specific, less melodramatic work — but some writers seize up entirely under it.

Pick deliberately. The recipient choice changes what the song can do.

content:
Plain prose. Date in the corner. "Dear ___" at the top. The user writes for thirty to sixty minutes without lifting the pen, addressing this person directly, in the present tense if they're alive and past tense if they're not. No line breaks, no rhymes, no choruses. Sensory specifics — what the room smelled like, what they said, the color of the jacket. The Pat Pattison object-writing discipline applies here: the seven senses, including the kinesthetic and organic (see [`corpus/lyrics/object-writing-and-sensory-imagery.md`](../../lyrics/object-writing-and-sensory-imagery.md)).

Two prohibitions: no abstractions and no universals. *Love* is an abstraction. *Loss* is an abstraction. *Hope* is an abstraction. The image of her standing at the sink in the green sweater is not. The line "everybody hurts" is universal. The line "you wouldn't get out of the car" is not.

provenance.section: What the letter looks like before it becomes a song
provenance.canonical-references: Nick Cave, *The Red Hand Files* (theredhandfiles.com); Nick Cave & Seán O'Hagan, *Faith, Hope and Carnage* (Canongate, 2022); Nick Cave interviews in Interview Magazine, NPR, Kill Your Darlings, Sharp Magazine

content:
Print or save the letter. Walk away for a few hours; ideally sleep on it. Then read it as a stranger would.

The song hides in the most concrete passages. Mark them. The chorus often appears as the line the writer keeps almost-saying and pulling back from — the line that's been building. The verses are the surrounding scenes. The bridge is frequently the moment the letter turns — the paragraph where the writer admits something they hadn't planned to admit.

Extract those. Reshape into meter and rhyme. Most of the letter will be cut. That's the design — the letter was the contact-restoration tool, not the finished artifact.

provenance.section: What to do when the letter is finished

content:
A letter is second-person by definition: *you*, addressed. The extracted song inherits this. Direct address is the default register of pop ([corpus/lyrics/point-of-view-tense-and-narrator.md](../../lyrics/point-of-view-tense-and-narrator.md)), but the letter method tends to produce a particular *kind* of direct address — specific second-person rather than generic second-person.

Generic "you": "you make me feel" (could be anyone). Specific "you": "you smoked at the funeral" (only the recipient). The second is what Aimee Mann calls earning the abstraction by way of the specific — and Cave's lyrics, line by line, are full of it (see [`aimee-mann-specificity-first.md`](./aimee-mann-specificity-first.md) for the adjacent workflow).

If the second-person address is going to alienate the listener, the writer can switch POVs in revision. But the letter method's gift — the *specificity* — should survive the POV change.

content:
Cave's own answer to writer's block, given in [Red Hand Files Issue #108](https://www.theredhandfiles.com/the-lyrics-just-arent-coming/): "when something's not coming, it's coming." His advice is patience plus showing up at the desk. The line "ideas are not in here, they're out there, struggling to get in" appears across multiple interviews and is consistent with his Red Hand Files cosmology.

Operationally: if the letter won't start, the user should write the date and "Dear ___" and the first three sentences of any conversation with that person. Often the bottleneck is the opener, not the content. Once the first paragraph is on the page, the rest usually follows.

If after a forty-five-minute attempt nothing has come, the workflow should be abandoned for the day — not the song. Cave has been clear that the discipline is showing up, not forcing output. The next day's session may unlock what today's did not.

content:
[*Faith, Hope and Carnage*](https://www.amazon.com/Faith-Hope-Carnage-Nick-Cave/dp/0374607370) is explicit that songwriting in its early stages is "agonising," and Cave describes himself as "wracked with anxiety." This isn't a problem to be solved. It's the texture of the work. The letter method does not eliminate the anxiety; it gives the anxiety something concrete to attach itself to — the recipient, the room, the smell of the jacket — instead of the impossible task of saying everything to everyone.

Telling the user that anxiety is the cost, not the bug, is part of what this workflow accomplishes.

content:
**The letter becomes a journal entry.** The writer reaches for catharsis instead of addressing the recipient. Fix: re-anchor with "Dear ___" and the recipient's eyes. If you're not still writing *to* them, you've drifted.

**The letter is too polished.** The writer self-edits in real time, producing a draft that's already pre-cooked into pop lines. Fix: instruct the user to handwrite, fast, no crossing out.

**The extracted song loses the letter's heat.** In the extraction pass, the specifics get sanded down into pop-able lines and what made the letter alive is gone. Fix: in revision, replace any sanded-down line with the original letter sentence verbatim. The pop will improve; the song will live.

**The writer cannot pick a recipient.** This is a signal that the song's subject matter may not be ready yet. Park the workflow. Consider [`david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md`](./david-lynch-catching-big-fish.md) or [`aimee-mann-specificity-first.md`](./aimee-mann-specificity-first.md) instead.

content:
**The letter you'll never send vs. the letter you might.** Already covered. Choose one before starting.

**The letter from the recipient back to you.** A second-pass variation. After extracting the song from the first letter, have the recipient write back. What would they say? This often unlocks the bridge — the moment of the song where another perspective is needed.

**The letter to a younger or older self.** When no other recipient surfaces, the self-at-a-different-age is a fallback. Sufjan Stevens' *Carrie & Lowell* circles his late mother but is also clearly written to and from his younger self ([cross-link `sufjan-research-then-write.md`](./sufjan-research-then-write.md)).

**The letter as bridge-only tool.** Some writers use the method only for the bridge, not the whole song — the bridge is where the song confesses something, and the letter format is the easiest way to find the confession.

content:
Almost never the whole letter. Sometimes a chorus is one verbatim line from the letter. Sometimes a verse is two letter sentences compressed to a couplet. Often the song is structurally a song while the letter is structurally prose, and the bridge is the one passage that survives almost unchanged because the prose was already singing.

The letter goes in a folder. Cave has said that for him the song is the survivor — the prose draft is process. The user should keep their letters; they're a record of what the songs were trying to do.

content:
Most stuck songs are not under-built; they are over-built. The song's essence has been buried under additions — a third synth pad, a sixteenth-note hat that "should be there," a doubled vocal "for thickness." Rick Rubin's central production move, across forty years of working as a producer, is *subtraction*. Remove until something speaks. The song you can hear inside the clutter is the song.

The Saint-Exupéry line Rubin uses in *The Creative Act* is the cleanest expression: "Perfection is finally obtained not when there is no longer anything to add, but when there's no longer anything to take away." Rubin treats this as a working law, not an aphorism.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
Two production touchstones — *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986) and *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994) — anchor the attribution. Both are records where Rubin's production decision was, structurally, to remove rather than add.

For *Reign in Blood*, Rubin in his own words: "I was more subtractive than additive. It was getting back to the essence. It wasn't doing the professional 'thing'. I wasn't using all the normal tricks of the craft. It was reducing them to only what was essential with the particular case in mind." ([Metal Injection](https://metalinjection.net/news/rick-rubin-explains-the-unique-production-behind-slayers-reign-in-blood-i-was-more-subtractive-than-additive-getting-back-to-the-essence)) The most famous specific subtraction: no reverb on guitars or vocals at a time when every metal record was drenched. The audible result is the "precise tightness" Rubin wanted instead of the "blur" of conventional metal production at that tempo.

For *American Recordings*, Rubin recorded Cash with voice and guitar alone — typically in Cash's Tennessee cabin or Rubin's living room — and stripped away the string sections, backing vocals, and reverb-rich ambience that had characterized Cash's late-Columbia and Mercury work. Cash's voice, in his late sixties, became the foreground because nothing else was there to compete with it. The series ran across six volumes and reframed Cash's late career.

The Rubin subtraction move is not a recipe for a particular sound. It's a question: *what would the song reveal if this were not here?*

provenance.section: Why "Rubin philosophy" is the right name
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
Rubin's invocation of the Saint-Exupéry line points to a workable diagnostic. For any element in the arrangement (or any line in the lyric), ask:

- If I removed this, what would be lost?
- If I removed this, what would be revealed?
- Is the loss greater than what is revealed?

The third question is the hinge. Most over-built songs fail it because the element was added for *adequacy* — to make the song "sound finished" — not because removing it would lose anything essential. Removing it reveals more than it loses.

provenance.section: The Saint-Exupéry test
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
The clean trigger: the user's demo is cluttered, has lost its focus, or feels like every layer is fighting every other. The signature: the user says some version of "I keep adding things and the song keeps getting worse" or "I can't tell what this song is about anymore."

Other fits:

- The user has 14 tracks open and can't remember what was on track 7
- The user's chorus is no longer landing because there's too much in it
- The user is in mix-procrastination, adding plugins to avoid finishing
- The user describes their song as "almost there" but won't ship — the gap is usually subtraction
- The user has a clear lyric but the production buried it

When this workflow does not fit:

- The user hasn't laid out enough material yet — there's nothing to subtract from
- The user is in early exploration (`david-lynch-catching-big-fish`, `eno-oblique-strategies`)
- The genre depends on density (wall-of-sound shoegaze, heavily-layered modern pop where the layers ARE the production identity)

provenance.section: When this workflow fits
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
The operational form of Rubin's subtraction:

1. Mute every track in the session.
2. Unmute the kick and the lead vocal. Play through the song.
3. Add one track back at a time. Each addition gets a verdict: does it make the song more itself, or is it noise?
4. The verdict has to be "more itself" — not "fine" or "doesn't hurt." If the addition is neutral, it's a subtraction candidate.
5. By the end of the pass, the user will likely have a session with 30–60% of the original tracks active.
6. Bounce. Listen. Listen elsewhere — phone, car, headphones.
7. If the bounce sounds *bigger* than the original session (despite having fewer elements), the protocol worked.

The "sounds bigger with less" phenomenon is one of the underrated production realities. It happens because the remaining elements have room to be heard.

provenance.section: The mute-and-add-back protocol
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
Subtraction applies to lyrics with equal force. The lyric-side protocol:

1. Read the lyric out loud, slowly.
2. For every line, ask: if this line were not here, would the song lose anything?
3. If the answer is "no" or "not much," the line is a subtraction candidate.
4. Cut the lyric by 20%. Read again.
5. Cut again by another 20%. Often this is where the song becomes itself.

Pat Pattison's prosody discipline (see [`corpus/lyrics/prosody-and-form-content-alignment.md`](../../lyrics/prosody-and-form-content-alignment.md)) is congruent: every line should earn its place. Rubin's reduction is the producer's version of the same discipline.

provenance.section: The lyric-side equivalent
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
Rubin's framing for the question of what to remove is essentialist: *what is this song about?* Then every element of the arrangement is judged against the answer. If the song is about loneliness and an element makes the song feel less lonely, the element fights the song's purpose. Subtract.

For a songwriter, the test surfaces a frequent buried problem: the song's *production* is at war with its *content*. A lyric about quiet grief over an arrangement that wants to be a stadium chorus. A lyric about violent anger over an arrangement that's smooth pop. Rubin's question forces this contradiction into the open, where it can be addressed by subtracting (or replacing) the offending production layer.

provenance.section: The "what is this song about" stress test
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
The two anchor records show the range. *American Recordings* used subtraction to reveal a 60-year-old voice at its most exposed. *Reign in Blood* used subtraction to make a thrash record clear at high tempo. Same move, opposite genres, identical premise: remove what's blurring the essential.

This is why ARLO can recommend the workflow without genre constraint. The question isn't "do you make folk or metal," it's "is your song over-built such that its essence is buried." For both genres, and most genres in between, the answer is often yes.

provenance.section: Cash and Slayer — different applications of the same move
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
**Subtracting the wrong layer.** The user removes the safest layer — usually a pad or a tambourine — rather than the most over-functional layer (often the second vocal harmony or a rhythm guitar that's been there since the demo). Fix: subtract from the *most prominent* layer first, the least prominent last. If the prominent layer was needed, you'll know within a bar.

**Subtracting and then re-adding from anxiety.** The mute-and-add-back protocol works because each addition has to *earn* its return. If the user adds back tracks because the song "feels too empty," they're adding to the producer's anxiety, not the song's need. Trust the space.

**Confusing subtraction with minimalism.** Rubin's move is not "every record should be sparse." It's *every record should remove what doesn't serve.* Some records require many layers and the subtraction pass leaves most of them. The principle is essential-ness, not sparseness.

**Subtracting before the song is fully drafted.** Rubin's move is most useful at the *production* or *late-arrangement* stage, when the song is structurally complete and the question is whether the production serves the song. Subtracting too early can starve the song before it's grown.

**Treating the lyric as untouchable.** The full Rubin move applies to lyrics too. Songwriters who consider production fair game for subtraction but lyrics sacred often miss the largest available win.

provenance.section: Common failure modes
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
Rubin's subtraction is in productive tension with several other workflows in this corpus.

**Vs. Bowie/Burroughs cut-up:** The cut-up *adds* surreal collisions. Rubin would ask, of each, "does it serve the song." Most don't. The two workflows can co-exist if cut-up is the seed and reduction is the editor.

**Vs. Tom Cosm 8-bar loop:** Cosm wants the loop iterated until it's undeniable, which often involves *additions*. Rubin wants subtractions from undeniable to essential. They work in sequence — Cosm to find the loop, Rubin to strip it for the arrangement.

**Vs. stems-first / production-first:** The production-first writer often loves their world and resists subtracting from it. Rubin would invite the question of which world elements the song actually needs. If the answer is "all of them, the world IS the song," the workflow doesn't fit. That's a legitimate aesthetic choice.

provenance.section: Where this clashes with other workflows
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
Some songs are sparse in production *because* they have not yet earned what they want to be. A pre-chorus that isn't lifting may need *more* — a second harmony, a synth swell, a building drum part. Rubin's move is the producer's, applied to over-built songs. An under-built song needs the opposite. ARLO should distinguish these before recommending.

The diagnostic: does the song feel cluttered (subtract) or under-realized (add)? The user's own description usually contains the answer. "I can't hear the song through the production" → subtract. "The song doesn't feel like enough" → add.

provenance.section: When subtraction is the wrong move
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
*The Creative Act* frames subtraction inside a larger practice: reducing life-maintenance overhead, protecting attention, treating creative work as the central practice rather than the leftover. The full Rubin philosophy isn't only "remove things from your song" — it's "remove things from your life that prevent you from doing the work, and the work itself will tend to come out cleaner."

ARLO can surface this larger frame when the user's stuck-ness is upstream of the song — when, say, the user describes being too overwhelmed to focus. But the song-specific subtraction move is the main retrieval target for this file.

provenance.section: What Rubin says about the broader practice
provenance.canonical-references: Rick Rubin, *The Creative Act: A Way of Being* (Penguin Press, 2023); Rubin interviews with Anderson Cooper (60 Minutes, 2023), the *Broken Record* podcast, *Tetragrammaton* (Rubin's own podcast); production credits on *American Recordings* (Johnny Cash, 1994), *Reign in Blood* (Slayer, 1986)

content:
The discipline is: **demo constantly, and the demo IS the writing.** Britt Daniel, the principal songwriter in Spoon, has built his entire practice around demoing as the primary creative act — not a draft of a song that will be "really" recorded later, but the *only* form the song ever lives in until it gets re-tracked with the band.

In a [Paste Magazine interview](https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/spoon/spoon-revisit-their-drafts-a-decade-later) Daniel says: *"The way that I write is through demos, so I'm putting together the words as I'm figuring out the one element of the song that's going to be the focus."* The demo is the workshop. The song is built inside it.

The forcing function is the discipline of finishing demos at a high rate — many per month — and treating the demo as the unit of completion. For *Gimme Fiction* alone there are reportedly 25 four-track cassettes of demos and attempts, [per the Spoon oral-history Substack](https://spoontheband.substack.com/p/gimme-facts-an-oral-history-of-spoons). This stream's research plan glosses the practice as "two demos a week"; the strict number is not verifiable, but the documented *behavior* is unmistakable: a steady, high-volume drip of finished demos that supplies the band's eventual album material.

provenance.section: The premise
provenance.canonical-references: [Britt Daniel — Songwriters on Process interview](https://www.songwritersonprocess.com/blog/2022/brittdanielspoon); [Paste Magazine — Spoon Revisit Their Drafts a Decade Later](https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/spoon/spoon-revisit-their-drafts-a-decade-later); [Rolling Stone — Britt Daniel on new songs and Spoon](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/spoon-interview-britt-daniel-new-songs-1235414652/); [Stereogum — Transference Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2069817/spoon-transference-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Stereogum — They Want My Soul Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2273727/spoon-they-want-my-soul-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Spoontheband Substack — An Oral History of Gimme Fiction](https://spoontheband.substack.com/p/gimme-facts-an-oral-history-of-spoons)

content:
A Spoon-school demo is **structurally a song**. It has an arrangement — intro, verse, chorus, bridge if there is one, outro. It has lyrics, even if they will change. It has a vocal performance and the rhythm-section feel. It does not need to be mixed. It does not need to be in tune to the cent. It does not need to be on real drums.

What it cannot be is half-finished. The discipline is: *finish the demo*. The demo is the unit. An unfinished demo is not a demo; it's an idea.

This is what makes the practice a *forcing function* — the rule isn't "have a great song." The rule is "have a song-shaped object by end of session." The bar is structural completion, not quality.

provenance.section: What "demo" means in this practice
provenance.canonical-references: [Britt Daniel — Songwriters on Process interview](https://www.songwritersonprocess.com/blog/2022/brittdanielspoon); [Paste Magazine — Spoon Revisit Their Drafts a Decade Later](https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/spoon/spoon-revisit-their-drafts-a-decade-later); [Rolling Stone — Britt Daniel on new songs and Spoon](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/spoon-interview-britt-daniel-new-songs-1235414652/); [Stereogum — Transference Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2069817/spoon-transference-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Stereogum — They Want My Soul Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2273727/spoon-they-want-my-soul-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Spoontheband Substack — An Oral History of Gimme Fiction](https://spoontheband.substack.com/p/gimme-facts-an-oral-history-of-spoons)

content:
In the [American Songwriter interview](https://americansongwriter.com/britt-daniel-looks-back-at-two-decades-of-spoon/) Daniel says: *"I feel like I am — maybe to a fault — thinking about the recording from the beginning. Or, at least, very early on."*

This is doctrinally important. For Daniel, lyric, melody, arrangement, and production are not sequential phases. They are entangled from the first session. The recording decisions (what synth, what drum sound, what guitar tone) are also songwriting decisions. Demos in this practice are not lyric-and-chords sketches that get produced later. They are productions whose structural skeleton happens to be the song.

This matches the *Transference* case ([Stereogum](https://stereogum.com/2069817/spoon-transference-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary)): about half of the album was reportedly left in demo form on release. The demo was the master. The discipline produced material that didn't need re-tracking.

provenance.section: Daniel's recording-as-writing principle
provenance.canonical-references: [Britt Daniel — Songwriters on Process interview](https://www.songwritersonprocess.com/blog/2022/brittdanielspoon); [Paste Magazine — Spoon Revisit Their Drafts a Decade Later](https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/spoon/spoon-revisit-their-drafts-a-decade-later); [Rolling Stone — Britt Daniel on new songs and Spoon](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/spoon-interview-britt-daniel-new-songs-1235414652/); [Stereogum — Transference Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2069817/spoon-transference-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Stereogum — They Want My Soul Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2273727/spoon-they-want-my-soul-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Spoontheband Substack — An Oral History of Gimme Fiction](https://spoontheband.substack.com/p/gimme-facts-an-oral-history-of-spoons)

content:
The deep insight underneath the practice is that **the quality of any single demo is not predictable from inside the writing**. You cannot tell, in the moment, which song is going to land. The defense is volume.

If you make four demos a month, your bar is "make four demos" not "make four masterpieces." Some demos will be obvious throwaways. Some will surprise you in three months when you re-listen. A few will earn band attention. The volume produces the selection pool from which the album emerges.

This connects to the general-corpus "throwaway song per week" practice in `corpus/workflow/finishing-work-and-completion.md`. The Daniel variant differs only in that *the throwaways are real songs by an end-of-demo standard*, not 30-second sketches.

provenance.section: Why volume matters more than quality
provenance.canonical-references: [Britt Daniel — Songwriters on Process interview](https://www.songwritersonprocess.com/blog/2022/brittdanielspoon); [Paste Magazine — Spoon Revisit Their Drafts a Decade Later](https://www.pastemagazine.com/music/spoon/spoon-revisit-their-drafts-a-decade-later); [Rolling Stone — Britt Daniel on new songs and Spoon](https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-features/spoon-interview-britt-daniel-new-songs-1235414652/); [Stereogum — Transference Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2069817/spoon-transference-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Stereogum — They Want My Soul Turns 10](https://stereogum.com/2273727/spoon-they-want-my-soul-turns-10/reviews/the-anniversary); [Spoontheband Substack — An Oral History of Gimme Fiction](https://spoontheband.substack.com/p/gimme-facts-an-oral-history-of-spoons)

content:
The research-plan's specific framing — "two demos per week" — is the kind of round number that's useful as a discipline but is not, as far as published interviews indicate, a verbatim Daniel-stated rule. What IS documented:

- Daniel demos *constantly*; demoing is "his preferred mode for songwriting" ([Songwriters on Process](https://www.songwritersonprocess.com/blog/2022/brittdanielspoon)).
- Albums are sourced from a much larger demo body than what's released. *Gimme Fiction*: 25 four-track cassettes; *Transference*: half the album left as demos.
- Daniel writes lyrics and demo simultaneously, "putting it together as I'm writing the song."

The honest version of the rule, then, is: **commit to a sustainable weekly demo cadence — whatever that means for your week — and treat the demo as the unit of completion.** For most writers that lands somewhere in the 1–3 demos-per-week range. Two is a reasonable starting target; pick the number you can actually hit.
