content: The problem is not that producers can't write — it is that they can't stop. Dennis DeSantis built *Making Music* around three categories of obstacle, and the third — Problems of Finishing — gets its own section because "almost (but not quite) everything is in place" is the most common stuck-state and the one that doesn't resolve itself with more inspiration [(Cycling '74 review)](https://cycling74.com/articles/a-review-of-making-music-74-strategies-for-electronic-music-producers). The fix is not motivation; it is process. This document collects the concrete, repeatable tactics that working producers use to close tracks: time budgets, decision criteria, shipping rituals, and the disciplines that turn 90% songs into 100% songs.

provenance.section: The finishing problem, framed
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The Pareto pattern reliably applies to mixing and arrangement: roughly 80% of the perceptible result comes from the first 20% of decisions — primarily balance, EQ, and arrangement — and the remaining 80% of effort produces 20% of the perceptible improvement [(Production Expert on the 80/20 rule in production)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/2019/12/10/how-to-use-the-8020-rule-in-music-production-to-jumpstart-your-productivity). The practical calibration: if a session has crossed the 80% mark, the producer should know it, and the work that follows should be deliberate polish on a small list of named issues, not exploratory tweaking. The trap is the polish phase that expands without bound — each additional hour produces less perceptible change, but the producer hears change anyway because the brain accommodates the small comparisons. The countermeasure is to write down the actual remaining issues before each session and refuse to touch anything outside that list.

provenance.section: The 80/20 calibration
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

citation_targets.title: (Production Expert on the 80/20 rule in production)

content: EDMProd's finishing-system writeup states a concrete time budget: the first session on a new track should be a minimum of 90 minutes, because it is where the most progress is made and the most ideas are committed [(EDMProd, finishing music)](https://www.edmprod.com/finishing-music/). The cognitive reason: starting cold burns warm-up time, so distributing track work across many short sessions multiplies that warm-up tax. The corollary rule: subsequent sessions can be shorter (30–60 minutes), but they should pick up a specific deliverable — finish the second verse, commit the drum bus, lock the arrangement — rather than re-open the entire track for inspection.

provenance.section: The first-session-is-longest rule
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: Set deadlines shorter than the producer's intuitive estimate. EDMProd's specific formula: if a track feels like a one-week job, set a four-day deadline [(EDMProd, finishing music)](https://www.edmprod.com/finishing-music/). Parkinson's Law — work expands to fill available time — applies in the DAW as cleanly as anywhere else: a track with two weeks to live tends to acquire two weeks of revisions, most of them neutral or negative. The deadline doesn't need external enforcement to work; the producer simply has to refuse to slip it. The accountability scale that EDMProd recommends runs from P2P (a friend checks weekly), to public (a shared spreadsheet or group channel), to reliant (a collaborator depends on the deliverable) — escalate only if self-enforcement fails [(EDMProd)](https://www.edmprod.com/finishing-music/).

provenance.section: Deadline compression as Parkinson's-law lever
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: DeSantis's pragmatic substitution — replace "how do I make this the best?" with "is this acceptable?" — is the single most consequential tactic for finishing [(EDMProd summary of DeSantis-aligned strategies)](https://www.edmprod.com/finishing-music/). "Acceptable" is a yes/no decision the producer can actually make; "best" is an asymptote. Apply it per element: is this snare acceptable? Yes — move on. Is this transition acceptable? No — fix it with one specific move, then re-ask. The test forces decisions because it has only two answers, and it forces motion because "acceptable" is permission to stop.

provenance.section: The "is this good enough" test
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The avoidance pattern in finishing sessions is consistent: the producer opens the track, fiddles with the kick for 20 minutes, and avoids the actual broken section (often the bridge, often the second verse vocal, often the outro). DeSantis's "slay the dragon" recommendation reverses the order [(EDMProd)](https://www.edmprod.com/finishing-music/). At the start of each session, name the worst section of the track and work on it first, while energy is highest. Put it off and the next session inherits the same dragon plus the accumulated dread. The tactic generalizes beyond DeSantis — Mixerman's framing on decision compounding has the same structure, just in different language [(Tape Op review)](https://tapeop.com/reviews/gear/93/zen-and-the-art-of-producing-book).

provenance.section: "Slay the dragon" — hardest task first
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: Ear fatigue is real and measurable. The Pro Audio Files protocol is specific: take a 15-minute break every two hours, and cap total mixing time per day with a hard ceiling, because perception of high-frequency content degrades measurably after extended exposure [(Pro Audio Files)](https://theproaudiofiles.com/7-ways-to-keep-your-ears-fresh-for-mixing/). The tactical move on a finishing day: limit yourself to three full passes — initial assessment, mid-session check, final closure — and between passes leave the room. Lower listening volumes during the polish phase, because both ear fatigue and confirmation bias scale with SPL. The cleanest test for "is the work done": bounce the mix, leave the studio for an hour, and listen on a system you haven't used during the session.

provenance.section: Fresh-ears protocols
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The bounce-and-listen-elsewhere ritual is the most reliable translation check. Rotate the bounced mix through at least three systems before declaring it done: studio monitors at reference level, a consumer headphone or earbud (AirPods Pro have become a working reference because they approximate how the majority of listeners actually hear music), and a real-world environment such as a car or kitchen speaker [(Gearspace discussion on AirPods as reference)](https://gearspace.com/board/so-much-gear-so-little-time/1416799-airpods-pro-amazing-reference-pros.html). Take notes on each pass; don't open the DAW until the rotation is complete. Mix translation problems usually reduce to four issues — the room is lying, only one playback system was checked, references weren't loudness-matched, and the low end is unbalanced [(adrianmilea.com)](https://adrianmilea.com/mix-translation/). The rotation catches all four.

provenance.section: The consumer-system rotation
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The decision to ship is not "I can't think of anything else to change" — that state never arrives. The criteria are practical: (1) the rough mix translates across the consumer-system rotation without obvious failures, (2) the artist (or producer in solo mode) has stopped finding new problems on consecutive passes, (3) the issues that remain are stylistic preferences rather than execution flaws, and (4) the deadline is here. Tape Op's "Working With a Mix Engineer" piece frames it from the mixer's side — when the rough is past the comping-and-tuning stage and into "the production decisions are made," it is ready to hand off [(Tape Op #158)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/158/working-mix-engineer). The mirror principle for solo finishing: when revisions stop changing the listener's experience, the track is done — even if the producer can still hear differences.

provenance.section: Shipping vs. iterating — the decision criteria
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The end-of-session ritual matters as much as the close-of-track ritual. The Production Expert workflow habits list recommends a short, mechanical end-of-session sequence: bounce a stereo rough dated to the day; document the session's state in a notes track or session log; back up to a second drive or cloud; walk away [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master). The mental component is critical — don't listen to the rough after closing the session. Fresh ears are an asset that can only be earned by stopping.

provenance.section: The session-close ritual
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content:
When a track is actually done — past the consumer-system rotation, past the artist's "no more changes" call — there is a longer ritual that ensures the track survives future recall. The canonical sequence from working producers:

1. **Master bounce** at the delivery format (typically 24-bit/44.1kHz or 48kHz WAV for digital distribution).
2. **Stems bounce** — every group bus rendered to its own file starting at bar 1, named consistently, exported to a `stems/` folder separate from session files [(Pro Mix Academy)](https://promixacademy.com/blog/how-to-bounce-stems-pro-tools/).
3. **Session freeze** — commit any live plugins, save a `_FINAL` version, and stop editing it. Future revisions get a new version number.
4. **Project archive** — collect all media into the session, save a "collect all" version, and back up to redundant storage (local drive + cloud).
5. **Project log** — a short text file noting the session's tempo, key, sample rate, the artist/collaborators, the mix engineer (if external), and any notes about plugin licensing or third-party dependencies. Future-recall sessions one or three years later depend on this note existing [(Sound on Sound on archiving)](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/studio-one-future-proof-your-song-archives).

The ritual exists because finished-but-unarchived projects are how producers lose tracks to plugin license changes, drive failures, and DAW version updates.

provenance.section: The finishing ritual for a closed track
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The single largest finishing accelerator is volume. EDMProd's recurring recommendation — finish one song a week, even if most of them are throwaways — is grounded in the deliberate-practice argument: a producer who finishes 52 tracks in a year goes through composition, arrangement, mixing, and shipping 52 times, while a producer with one perfect album goes through each stage perhaps once [(EDMProd, why finish more music)](https://www.edmprod.com/why-you-should-finish-more-music/). Finishing requires going through every stage; not finishing means skipping the stages that are hardest. The "throwaway" framing matters because it removes release pressure: the song doesn't need to be released, listened to, or even shared. It needs to be bounced, archived, and ended. Improvement compounds across volume in a way it doesn't across polish.

provenance.section: The "throwaway song per week" practice
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: The structural opposite of the polish-without-bound trap is the time-boxed completion exercise — a track started and finished in a single 60–120 minute session. The exercise forces every decision into the "is this acceptable" frame because nothing else fits. The educational value isn't the resulting track; it is the calibration the producer develops about how much of their normal session time is genuine decision-making versus exploratory drift [(eMastered on production challenges)](https://emastered.com/blog/music-production-challenges). Run the exercise periodically — once a month is a reasonable cadence — and the calibration transfers back to the longer-form work.

provenance.section: The time-constrained completion exercise
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content:
- **The endless "alt mix" stack.** If the session has more than two alternate mixes, finishing has failed. Pick one, freeze the others, and stop.
- **Tweaking after the consumer rotation.** Once the bounced mix has passed the rotation, every additional change risks breaking what works. Cap revisions at one or two named fixes; if more emerge, the rotation needs to be redone.
- **The "one more reference track" loop.** Reference tracks are calibration, not target. Three references is enough; ten is procrastination.
- **The mix that lives forever because no one called it.** Self-imposed deadlines work; absent deadlines invite indefinite revision. Set a date, ship on it.
- **Re-opening a finished track to "improve" it.** Don't. The version on the master bounce is the version that exists. Future improvements belong in the next track.

The Mixerman framing applies across all of these: producing is the management of decisions, and finishing is the management of the last decisions — the ones the producer is most tempted not to make [(Tape Op review of Zen)](https://tapeop.com/reviews/gear/93/zen-and-the-art-of-producing-book).

provenance.section: Common failure modes and their countermeasures
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: A finished track has four properties: it has been mastered (or rendered through a mastering chain that the producer trusts), it has been bounced as stems and archived, it has been logged with enough metadata that the producer can recover it in two years, and the producer has decided in writing that it is finished. The decision is the load-bearing element. Tracks that are finished-but-the-producer-hasn't-said-so tend to drift back into the active queue. Tracks that are stems-bounced, archived, dated, and marked done in a project log tend to stay done. The discipline is administrative, not creative — and that is exactly why it works.

provenance.section: What "done" actually means
provenance.canonical-references: Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; EDMProd finishing-system writeups; Production Expert workflow guides

content: Every problem solved at the songwriting and arrangement desk costs an order of magnitude less than the same problem solved at the mix desk. Sound on Sound's preproduction overview is explicit on this: spending more time at the planning stage saves far more time downstream, and most "mix problems" are actually unmade preproduction decisions wearing a different hat [(SOS, Pre-production)](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/pre-production). Howard Massey's *Behind the Glass* interviews with top producers — originally Musician magazine's First Take series — converge on the same observation across 37 different producers: the producers who routinely deliver finished records on schedule are the ones who arrive at tracking with the song already decided, not the ones who plan to "find it in the studio" [(Behind the Glass, Internet Archive)](https://archive.org/details/behindglasstopre00mass). This document collects the concrete decisions, conventions, and handoff formats that turn that observation into a process.

provenance.section: Why preproduction is the highest-leverage stage
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content:
Five elements must be locked before a single mic is hung. Each one is a decision that compounds; each one costs an order of magnitude more to revisit after tracking starts.

1. **Key** — verified against the artist's actual vocal range at performance volume. Range checks done at speaking volume routinely produce keys that the vocalist can't sustain over a full take.
2. **Tempo** — entered as a metronome BPM, with intentional tempo changes mapped explicitly. Tracking studios' preproduction guidance is direct on this point: even a couple BPM can change the song's feel, and tempo is the cheapest thing to decide and the most expensive thing to revisit [(Island Recording Studios)](https://www.islandrecordingstudios.com/post/recording-prep-checklist).
3. **Arrangement and song length** — bar counts named for every section, intro/outro length decided, total runtime within ~20 seconds of target. "Knowing how many bars the intro is, the order of the verses, choruses and bridges, how the song finishes" is on essentially every preproduction checklist published by working studios [(2201 Recording)](https://www.2201.co.uk/blog-1/music-producers-pre-recording-checklist).
4. **References** — 2–4 commercial records that define tone, density, and arrangement. References are a vocabulary, not a target.
5. **Instrumentation** — every part on the track named, with performers booked and parts charted where appropriate.

The simplest test for preproduction completeness: can the producer write down the song's structure on a single index card without consulting the DAW? If not, preproduction isn't finished.

provenance.section: What to lock before tracking
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: A demo is not a rough version of the final record; it is a structural blueprint that the final record will reference. Producer Mikko Gordon's Tape Op interview frames the distinction: the demo's job is to establish aesthetic direction before tracking starts, so that "there should be a sense of the direction the production is going in, from the very first moment people start making sounds" [(Tape Op #157)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/157/mikko-gordon). A well-built demo settles arrangement, tempo, key, instrumentation, and tonal references. A poorly-built demo establishes none of these and forces tracking to do the work — which is what produces the 30-tracks-of-drums sessions Gordon describes [(Tape Op #157)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/157/mikko-gordon).

provenance.section: The demo's structural role
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content:
The empirical pattern across published producer interviews and writeups: the elements that survive from demo to final are the ones that establish identity, not the ones that establish quality. The conventions:

- **Songwriting and arrangement** almost always survive. If the chord progression, melody, lyric, and section order are working in the demo, they shouldn't change at tracking.
- **Tempo and key** survive almost always, occasionally adjusted by a half-step or a few BPM.
- **Scratch/demo vocals** are usually re-tracked, but exceptions are common enough to be worth taking seriously. The Killers kept Brandon Flowers' scratch vocals on roughly half of *Day & Age* because re-tracking lost the energy, and "Superstar" by the Carpenters used the original scratch vocal in the final master [(Wikipedia, Scratch vocal)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scratch_vocal). Always record scratch vocals well enough that they could survive — through a real mic, into a clean preamp, with usable headphone monitoring.
- **Demo drums and demo synths** usually get re-tracked or replaced, but the parts they played survive — the drummer plays what the programmed kit established, the keyboard player voices what the demo synth voiced.
- **Vibe and energy** survive in the form of a reference rough mix that the tracking team listens back to before takes. The first rough is the record at its most honest; subsequent versions tend to chase polish at the expense of energy [(Sweetwater on rough mixes)](https://www.sweetwater.com/insync/rough-mix/).

The decision discipline: before retracking any element, the producer should be able to say what the retracked version will gain that the demo version doesn't already have. "Better quality" is not an answer; "tighter time" or "different harmonic density" or "real-room ambience" is.

provenance.section: What survives the demo-to-final transition
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: The discipline of building a rough mix during tracking — not after — is recommended consistently by tracking-studio engineers. The Production Expert workflow habits article phrases the principle bluntly: comp, fade, and balance during tracking so playback sounds good the next time the session opens [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master). The corollary from Sweetwater's rough-mix entry: the rough mix is shared, listened to, and heard by people who will form opinions about the song based on it — leaving a tracking day with a rough mix the producer isn't proud of is a mistake [(Sweetwater)](https://www.sweetwater.com/insync/rough-mix/). The rough should pass through the full mix bus, include all stems at workable balance, and be exported at the end of each tracking day with a date in the filename.

provenance.section: The "rough mix first" rule
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content:
When a track is heading to a mix engineer, the stems must conform to format conventions the engineer can rely on. The consensus across producer-prep guides:

- **Format:** 24-bit WAV at the session's sample rate (44.1 or 48 kHz typical, 96 kHz if the session was tracked there). Lossy formats are unacceptable [(Tyler Gunz)](https://www.tylergunz.com/new-blog/2017/11/18/submitting-stems-to-your-mixing-engineer).
- **Start point:** every stem starts at bar 1, regardless of when the source track has audio. This guarantees alignment when the mix engineer imports.
- **Length:** every stem is the same length as every other stem. Pad with silence as needed.
- **Headroom:** no clipping anywhere in the chain. Pull individual track faders down if necessary; do not rely on master-fader attenuation to fix pre-fader clipping [(Pro Audio Files)](https://theproaudiofiles.com/preparing-files-for-a-mix-engineer/).
- **Master-bus processing:** removed before bounce. The mix engineer needs the raw stems, not the producer's master-bus chain [(Tyler Gunz)](https://www.tylergunz.com/new-blog/2017/11/18/submitting-stems-to-your-mixing-engineer).
- **Naming:** descriptive (Kick, Snare-Top, Vox-Lead, Synth-Bass), not creative (MEGA-OOTS, GoodOne-3). The Pro Audio Files header format `artist_track_120BPM_STEM` is one widely-used convention [(Pro Audio Files)](https://theproaudiofiles.com/preparing-files-for-a-mix-engineer/).

The Gearspace consensus naming pattern for film/TV work — `ShowID_Identifier_Channels_Date_versionNN` — is the formal version of the same idea, with version numbers incrementing on every redelivery [(Gearspace, Printmaster/Stems naming)](https://gearspace.com/board/post-production-forum/1014111-printmaster-stems-naming-convention.html).

provenance.section: Stem hand-off conventions: format
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content:
A complete hand-off package, by working-engineer convention, includes more than the stems themselves:

- **The stems**, in a single zipped folder named for the project and version.
- **A reference rough mix** as a stereo bounce — the version the producer wants the mix engineer to use as the emotional and tonal compass [(Tyler Gunz)](https://www.tylergunz.com/new-blog/2017/11/18/submitting-stems-to-your-mixing-engineer).
- **Notes** in a plain-text or PDF file: tempo, key, sample rate, intended deliverable format, any sections that need attention, anything unusual (e.g., a delay throw the producer wants preserved, an intentional clip, a vocal moment that must read).
- **Reference tracks** (commercial records) named in the notes — not bounced into the package, just identified by artist and track title.
- **DAW session file** as backup, if the mix engineer uses the same DAW. The stems remain the primary deliverable.

The "compress to .zip before sending" rule is small but matters: it cuts transfer size and prevents Finder/Explorer file-reordering on the recipient's machine [(Tyler Gunz)](https://www.tylergunz.com/new-blog/2017/11/18/submitting-stems-to-your-mixing-engineer).

provenance.section: Stem hand-off conventions: what to include
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content:
The producer's pre-handoff checklist, drawn from working-engineer guidance:

1. Delete unused or muted tracks.
2. Rename every track from generic labels (Audio-12, Inst-3) to source-specific names (Kick-In, Vox-Lead, Pad-Wide).
3. Verify start and end points across all stems.
4. Clean audio artifacts — clicks, breaths if not wanted, unintended silence.
5. Confirm no clipping anywhere, especially on the master bus.
6. Group multi-mic sources (drums, guitar amps, layered vocals) into clearly-named folders.
7. Bounce dry stems and wet stems if both are wanted; keep them in separate folders.
8. Render a reference rough mix as a stereo file.
9. Compile session notes with tempo, key, references, and special instructions.
10. Zip the whole package and version-number it [(Pro Audio Files)](https://theproaudiofiles.com/preparing-files-for-a-mix-engineer/).

Items 1, 2, and 5 are the most commonly skipped — and they are the most expensive when skipped, because the mix engineer's first hour gets spent on them instead of on mixing.

provenance.section: Session-prep checklist for the producer
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: Modern preproduction blurs the historical separation between artist, songwriter, and producer — particularly in pop and hip-hop, where the producer is often in the room from the first idea. The Audiospring breakdown of roles makes the practical distinction: the songwriter crafts the song into existence (structure, melody, chords, lyric), and the producer enhances, arranges, edits, and directs the recording toward a polished outcome [(Audiospring)](https://audiospringmusic.com/the-roles-of-songwriter-vs-producer-in-making-songs/). When the same person plays both roles, the discipline that protects the work is mode-switching: songwriting mode is open and exploratory, producer mode is decisive and structural. Mixerman's framing — producing is decision management — applies most acutely to the producer-side decisions an artist-producer is making on their own behalf, where the lack of a second voice in the room amplifies both perfectionism and avoidance [(Tape Op review)](https://tapeop.com/reviews/gear/93/zen-and-the-art-of-producing-book).

provenance.section: Artist-vs-producer role separation
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: The Sound on Sound Inside Track feature on Lewis Capaldi's "Someone You Loved" is one of the most concrete preproduction case studies in print. TMS LDN — the production trio behind the track — works on a five-day cycle split into three writing days and two production days, with different two-person configurations each week. They create 15-second musical "starters" — keyboard parts, drum sketches, vocal ideas — and present a portfolio of these to the visiting artist [(SOS, Capaldi Inside Track)](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/inside-track-lewis-capaldis-someone-you-loved). The methodological insight: the starter is a preproduction artifact that gives the artist options without committing them to a fully-built backing track. It balances preparation (the team has done work) with spontaneity (the artist doesn't walk into a finished song). The writing room itself is designed to support the mode — a living-room layout, no vocal booth, lyrics on a projector screen so everyone is working from the same surface [(SOS)](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/inside-track-lewis-capaldis-someone-you-loved).

provenance.section: The TMS LDN model: starters as preproduction artifacts
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: A tracking sheet is the in-session document that captures every take, comp, and decision during recording. Standard fields: song name, take number, performer, mic, signal path, time-of-day, producer notes ("V2 — keeper, comp in for chorus"). The discipline is administrative — tracking sheets exist so the producer in three months can identify which take is on which track, and so the mix engineer can be told "use take 4 of the bridge vocal" without ambiguity. Pro audio guidance treats this as part of the session-prep package: the tracking sheet stays with the session files, and a summary travels with the stems to the mix engineer.

provenance.section: The "tracking sheet" as preproduction artifact
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: Producers occasionally discover that the demo version is the version. The pattern across published cases — Brandon Flowers' Day & Age scratch vocals, "Superstar" by the Carpenters, Mick Jagger demos that became finals — is that the demo had energy and intention that the retracked version couldn't recapture [(Wikipedia, Scratch vocal)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scratch_vocal). The practical implication for preproduction: track every demo through good enough signal chain that the demo could survive. A demo vocal cut through a USB interface and a $50 mic into a noisy preamp can't be promoted to master no matter how good the performance. A demo vocal cut through a real preamp into a quiet 24-bit converter can be. The cost of treating demos like real takes is small; the cost of having to retrack a magic performance is large.

provenance.section: When the demo becomes the master
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: The single message to send to a mix engineer alongside stems should answer five questions: what is the song's tempo and key, what are the references, what is the intended delivery format, what is the deadline, and what does the producer want the mix engineer to know that isn't audible in the stems. Everything else can be inferred from a well-named stem package and a reference rough. The mix engineer's job is to mix; the producer's job is to make that job tractable. The Production Expert workflow rule applies: another engineer should be able to open the package and understand the project without a phone call [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master).

provenance.section: What to send the mix engineer, restated
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: The producers profiled across Massey's *Behind the Glass* converge on a consistent observation: the records that finish well are the records whose preproduction was complete. The mechanism is structural, not motivational — preproduction decisions are the cheapest decisions in the project, and deferring them just makes them more expensive without making them better. A producer who locks key, tempo, arrangement, references, and instrumentation before tracking, who builds a structurally-honest demo, who runs a rough mix in parallel with recording, and who hands off stems in conventional format with conventional notes, has spent perhaps two days on preproduction and saved a week of mixing. The leverage is empirical and reproducible — which is why the same conventions appear, in slightly different language, in essentially every working-producer source.

provenance.section: How preproduction discipline pays back
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Howard Massey, *Behind the Glass*; SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus); Pro Audio Files and Production Expert workflow guides

content: The producers behind hit records describe a recurring pattern: the records that finish are the ones whose sessions were organized before tracking began, and whose decisions were committed early rather than deferred. Mixerman, in his book on producing, argues that producing is fundamentally a sequence of decisions whose downstream cost compounds — every undecided element forces another set of options in the next stage, and the bill arrives at mix [(Tape Op review)](https://tapeop.com/reviews/gear/93/zen-and-the-art-of-producing-book). Producer Mikko Gordon makes the same point in plain language: "I hate when decisions are left until the mixing stage. Like when the session has 30 tracks of drums and loads of different microphones, but there's nothing defined aesthetically. For me there should be a sense of the direction the production is going in, from the very first moment people start making sounds" [(Tape Op interview)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/157/mikko-gordon). The methodology in this document is the structural scaffolding that makes those early decisions possible — it is not motivation, it is process.

provenance.section: Why session methodology matters more than gear
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content:
Lock these five elements before a session begins. None of them require commitment in the studio; all of them cost money to revisit there.

1. **Key** — confirmed against the artist's actual vocal range, sung at full performance volume, not muttered into a phone.
2. **Tempo** — entered as a metronome BPM, with any intentional tempo changes mapped as a tempo map. The recording-prep guidance from working studios is explicit: a couple BPM can change the entire feel of a song, and tracking at the wrong tempo is one of the most expensive mistakes to discover late [(Island Recording Studios)](https://www.islandrecordingstudios.com/post/recording-prep-checklist).
3. **Arrangement and song length** — bar counts for every section, total runtime within ~20 seconds of target, intro and outro lengths decided. "Knowing how many bars the intro is, the order of the verses, choruses and bridges, how the song finishes" is the literal checklist item recommended by tracking studios before drums are recorded [(2201 Recording)](https://www.2201.co.uk/blog-1/music-producers-pre-recording-checklist).
4. **Reference tracks** — 2–4 commercial records that define tone, density, and arrangement target. References are not for copying; they exist so the producer, artist, and mix engineer share a vocabulary for what "right" sounds like.
5. **Instrumentation** — every part that is going to be tracked, named, with the relevant performer booked.

The Sound on Sound preproduction overview frames the rule simply: every problem you can solve at the songwriting desk costs an order of magnitude less than the same problem solved at the mix desk [(SOS, Pre-production)](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/pre-production).

provenance.section: Preproduction checklist: what to lock before tracking
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: Working producers don't open empty sessions. They open a template that already contains the expected track list, color-coded by instrument family, with sends, busses, and VCA/track-stack groups wired and labelled. Pro Tools and Logic Pro guides describe the canonical pattern: drums on one color, bass on another, guitars on a third, vocals on a fourth, FX returns on a fifth, with the visual grouping making a 40-track session legible at a glance [(Sweetwater on Pro Tools templates)](https://www.sweetwater.com/insync/using-pro-tools-templates-tracking/). In Logic Pro, summing track stacks let the producer collapse the drum kit into a single visual lane while still routing through a shared bus for parallel processing or VCA-style level control [(Apple, Logic Pro track stacks)](https://support.apple.com/guide/logicpro/track-stacks-overview-lgcp9bc4b63d/mac). The template should also include go-to reverb and delay sends on aux returns so the rough mix grows as tracking happens, not as a separate later phase.

provenance.section: The session template — built before the artist arrives
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: Track names are not for the producer who created the session; they are for the producer who opens it three months later, and for the mix engineer who has never seen it. The Pro Tools naming convention guidance from professional engineers is consistent: name every track to the source, not the slot — "VOX-LD" instead of "Audio 12", "KICK-IN" and "KICK-OUT" instead of "Kick 1" and "Kick 2" [(Pro Tools Training)](https://www.protoolstraining.com/blog-help/pro-tools-blog/tips-and-tricks/456-5-tips-for-organizing-your-pro-tools-session). Color-coding follows the same logic: a consistent palette across all sessions (e.g., drums red, bass orange, keys yellow, guitars green, vocals blue, FX purple) means muscle memory transfers across projects. The "universal handoff test" applies — another engineer should be able to open the session and understand it without a phone call [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master).

provenance.section: Track naming and color discipline
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: The naming format that working producers converge on is `ArtistName_SongTitle_vNN` or `SongTitle_location_vNN`, with the version number incrementing at the start of every working day. The Pro Audio Files convention is explicit: every new working session starts with a "Save As" to a new version number, even if no changes are made yet — this protects against corruption and creates a daily restore point [(Pro Audio Files, The Name Game)](https://theproaudiofiles.com/the-name-game/). Avoid "final," "FINAL2," and "final_real_thisone" — version numbers must remain strictly monotonic. When working across multiple drives or DAWs, include the location in the filename and continue the version sequence rather than resetting it; two `_v07` files in different locations is the most common source of "which one is current" confusion [(Pro Audio Files)](https://theproaudiofiles.com/the-name-game/).

provenance.section: Session naming and versioning
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: The single largest workflow lever during tracking is building the rough mix in parallel with recording, not after it. As each part lands, set its level against the existing rough, decide whether the take is a keeper, and commit. Mike Senior's mixing workflow assumes that the tracking team has already comped playlists and made performance decisions before the mix engineer opens the session — the mix is not where you decide which take to use [(Sound on Sound on Mixing Secrets)](https://www.soundonsound.com/reviews/mixing-secrets-small-studio). The Production Expert workflow guidance phrases it directly: "comping playlists, fades, literally while you're recording, so playback sounds good next time" is the habit that separates sessions that finish from sessions that stall [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master).

provenance.section: Tracking-day flow: rough mix as you go
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: Mixerman's argument runs that producing is the management of decisions and their consequences, not the deferral of them [(Tape Op review)](https://tapeop.com/reviews/gear/93/zen-and-the-art-of-producing-book). Every unmade decision becomes a track that needs to stay live, an option that needs to be A/B'd, a fader that has to be automated rather than set. The Production Expert workflow framing is harder still: "Select definitive takes rather than accumulating multiple options. Print comps and remove unnecessary parts rather than deferring choices. Prevent 'digital hoarder' sessions that create confusion instead of flexibility" [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master). The practical move: at the end of each tracking session, comp the chosen take, bounce the comp to a single audio file, and archive (don't delete) the playlist of alternates on a hidden track. The session moves forward with one vocal track, not eight.

provenance.section: The "decide once, move on" principle
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: "Print" and "commit" mean the same thing in modern DAW terminology, borrowed from the tape-era practice of playing a signal through outboard and recording the processed output [(Avid Pro Audio Community discussion)](http://duc.avid.com/showthread.php?t=378440). The discipline: when a sound is right, bounce it to a new audio track with its processing baked in, and disable the source. This removes the temptation to re-tweak, frees CPU for downstream work, and ensures the mix engineer hears the producer's intent rather than a tower of toggleable plugins. Always keep the unprocessed original muted on a separate playlist so the decision is reversible — the discipline is commitment, not destruction.

provenance.section: Print and commit — making decisions audible
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: Dennis DeSantis structures *Making Music* around three categories of creative obstacle — Problems of Beginning, Problems of Progressing, and Problems of Finishing — and his core argument is that the strategies for each are different and should not be mixed [(Making Music, About)](https://makingmusic.ableton.com/about). The pragmatic consequence for sessions: writing, arranging, and mixing are different mental modes, and the producer who tries to mix while writing tends to do both badly. The cleanest pattern is single-mode sessions — a writing day produces a sketch, an arranging day commits the structure, a tracking day records performances, a mixing day balances. Mixerman's framing is the same in different language: every stage hands a defined deliverable to the next stage, and the producer's job is preventing the modes from collapsing into one another [(Tape Op review)](https://tapeop.com/reviews/gear/93/zen-and-the-art-of-producing-book).

provenance.section: Separating composing, arranging, and mixing modes
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: The methodology TMS LDN used to write "Someone You Loved" with Lewis Capaldi is the most concrete model in the corpus: a five-day week split into three days of writing and two days of production, with the writing days happening in a living-room-style room with no vocal booth and lyrics projected on a wall screen, and the production days happening in the technical room [(SOS Inside Track, Capaldi)](https://www.soundonsound.com/techniques/inside-track-lewis-capaldis-someone-you-loved). The same article describes the team's "starters" practice — 15-second musical sketches created in advance so the artist arrives to options rather than a blank session. The general principle generalizes beyond TMS: a producer who writes and produces on the same day will tend to overproduce thin songs and underwrite strong ones; separating the modes by day-of-week is a low-cost structural fix.

provenance.section: Weekly cadence: writing days vs. production days
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: The Production Expert workflow habits list places comping during tracking, not after, as a core discipline — the producer compes vocal takes between songs while the artist takes a break, rather than accumulating raw playlists for a later editing pass [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master). The reason is empirical: editing decisions made an hour after the performance, with the performance still in the room's memory, are more musically grounded than decisions made a week later from headphones alone. The mix engineer's perspective in Tape Op's "Working With a Mix Engineer" piece reinforces the rule from the other direction — when comping is deferred to mix, the mix budget is spent on comping instead of mixing [(Tape Op #158)](https://tapeop.com/interviews/158/working-mix-engineer).

provenance.section: Comping and editing during tracking, not after
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: The end of a working session is its own discipline. The Production Expert habits list and Pro Tools organizing guides converge on a short ritual: bounce a stereo rough mix dated to the day; commit any plugin chains the producer doesn't want to re-tweak next session; write a short note in the DAW's text-track or a session log describing where things stand and what the next session should tackle [(Production Expert)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master). Daily backup to a second drive or cloud is non-negotiable. The mental component matters too: walk away from the rough mix and don't listen until the next session — fresh ears are a tool, and the only way to get them is to stop listening.

provenance.section: Session-end ritual: archive, document, walk away
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content:
A handful of patterns reliably break sessions and should be designed out of the template:

- **Multiple "alt" mixes on the same fader.** Decide once and remove alternates from the playable set. If they need to survive, freeze and hide them.
- **Plugin chains the producer doesn't fully understand.** The Tape Op preset-trap warning generalizes — if a chain works but the producer can't explain why, it will be impossible to translate to a different song.
- **Markers that describe technical state instead of musical structure.** Markers should read "Chorus 2," "Bridge," "Drop" — not "fix vox" or "comp here." Use a notes track or task list for the latter.
- **Saving versioned files in the same folder as the renders.** Keep `bounces/` separate from session files so the version count doesn't bleed into the deliverable count.

The general rule from Mike Senior's school of thought — make the session legible to a stranger, because in three months that stranger will be you [(Production Expert, paraphrasing the universal handoff test)](https://www.production-expert.com/production-expert-1/the-workflow-habits-every-audio-engineer-should-master).

provenance.section: What to skip — common methodology anti-patterns
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

citation_targets.title: (Production Expert, paraphrasing the universal handoff test)

content: Used together — locked preproduction, template-based session, color and naming discipline, rough mix during tracking, decide-once commitment, mode-separated days, ritual session close — these practices move the producer's attention from where-is-everything plumbing to actual musical decisions. None of them are exotic; all of them are described, in slightly different language, by the working producers cited above. The leverage is cumulative: each habit reduces the cognitive load of the next stage, and the savings compound across the project lifetime.

provenance.section: How the methodology compounds
provenance.canonical-references: Mixerman, *Zen and the Art of Producing*; Dennis DeSantis, *Making Music* (Ableton); SOS Inside Track features (TMS LDN / Capaldi in corpus)

content: TMS LDN — Tom 'Froe' Barnes, Ben Kohn, and Peter 'Merf' Kelleher — formed as The Musical Shed in 2002. They created "Someone You Loved" with Lewis Capaldi during an afternoon writing session.

provenance.section: TMS LDN Production Trio

content:
Moved to State Of The Ark studio in London (formerly Terry Britten's). Years of incremental development preceded this, including:

- Original garden shed with inadequate soundproofing
- Chiswick's RDS studio
- Grand Prix House (converted call centre, 12 years)
- State Of The Ark (current)

provenance.section: Studio: State Of The Ark

content:
- **DAW:** Apple Logic
- **Interface/cards:** UAD interfaces and expansion cards
- **Monitoring:** Barefoot Sound MicroMain 27s (primary), Yamaha NS10s, Auratones
- **Plugins:** Waves, Softube, FabFilter, iZotope, Soundtoys

Stated workflow principle: **"simplicity and quick workflow are essential"** — applies to plugin selection and DAW familiarity.

provenance.section: Technical Setup

content:
TMS operates as **rotating pair-and-solo configurations**, not as a complete trio. Five-day weeks split as:

- **3 days writing**
- **2 days production**

Different member pairings rotate weekly to prevent creative stagnation.

provenance.section: Weekly Methodology

content:
The team creates **starters** — 15-second musical sketches featuring keyboard parts, drums, or vocal elements. Each member individually scores these. Selected options presented to the visiting artist or topliner.

The rationale: balance preparation with spontaneity, avoid intimidating the artist with a completely finished backing track.

provenance.section: "Starters" Pattern

content:
Writing room mimics a living-room environment, not a traditional studio:

- Unconventional monitor placement prioritizes mood over acoustic precision
- Lyrics displayed on a projector screen throughout sessions
- No vocal booth — everyone in the same space to enhance communication

Kohn: production sessions are *"like therapy, a lot of the time"* — extended conversations establish emotional core before musical development.

provenance.section: Writing Room Design

content:
- Lewis Capaldi visited the studio multiple times before the August 2018 writing session
- Final version emerged largely from **one three-hour afternoon session** following completion of another track that day
- Capaldi explored piano chords; team recorded on iPad to preserve musical ideas

content:
Bake-the-Grit Resample — SP1200/MPC60 Authentic Crush
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Tune Semi (step 1): +6 (pitch the source UP)
- Vintage Emulator K1 Type: SP1200 / MPC60 / SP1200Ring
- Resample (Pad 11): crush hits the pitched-up signal (recreates aliasing)
- Tune Semi (step 4): ~−6 (tune the resample back DOWN)
- LoFi Bitcrush (heavier): ~8 → 4
- LoFi Decimator (heavier): 20–60%
- Color (stack): Cassette / Vinyl (for hiss)
- Slot/Bank: Knob FX = Vintage Emulator / LoFi → resampled pad

## Concept

Authentic vintage-sampler grit on breaks/one-shots — the degraded "recorded-wrong" sound. Pitch the source up, crush it, resample, then pitch back down: this recreates the original memory-limit aliasing of a 12-bit/26 kHz SP1200. The emulations are flavor curves, not converter clones (matches the Sarah2ill A/B finding), but the pitch-up-then-resample is the genuine technique.

## How to play it

1. Tune the source UP +6 semitones (Tune Semi=+6).
2. Put Vintage Emulator Knob FX on the pad: K1 Type = SP1200 (grainy snare bite) / MPC60 (dark glue) / SP1200Ring (metallic edge).
3. Resample (Pad 11) so the crush hits the pitched-up signal (recreates the original memory-limit aliasing).
4. Tune the resample back DOWN ~−6 st.
5. Heavier: add LoFi (Bitcrush ~8→4, Decimator 20–60%) before resampling; stack Color = Cassette/Vinyl for hiss.

## Notes

- Honest: the emulations are flavor curves, not converter clones — subtle (matches the Sarah2ill A/B finding).
- The pitch-up-then-resample is the genuine SP1200 12-bit/26 kHz technique.

Banjo-as-Lead Tuned Kit — 16 Levels Chromatic
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Warp: OFF first (16 Levels refuses with Warp on)
- 16 Levels Type: Tune (one note spreads chromatically across all 16 pads)
- Scale map: root on pad 4, ascends; skip out-of-scale pads (≥4 in-key/scale; no native scale lock)
- Amp Attack: 0 (keep the pluck transient)
- Amp Decay: medium (rings as a lead)
- Vinyl Emulator Crackle: ~20% (degraded character)
- Vinyl Emulator Tone: ~40
- Wider range/chords: drive from 61SL MkIII over MIDI In, or pre-sample the chord
- Slot/Bank: 16 pads (16 Levels = Tune)

## Concept

Playing the banjo (GK-5 → VG-800) as a melodic LEAD voice across the pads. Sample single plinks, spread one note chromatically across all 16 pads with 16 Levels = Tune, keep the pluck transient, and let it ring as a lead. HIGH fit — banjo-as-lead. "Warp off first" is a real gotcha (16 Levels refuses with Warp on).

## How to play it

1. Sample single banjo plinks (line in or built-in mic).
2. Turn Warp OFF first (16 Levels refuses with Warp on).
3. Press 16 Levels → Type = Tune: one banjo note spreads chromatically across all 16 pads (community map: root on pad 4, ascends; skip out-of-scale pads following the major/minor shapes — usually ≥4 in-key notes per scale, no native scale lock).
4. Amp Attack = 0 to keep the pluck transient; medium Decay so it rings as a lead.
5. Add Vinyl Emulator (Crackle ~20%, Tone ~40%) for degraded character.
6. For wider range/chords, drive from the 61SL MkIII over MIDI In or pre-sample the chord.

## Notes

- HIGH fit — banjo-as-lead.
- The exact pad-skip shapes live in the imgur cheat-sheet image (t/220653), not transcribable as text.
- "Warp off first" is a real gotcha.

Baritone Sub-Bass Bed — Repitch Down
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Warp: Pitch (repitch mode), value < 100% (e.g. 50% = down an octave + slower)
- Tune Semi (alt): −12 with Warp = Off (octave-down, same length)
- Tune root: MATCH the kick's key (reinforce)
- Filter: LPF4
- Filter Cutoff: ~60 (sub-only)
- Loop + Loop Lock: endless bed
- Per-pad Volume: lowered — DO NOT Normalize sub-heavy hits (low-freq output clips)
- Slot/Bank: Per-pad (Tune > Warp Pitch + Filter LPF4)

## Concept

A low, sustained baritone Jazzmaster / VG-800 drone repitched into a doom sub-bed. Repitch-down (Warp = Pitch < 100%, or Semi −12) is the dossier's route to baritone sub-bass; tune the root to match the kick so they reinforce, then low-pass it sub-only and loop it endless. The sub-clip warning is rig-critical.

## How to play it

1. Sample a baritone drone off the Apollo bus.
2. Tune page: Warp = Pitch (repitch mode), value < 100% (e.g. 50% = down an octave + slower) OR Semi −12 with Warp = Off for octave-down, same length.
3. Tune the root to MATCH the kick's key so they reinforce.
4. Filter = LPF4, Cutoff ~60 to keep it sub-only.
5. Loop + Loop Lock for an endless bed.

## Notes

- ⚠️ CRITICAL: lower the pad Volume (don't Normalize sub-heavy hits) — low-freq output clips on the box; finalize lows in the Apollo.
- Repitch-down is the dossier's route to baritone sub-bass; the sub-clip warning is rig-critical.

content:
Chop → Transients — Break-Flip
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Chop mode: By Transients
- Threshold (Shift+K3): 0–100% (higher = fewer slices)
- Slice edit: enter slice → edit start/end with the knobs
- Zoom (Shift + encoder): zooms straight to the transient
- Chop toggle: off = original break; on = slices
- Slot/Bank: 16 pads (chop layout)

## Concept

Flipping a drum break — or a fuzz-wall / banjo phrase — into a new re-sequenceable pattern. Transient detection finds peaks and spreads slices across 16 pads, which you re-order over the loop. The Threshold control (`Shift+K3`) trades slice count for cleanliness.

## How to play it

1. Select sample → press Chop → mode = By Transients (detects peaks; `Shift+K3` = Threshold 0–100%, higher = fewer slices).
2. Slices spread across 16 pads. Re-sequence them in a new order over the loop.
3. Tighten each slice: enter the slice → edit start/end with the knobs; `Shift` + encoder zooms straight to the transient.
4. Chop off = original break; Chop on = slices.

## Notes

- Threshold detection is laggy/sample-dependent — fix split points by hand.
- LIMITATION: chopped slices share pitch/filter — use Extract (patch "Extract Slice to Own Pad") to edit one independently.

content:
Cohesive Tuned Kit — Whole-Kit Build
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Tune (all drums): one song key (Semi −24…+24 / Fine ±90 ¢)
- Per-pad Volume: −INF…+6 dB (level the kit)
- Normalize (Shift in Trim/Mix/Amp): each one-shot to 0 dB
- Kit Volume (Shift+K2): leave headroom, don't slam to +6
- Mute Group (Play page): closed + open hat = same group (closed chokes open)
- Vel Sens (per-pad): 0–127 (127 = most dynamic; 0 = always-full)
- Filter (per-pad = EQ): HPF hats/perc; LPF busy melodic bed
- Pan (per-pad): 50L–C–50R (kick/snare/sub center; hats/perc/FX out)
- Slot/Bank: Kit / all 16 pads of one bank

## Concept

A whole-kit build recipe so a kit sounds finished instead of amateur. The AC50 has no parametric EQ, so the per-pad Filter is your EQ. The six-step routine (tune, level/normalize, mute-group, velocity, filter, pan) is designed craft layered onto AC50-confirmed controls.

## How to play it

1. Tune all drums to one song key.
2. Level with per-pad Volume (−INF…+6) plus Normalize each one-shot (`Shift` in Trim/Mix/Amp = Normalize to 0 dB); leave kit-bus headroom (Kit Volume = `Shift+K2`, don't slam to +6).
3. Closed + open hats → same Mute Group so closed chokes open.
4. Per-pad Vel Sens 0–127 (127 = most dynamic; 0 = always-full for a machine-tight hat).
5. Per-pad Filter is your EQ (no parametric EQ): HPF hats/perc, LPF a busy melodic bed.
6. Pan per pad (50L–C–50R): kick/snare/sub center, hats/perc/FX out to the sides.

## Notes

- ⚠️ Don't Normalize sub-heavy hits (worsens low-end output clipping).
- Judge bass on headphones/LSR305s, not the mono speaker (dies below ~200 Hz).

provenance.title: Cohesive Tuned Kit — Whole-Kit Build
provenance.description: A whole-kit build recipe — tune, level, mute-group, velocity-shape, filter-as-EQ, and pan — so the kit sounds finished instead of amateur.

Cycle-Kit / Round-Robin — Humanized Drums
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Takes per voice: 2–4 (vary velocity/strike); up to 4 RR/voice
- Mute Group (Play page): same number 1–16 for all takes of a voice

## Concept

Sampled drums that feel alive — no machine-gun effect — the way the official Sample-Edition packs do it. The AC50 has no native round-robin engine, so this is the manual fake: record multiple takes of the same hit and rotate them. Up to 4 round-robins per "voice" matches The Downbeat Kit's config.

## How to play it

1. Record 2–4 takes of the same hit (vary velocity/strike).
2. Spread them across adjacent pads in one Mute Group (Play page: Mute Group = same number 1–16 for all).
3. Trigger them in rotation while finger-drumming, OR assign one source to 16 Levels spread across all 16 pads.
4. Save the kit WITH a matching demo groove sequence in the same Project (the Sample-Edition packaging template).

## Notes

- The AC50 has no native round-robin engine — this is the manual fake.
- Counts are vendor-stated (Dirty Drummer = 60 cycle-kit projects; Downbeat = 17 kits, up to 4 RR/pad).

content:
Dilla Feel — Quantize-Off, Hand-Played Micro-Timing
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Quantize: OFF (mix quantized + unquantized in one beat)
- Micro-timing: kick ~30 ms early, snare ~20 ms late (direction reported inconsistently; magnitude + asymmetry is the load-bearing fact — nudge by feel)
- Step Edit (Shift+Seq) fader nudge: ~20–30 ms on a selected event
- Offset: 0–100% (silence-in-front, drag a pad late)
- Pad Link (hand-built hat swing): DIBIA$E links pad 4→3, varies linked hat velocity
- Velocity (poly-aftertouch): vary hard — accents vs ghosts
- Slot/Bank: Sequence (quantize off)

## Concept

Off-grid human boom-bap feel on chopped breaks and the rig's drones/banjo. Quantize off, finger-drum by hand, and apply deliberate asymmetric micro-timing. INFERRED mapping — Dilla never touched the AC50 (died 2006); the 30/20 ms figures are his documented micro-timing, the AC50 application is the mapping. The DIBIA$E Pad-Link/Offset half is REAL on this box.

## How to play it

1. Quantize OFF; finger-drum kick/snare/hat by hand (the Sample sequences quantized OR unquantized — mix both in one beat).
2. Deliberate micro-timing (Dilla: kick ~30 ms early, snare ~20 ms late — direction is reported inconsistently across sources; magnitude + asymmetry is the load-bearing fact, nudge by feel).
3. In Step Edit (`Shift+Seq`) move the fader to nudge a selected event ~20–30 ms; OR drag a pad late with Offset (0–100%, silence-in-front).
4. Combine with Pad Link to hand-build per-pad hat swing (DIBIA$E links pad 4→3, then varies the linked hat's velocity).
5. Vary velocity hard (accents vs ghosts) via poly-aftertouch.

## Notes

- INFERRED mapping — Dilla never touched the AC50 (died 2006); the 30/20 ms figures are his documented micro-timing, the AC50 application is the mapping.
- The DIBIA$E Pad-Link/Offset half is REAL on this box.
- Free Dilla-style practice kit at mpc-tutor.com.

content:
Finger-Drum Pad Layout — Bank A Standard
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Bank A pads 1–4: kick(alt) / perc / hat / kick(main)
- Bank A pads 5–8: tom-perc / perc / closed hat / snare
- Bank A pads 9–12: clap / perc / open hat / snare(ghost)
- Bank A pads 13–16: FX-fill / perc / crash-ride / melodic-bed
- Hand split: R = kick/snare/hat column; L = ghosts/open hat/claps/rolls
- Mute Groups: closed + open hat choke
- Vel Sens (per-pad): 0–127
- Slot/Bank: Bank A (16 pads)

## Concept

A fast, comfortable, muscle-memory finger-drum layout — the same map on every kit. Community consensus (mpc-samples/xpresspads) centers the hands on row 2 rather than the factory default, which puts kick/snare/CH/OH on the bottom row A01–A04. The #1 rule is consistency: pick one layout and keep it identical across every kit.

## How to play it

1. Map Bank A: Pad1 kick(alt), Pad2 perc, Pad3 hat, Pad4 kick(main); Pad5 tom/perc, Pad6 perc, Pad7 closed hat, Pad8 snare; Pad9 clap, Pad10 perc, Pad11 open hat, Pad12 snare(ghost); Pad13 FX/fill, Pad14 perc, Pad15 crash/ride, Pad16 melodic/bed.
2. Right hand plays the kick/snare/hat column; left hand plays ghosts/open hat/claps/rolls.
3. Set Mute Groups (closed+open hat choke) plus per-pad Vel Sens.
4. #1 rule: pick one layout and keep it identical across every kit.

## Notes

- Community consensus layout (mpc-samples/xpresspads).
- Factory default puts kick/snare/CH/OH on the bottom row A01–A04; community prefers centering hands on row 2.

content:
Fuzz-Wall Chop-to-Drone Bed
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Input Config Source: Rear (stereo)
- Chop Type: Threshold (or Regions 8)
- Threshold (Shift+K3): high ~70–90% (fewer, longer slices)
- Loop + Loop Lock (Shift+B1): engage for sustained drone
- Polyphony / Note On (Shift+Chop): Note On (gate-while-held)
- Tune Semi: to song key
- Reverb Large K Time: +inf s (infinite wall)
- Reverb Large K Mix: ~40%
- Reverb Large K Pre-Delay: ~30 ms

## Concept

Turning a sustained Board-1 fuzz/baritone wall (off the Apollo bus) into a tuned, loopable drone instrument. Chop into a few rich long slices, sustain one with Loop Lock + Note On, tune it to key, and drown it in Reverb Large with the infinite tail. "Use sources nobody else has" (DJ Shadow) applied to the rig.

## How to play it

1. Sample a 10–20 s wall (Input Config Source = Rear, stereo).
2. Chop → Type = Threshold, `Shift+K3` Threshold high ~70–90% (fewer, longer slices) OR Regions 8.
3. Pick one rich slice → engage Loop + Loop Lock (`Shift+B1`), set Polyphony = Note On (`Shift+Chop` = NOTE ON gate-while-held) for a sustained drone.
4. Tune to song key (Semi).
5. Add Reverb Large Knob FX (Time = +inf s, Mix ~40%, Pre-Delay ~30 ms) for the infinite wall.
6. Resample with LoFi/Color baked.

## Notes

- Reverb Time → +inf s is the manual-confirmed infinite tail.
- "Use sources nobody else has" (DJ Shadow) applied to the rig.

3. Add the broken element with the LoFi Bitcrush FX (24 → ~6-bit) on a couple of hits + loose 16th timing.
4. Send the bus to the Delay FX (the Line 6 / MIDIverb role).
5. Keep dry-forward.

## Notes

- MPC-E3.

content:
Layered Kick — Sub-Body + Click via Pad Link
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Pad A Filter: LPF2
- Pad A Cutoff: ~50–60 (of 127, sub/body only)
- Pad A Tune: to song key
- Pad A Amp Decay: medium
- Pad B Filter: HPF2
- Pad B Cutoff: ~70–90 (of 127, attack/click only)
- Pad B Amp Attack: 0
- Pad B Amp Decay: very short
- Pad Link (Tune pg, Shift+K2): Pad A → B's pad number
- Per-pad Volume: −INF…+6 dB (even the two layers)
- Resample (Pad 11): Bake the pair into one one-shot
- Slot/Bank: Two linked pads → resampled to one free pad

## Concept

A fat, full-range kick built from two samples in different frequency bands: a sub/body layer (low-passed) and a click/top layer (high-passed). Pad Link is the AC50's only layering route (no keygroups), so one strike fires both pads. Resample-to-one is the AC50-specific commit step that frees the linked pad and allows further chop/tune.

## How to play it

1. Pad A = sub/body kick: Filter LPF2, Cutoff ~50–60 (of 127) to keep only the low end; tune to song key; medium Amp Decay.
2. Pad B (same bank) = click/top: Filter HPF2, Cutoff ~70–90 to keep only the attack; Amp Attack=0, very short Decay.
3. Link them: on Pad A, Tune page → `Shift+K2` Pad Link = B's pad number so one strike fires both.
4. Even the levels with per-pad Volume (−INF…+6 dB) so the layers don't cancel.
5. Resample (Pad 11) the pair into one tight one-shot to free the linked pad and allow further chop/tune.

## Notes

- Pad Link is the AC50's only layering route (no keygroups).
- Frequency-band split = a general layering principle; resample-to-one is the AC50-specific commit step.

Finding the human pocket live and non-destructively. In Sequencer mode, Real-Time Swing = K3 (bottom-right of the screen) — ride it live. 4. Time Correct → Swing (K3) is the destructive/global version (also governs Note Repeat feel).

## Notes

- Percentages are Roger Linn's own engine math + Audeobox's "58% classic".

The signature DFA method — synthesize the kit from one polysynth's voices and resample them in (the "Get Innocuous!" CS-60 move), AC50-mapped. One synth becomes the whole kit. Designed (MPC-E2) — the DFA method, not LCD's actual CS-60.

## Concept

Printing Knob FX / Color / LoFi into a clean loop, then chopping and rebuilding — the core "resample bed → re-mangle" move for the recorded-wrong aesthetic, and the workaround for every "FX/character is global" limit on the box.

content:
Snappy One-Shot — Transient + Tight Decay
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Polyphony: Mono (One Shot, Note On off)
- Amp Env Attack: 0
- Amp Env Decay: 25–45 (of 127)
- Decay From (Shift+K2): Start
- Vel Sens: 90–110 (of 127)
- Transient Knob FX K1 Attack: +30…+60%
- Transient Knob FX K2 Shape: ~40%
- Transient Knob FX K3 Sustain: −20…−50%
- Normalize (Shift in Trim/Mix/Amp): Normalize to 0 dB before baking
- Resample (Pad 11): Bake to make permanent
- Slot/Bank: Per-pad (Sample > Amp Env + Knob FX = Transient)

## Concept

The single biggest "snap" move on the AC50 — turning any sampled drum hit (kick/snare/perc) into a tight, punchy one-shot. The Amp Env clips the tail for punch and space, and the Transient Knob FX exaggerates the attack while cutting the ring. This corrects the old "no transient shaper" claim: the Transient Knob FX is the confirmed designer (manual p.54).

## How to play it

1. On the Play page, set Polyphony = Mono so the pad behaves as a One Shot (Note On off).
2. Amp Env: Attack = 0; Decay ≈ 25–45 (of 127). `Shift+K2` set Decay From = Start so the tail is clipped (punch + space).
3. Set Vel Sens ≈ 90–110 for dynamics.
4. Add the Transient Knob FX on that pad: K1 Attack +30…+60%, K2 Shape ~40%, K3 Sustain −20…−50% (cuts ring, exaggerates the hit).
5. Normalize first (`Shift` in Trim/Mix/Amp).
6. Bake it permanent with Resample (Pad 11).

## Notes

- The Transient FX is the confirmed designer (manual p.54) — corrects the older "no transient shaper" claim.
- The Decay=0 / Decay-From-Start variant doubles as the fix for "my samples fade out unexpectedly."

3. Then Chop.

Tune-Drums-to-Key — In-Key Kit
Device: Akai MPC Sample

Settings:
- Tune Semi: −24…+24 (to nearest in-key note)
- Tune Fine: −90…+90 ¢ (for cents)
- Warp: Off (keep length)
- Kick target: fundamental ~50–90 Hz, thump 150–250 Hz; C in C minor
- Snare target: ~E3–B3 (~170–200 Hz); D♯ (minor 3rd) in C minor
- Slot/Bank: Per-pad (Sample > Tune); whole kit

## Concept

The most actionable "better drum samples" move: tune the whole kit to one song key so it sounds cohesive and musical, and tie the low end to the rig's baritone sub-bed. The AC50 has no tuner, so pitch is analyzed off-device; only the semitone/cent result lands on the box. ±24 st / ±90 ¢ are real AC50 ranges; the frequency targets are the craft method.

## How to play it

1. Analyze pitch off-device (free Voxengo SPAN High-Res + Hold, or FabFilter Pro-Q).
2. On the box: Tune page → Semi (−24…+24) to the nearest in-key note, Fine (−90…+90 ¢) for cents.
3. Targets: kick fundamental ~50–90 Hz, harmonic thump 150–250 Hz; snare ~E3–B3 (~170–200 Hz). In C minor: kick = C, snare = D♯ (minor 3rd).
4. Keep Warp = Off so length doesn't change.
5. Tune the baritone sub-bed to the SAME root as the kick so they reinforce instead of fight.

## Notes

- ±24 st / ±90 ¢ are real AC50 ranges; the frequency targets are the craft method.
- Only the semitone/cent result goes on the box.

Device: Boss BF-3

Settings:
- MODE: Standard
- MANUAL: ~10:00
- RES: 9–10:00 (modest — too high thins the fundamental)
- DEPTH: ~11:00
- RATE: ~8:00 (slow)
- Input: BASS IN (disables GUITAR IN — either/or repatch)
- Output: OUTPUT A (mono)

## Concept

Movement on bass — a Jazz Bass or VG-800 baritone — without losing the fundamental. The BASS IN jack re-ranges MANUAL and is voiced to retain low end where a guitar-input flanger would eat the bottom. Here it's a low-end-safe drift under a baritone drone, adding motion while keeping the weight intact.

## How to play it

1. Plug into BASS IN (this disables GUITAR IN — it's an either/or repatch).
2. Set MODE to Standard, RATE slow (~8:00), DEPTH ~11:00, RES modest (9–10:00), MANUAL ~10:00.
3. Play a bass or baritone drone through it for low-end-safe drift.

## Notes

- Designed. Delay range on BASS IN is shorter (0.3–6.3 ms vs 0.3–14.4 ms) to keep bass clear.
- Keep RES modest so notches don't gut the fundamental — too high thins it out.
- Under-used asset for baritone-weight drone.

Chorus-Like Shimmer
Device: Boss BF-3

Settings:
- MODE: Standard
- MANUAL: ~7:00 (low)
- RES: ~7:00 (low)
- DEPTH: 10:00
- RATE: ~1:00
- Input: GUITAR IN
- Output: OUTPUT A (mono)

## Concept

A low-RES, shallow, faster setting that reads as a thin chorus or shimmer rather than a jet flange. Gentle thickening for a cleaner banjo/baritone or a clean-ish bed before the wall builds — the notches stay subtle so the source keeps its character.

## How to play it

1. Set MODE to Standard, DEPTH 10:00, RATE ~1:00, RES and MANUAL both low (~7:00).
2. Play an exposed banjo lead or a clean bed through it for a thin chorus shimmer.
3. To add panning, run it in stereo via Gate/Pan with both outputs (Messano demos both mono and stereo).

## Notes

- Best on exposed banjo lead, which otherwise goes thin/metallic through deep flange (the notches hit its 2–4 kHz spike) — keep RES/DEPTH low on bare banjo.
- In stereo (via Gate/Pan) it gains panning.

content:
Classic Jet-Plane Flange
Device: Boss BF-3

Settings:
- MODE: Standard (12:00)
- MANUAL: 12:00
- RES: ~3–4:00 (cranked)
- DEPTH: 12:00
- RATE: 12:00
- Input: GUITAR IN
- Output: OUTPUT A (mono)

## Concept

The textbook jet-plane flange — the dramatic talking whoosh that every flanger is judged on. All knobs sit at noon while RES is cranked to roughly 3–4:00 to push the resonance into that screaming, spectrum-sweeping rush. In this rig it's the literal jet-swell-on-the-wall target: engage it on a sustained fuzz wall for a dramatic sweep across the whole frequency range.

## How to play it

1. Set MODE to Standard, MANUAL/DEPTH/RATE all to 12:00, RES cranked to ~3–4:00.
2. Build the dirt stack into a sustained wall first.
3. Engage the BF-3 and let the comb sweep talk across the spectrum.

## Notes

- Watch output when feeding the Somersault — high RES + fuzz is additive gain. Trim downstream.
- The single most-copyable jet recipe on disk (spoken while playing by Messano).

content:
EVH Momentary Bursts
Device: Boss BF-3

Settings:
- MODE: Momentary
- MANUAL: 12:00
- RES: ~3–4:00
- DEPTH: 12:00
- RATE: 12:00
- Input: GUITAR IN
- Output: OUTPUT A (mono)
- Pedal footswitch (momentary): Effect is ON only while depressed — hold for the phrase, release to drop

## Concept

Flange that exists only while you hold the footswitch down — Van-Halen-style on-demand bursts for a single phrase, note, or the last chord of a song. There's no double-tap and no tap-tempo in this mode; the effect is purely momentary. Flanging starts in the low end (Standard voicing) and drops the instant you release.

## How to play it

1. Set MODE to Momentary, keep the Classic-Jet knobs (MANUAL 12:00, DEPTH 12:00, RATE 12:00, RES ~3–4:00).
2. Hold the pedal switch for the phrase you want flanged.
3. Release to drop the effect — it's on ONLY while depressed.

## Notes

- The EVH reference is the technique only — EVH used an MXR M117, NOT a BF-3; Momentary mode merely recreates the move. Not a BF-3 artist credit.

content:
Gate Slicer (Mono Chop)
Device: Boss BF-3

Settings:
- MODE: Gate/Pan (~9:00)
- MANUAL: ~6–7:00 (way down)
- RES: ~6–7:00 (way down)
- DEPTH: ~9:00
- RATE: ~9:00
- Input: GUITAR IN
- Output: OUTPUT A (mono)
- Pedal footswitch (tap-tempo): Hold ≥2 s → tap to sync the chop to the beat (optional)

## Concept

In a mono slot, the BF-3's Gate/Pan mode is not the L/R rotary — it becomes a hard-cutoff volume slicer / extreme tremolo with swirl. The flanger's rise-and-fall drives 32 on/off cycles, chopping the signal into a rhythmic gate. Good for rhythmic stutter over a sustained wall or pad; tap-sync to land the chop on the beat.

## How to play it

1. Set MODE to Gate/Pan (~9:00), RATE and DEPTH ~9:00, MANUAL and RES way down (~6–7:00).
2. Run a sustained wall or pad into it so the gate has something to chop.
3. Optionally hold the pedal ≥2 s and tap to sync the chop to the song's beat.

## Notes

- Electronic/sliced + post-punk rhythmic-build fit.
- In mono this is a slicer, NOT the L/R rotary — for the rotary you need OUTPUT B / a post-CE-2W stereo repatch (see Stereo Rotary / Leslie Spin).
- Output jumps in Gate/Pan + tap — trim downstream.
